Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Luther called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.

Meaning first. Romans 4 proves from the Old Testament that justification has always been by faith. Paul takes the greatest example in Jewish history, Abraham, and shows that he was counted righteous because he believed God, not because he worked, and before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile. His faith trusted the God who gives life to the dead, and ours does the same: we believe in the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification. The chapter is the Old Testament foundation of “by faith alone.”

What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? Key words. Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man, who kept the law before it was given. If anyone was justified by works, surely Abraham was.

For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. If works justified him, he could boast. But no one can boast before God (3:27).

In a sentence. What did Abraham, the forefather of the Jewish people, discover? If he was justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God.

On a Tuesday. Even the greatest believers had nothing to boast of before God. Neither do you, and that is freedom.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.

For what does the Scripture say? Key words. Paul settles it by Scripture, not by tradition or argument.

Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Key words. From Genesis 15:6, the key verse of the chapter, quoted also in Galatians 3:6 and James 2:23. God promised Abraham descendants as many as the stars, when he had no child. Abraham believed. And God credited righteousness to him. “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account (logizomai). Used eleven times in this chapter. Righteousness was put on Abraham’s account, though he didn’t earn it.

Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. Key words. A simple illustration. Wages are earned; a gift is free. You can’t have it both ways. If righteousness were earned, it would be wages. It is credited as a gift.

But does James not say the opposite? James 2:21–24 says that Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Readers rightly ask how Paul and James fit together. Three things resolve it. First, they are speaking of different moments in Abraham’s life: Paul quotes Genesis 15, when Abraham first believed and was counted righteous; James points to Genesis 22, perhaps thirty years later, when Abraham’s faith was tested and proved real. Second, they are answering different errors: Paul opposes those who think they can earn acceptance with God by works; James opposes those who think a faith that produces no works can save. Third, they use justified in different senses: Paul means declared righteous before God; James means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine before others (James 2:18, show me your faith). James himself quotes Genesis 15:6 and says Abraham’s works fulfilled it (James 2:23): his obedience showed what his faith had always been. So the two agree. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it always works (Galatians 5:6).

In a sentence. Scripture says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, and wages are not credited to a worker as a gift but as what he is owed.

For worship. Righteousness is credited to your account by faith. You didn’t earn it. Thank God for the gift.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,

And to the one who does not work. Key words. Not that believers don’t do good works, but that they don’t work to be justified. They stop trying to earn it.

But believes in him who justifies the ungodly. Key words. One of the most astonishing phrases in Scripture. God justifies the ungodly. Not the good, not the improving, not the religious, but the ungodly. The law said a judge who justifies the wicked is an abomination (Proverbs 17:15; Exodus 23:7). Yet God does it, justly, because Christ bore their punishment (3:26). Good news for the worst sinner.

His faith is counted as righteousness. Faith is not itself the righteousness, as if faith were a good work God accepts instead of obedience. Faith is the hand that receives Christ’s righteousness. It is counted “for” righteousness because it unites us to Christ, who is our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30; Philippians 3:9).

In a sentence. To the one who does not work but trusts God who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.

On a Tuesday. God justifies the ungodly. If you feel ungodly, you qualify. Trust him.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;

Just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works. Key words. A second witness, from the Psalms (Deuteronomy 19:15). Abraham before the law; David under the law. Both justified by faith.

Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Key words. From Psalm 32:1, written after David’s adultery and murder. Not the man who never sinned, but the man forgiven. “Covered”: hidden from God’s judgment, under the blood (Psalm 85:2).

In a sentence. David also speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: blessed are those whose lawless acts are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

For worship. Blessed are you if your sins are forgiven. That is the greatest happiness there is.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”

Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin. Key words. Psalm 32:2. The other side of imputation. God credits righteousness to the believer (v. 6) and does not credit his sin to him. Both. The negative and the positive. Sin not counted against us, because it was counted against Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19–21). Righteousness counted to us, because Christ’s righteousness is ours. The great exchange.

In a sentence. Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord will never count against him.

On a Tuesday. God will never count your sin against you, if you are in Christ. Live in that freedom.

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.

Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? The key question for Jew and Gentile.

How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? A brilliant argument from the order of events.

It was not after, but before he was circumcised. Key words. Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, at least fourteen years later. He was justified as an uncircumcised man. So circumcision was not necessary for justification. Gentiles can be justified without it.

In a sentence. Is this blessing only for the circumcised, or for the uncircumcised too? Faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness, and when? Before he was circumcised, not after.

For worship. God accepted Abraham before any ritual. He accepts you the same way: by faith.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.

He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith. Key words. A sign points to something; a seal confirms it. A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine, like a wax seal on a document. Circumcision didn’t make Abraham righteous; it confirmed the righteousness he already had by faith.

The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised. Key words. Abraham is the father of Gentile believers. Spiritual descent, by faith, not by blood (Galatians 3:7, 29).

And to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith. And of believing Jews: not merely circumcised, but following his faith. Abraham’s true children are those who believe.

Where Christians differ: circumcision, baptism and infants. Paedobaptists argue that baptism replaces circumcision as the sign and seal of the covenant (Colossians 2:11–12), and since circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too. Verdict: Paul says circumcision sealed the righteousness Abraham had by faith; it followed faith in Abraham’s case. In the new covenant, all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and the sign is given to those who believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12). Credobaptists hold that baptism belongs to believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters as fellow heirs of Abraham.

In a sentence. Abraham received circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness he had by faith while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe without being circumcised, and also of the circumcised who walk in the footsteps of his faith before circumcision.

On a Tuesday. Walk in Abraham’s footsteps of faith. You are his child if you believe.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul argues that God’s promise that Abraham and his descendants would inherit the world never depended on keeping the law but on the righteousness that comes by faith. If it rested on law, faith would be pointless and the promise void, since the law exposes transgression and brings wrath. So the promise rests on grace through faith, and it is guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, Jews and Gentiles who share his faith, for he is the father of many nations. Abraham trusted the God who gives life to the dead and creates out of nothing. Though he was about a hundred and Sarah was barren, he kept hoping when there was no human ground for hope, grew strong in faith, gave God glory and was fully convinced God would do what he had promised. That is why it was counted to him as righteousness, and Scripture records it for our sake too: righteousness will be counted to us who trust the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of his deity but the declaration that his atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in his death; it is faith in the God who raised him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.

For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world. Key words. God promised Abraham the land of Canaan (Genesis 12:7; 15:18). Paul sees that the promise was bigger: the whole world. All nations blessed in him (Genesis 12:3), and his offspring, Christ, inheriting the earth (Psalm 2:8; Matthew 5:5). The land was a down payment on the new creation.

Did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. The law came 430 years later (Galatians 3:17).

For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void. Key words. If inheritance depended on law-keeping, no one would inherit, since no one keeps it, and the promise would be empty. Law and promise work on different principles.

In a sentence. The promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would inherit the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith, for if those who rely on the law are heirs, faith means nothing and the promise is worthless.

For worship. In Christ you will inherit the world. The meek shall inherit the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,

For the law brings wrath. Key words. “Wrath” (orgēn). The law is good (7:12), but given to sinners it cannot give life; it exposes and condemns. It turns sin into transgression, and transgression brings God’s judgement.

But where there is no law there is no transgression. Key words. “Transgression” (parabasis, stepping over a line). This does not mean that people without the law do not sin, or are innocent. Paul will say that sin was in the world before the law was given, and death reigned from Adam to Moses (5:13–14), and that Gentiles without the law still perish for their sin (2:12). Transgression is a particular kind of sin: the deliberate breaking of a known, stated command. When God gave the law, sin became visible and wilful rebellion against his spoken word, and so more serious (5:20; 7:13). The point for Paul’s argument is that if the promise depended on the law, it would bring wrath, not blessing; so the promise must rest on faith and grace instead.

That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace. Key words. Faith and grace go together. Faith receives what grace gives. If it depended on us, it would be uncertain.

And be guaranteed to all his offspring. “Guaranteed” (bebaian): firm, sure. Because it rests on grace, not on our performance, it is certain. Assurance is possible because salvation is by grace through faith.

Who is the father of us all. Jew and Gentile believers alike.

In a sentence. The law brings wrath, and where there is no law there is no transgression, so the promise depends on faith, so that it may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, not only to those of the law but to those who share Abraham’s faith, for he is the father of us all.

On a Tuesday. Because your salvation rests on grace, it is guaranteed. You can be sure.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations” — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”

I have made you the father of many nations. From Genesis 17:5, when God renamed Abram (“exalted father”) as Abraham (“father of a multitude”). Already said in the past tense: God speaks of the future as done.

In the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. Key words. What kind of God did Abraham trust? The God of resurrection and creation. Who gives life to the dead: to Abraham’s and Sarah’s dead bodies (v. 19), to Isaac on the altar (Hebrews 11:19), and supremely to Jesus. Who calls into existence things that don’t exist: creation out of nothing. Faith trusts a God who can do the impossible.

In hope he believed against hope. Key words. Humanly, no hope. But he hoped in God. Faith hopes beyond human possibility.

So shall your offspring be. From Genesis 15:5. As the stars.

In a sentence. As Scripture says, God made him the father of many nations, in the sight of the God he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist, and against all hope Abraham believed in hope that he would become the father of many nations, just as he had been told his offspring would be.

For worship. Your God gives life to the dead and calls things into being from nothing. Nothing is impossible for him.

parallels.desc: the father of a multitude of nations
so shall your offspring be

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,

He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead. Key words. Faith is not ignoring reality. Abraham faced the facts: about a hundred, and Sarah ninety and barren. He considered them honestly. And still believed.

No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God. But didn’t Abraham laugh (Genesis 17:17) and take Hagar (Genesis 16)? Yes. His faith wasn’t perfect. But in the end, it did not waver from the promise itself. God graciously remembers Abraham’s faith, not his failures (Hebrews 11).

But he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God. Key words. Faith grows by looking at God, not at ourselves. And faith gives glory to God, trusting him to keep his word. Unbelief calls God a liar (1 John 5:10).

In a sentence. Without weakening in faith, he faced the fact that his body was as good as dead, since he was about a hundred, and that Sarah’s womb was also dead, yet he did not waver in unbelief at God’s promise but was strengthened in faith and gave glory to God.

On a Tuesday. Face your impossible situation honestly. Then look at God and give him glory by trusting his promise.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.

Fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised. Key words. The definition of faith: full conviction that God can and will do what he says. Faith rests on two things: God’s promise and God’s power. Not on our feelings, or our ability.

In a sentence. He was fully persuaded that God had power to do what he had promised.

For worship. Be fully convinced: God is able to do what he has promised you.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also.

That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” Repeating Genesis 15:6.

But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. Key words. Scripture was written for us (15:4; 1 Corinthians 10:11). Abraham’s story is the pattern of every believer’s salvation. What was true for him is true for you.

In a sentence. This is why his faith was credited to him as righteousness, and the words “it was credited to him” were written not for him alone, but also for us.

On a Tuesday. Read the Bible as written for you. It is.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord. Key words. Our faith is like Abraham’s: trust in the God who gives life to the dead. Abraham believed God would bring life from his dead body; we believe God brought life from Jesus’ dead body.

Who was delivered up for our trespasses. Key words. “Delivered up” (paredothē): handed over, the word of Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament, and of Judas’s betrayal. By God, for our sins. Because of our sins, to pay for them.

And raised for our justification. Key words. Because of our justification, or to secure it. The resurrection proves that the payment was accepted. If Christ had stayed dead, we would not know our sins were paid. His resurrection is God’s receipt, declaring the debt settled, and the living Christ applies his righteousness to us (5:10; 8:34).

In a sentence. Righteousness will be credited to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was handed over to death for our sins and raised to life for our justification.

For worship. He was handed over for your sins and raised for your justification. Your sins are paid; you are declared righteous. Rejoice.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh?<sup>2</sup>For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.<sup>3</sup>For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>4</sup>Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.<sup>5</sup>And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,<sup>6</sup>just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:<sup>7</sup>“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;<sup>8</sup>blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”<sup>9</sup>Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.<sup>10</sup>How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.<sup>11</sup>He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well,<sup>12</sup>and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.<sup>13</sup>For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.<sup>14</sup>For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.<sup>15</sup>For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression.<sup>16</sup>That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring—not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,<sup>17</sup>as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.<sup>18</sup>In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”<sup>19</sup>He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.<sup>20</sup>No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,<sup>21</sup>fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.<sup>22</sup>That is why his faith was “counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>23</sup>But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,<sup>24</sup>but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,<sup>25</sup>who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Romans 5 is the hinge of the letter. Behind us lie three chapters of diagnosis and one chapter of remedy; ahead lie three chapters of Christian experience and life. Chapter 5 stands at the turning point, summarising the achievements of justification (vv. 1–11) before setting those achievements within the grandest possible framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose actions determined the destiny of all humanity (vv. 12–21).

The opening "therefore" connects everything that follows to everything Paul has argued. Because we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God. We have access to grace. We stand in hope. We can even boast in our sufferings. And the love of God — poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit — is the guarantee that the hope will not put us to shame. The person justified by faith does not merely have a changed legal status; she has entered a new world, a new relationship, a new story whose ending is already written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." This sentence is the great sigh of relief at the centre of the letter. Three chapters of accumulated guilt — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the universal verdict of Scripture, the silencing of every mouth — and now: peace. Not merely the absence of war, but the shalom of a relationship fully restored. The hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has been dealt with at the cross, and the one who has received the verdict of justification stands in the peace of a fully settled relationship with God.

Paul adds to peace the gift of access (v. 2) — "through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand." Access was a technical term for the privilege of being brought into the presence of a king. The justified sinner has not merely been acquitted; she has been given permanent, unimpeded access to the throne of God. She does not approach on the basis of her spiritual performance on any given day; she stands in grace — a position of favour that does not fluctuate with her feelings or her faithfulness.

The boasting in sufferings (vv. 3–5) is one of the most counter-intuitive things Paul writes. He does not merely say we can endure suffering; he says we rejoice in it — because suffering produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame because the love of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit. The chain is unbreakable. And the certainty of hope rests not on our own resilience but on the Spirit-given experience of being loved by God.

And then Paul does something the rest of the section depends on: he proves that love rather than asserting it. Verses 6 to 8 fix the timing of the cross — Christ died for us while we were still weak, still ungodly, still sinners. Not after we improved, and not in anticipation of our improving. He sets it against the best human parallel he can find and shows that there is none: one might barely die for a good man, but God shows his love in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us (v. 8). From there the argument runs from the harder thing to the easier. If God did that for enemies, the lesser question of whether he will finish the work in friends answers itself — since we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved from wrath through him (vv. 9–10). The section ends where it must: not with the benefits but with the giver. We rejoice, finally, not in peace or access or hope, but in God himself, through whom we have now received reconciliation (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and the Assurance of Faith

Romans 5:1 is a foundation stone of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer has peace with God — not the peace she feels on spiritually good days, but the objective peace established by the accomplished work of Christ received by faith. The Reformation recovered this against the Roman Catholic teaching that assurance is presumption: on the contrary, to doubt one's justification when God has spoken the verdict is to call God's word into question. As Calvin taught, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament. The peace of Romans 5:1 is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the finished work of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first-century world had no shortage of philosophical frameworks for enduring suffering — Stoic resignation, Epicurean avoidance, Platonic transcendence. None of them grounded suffering in the love of a personal God or gave it redemptive purpose. Paul's rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was genuinely new: suffering has a trajectory, and that trajectory ends in hope that is guaranteed by the Spirit. Now: In an age that treats suffering as the enemy of the good life, to be medicated, minimised, or avoided at all costs, Romans 5:3–5 offers a radically different framework. Suffering is not the enemy of Christian hope; it is one of its primary instruments. The Christian who suffers well — who endures, who builds character, who hopes — is not an anomaly but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.

Meaning first. Romans 5 shows what justification brings. First, its fruits: peace with God, access to his grace, hope of glory, joy even in suffering, the love of God poured into our hearts, and certainty of final salvation, since if God loved us when we were enemies, he will surely save us now we are his friends (vv. 1–11). Then the great comparison of Adam and Christ (vv. 12–21): through one man’s sin, condemnation and death came to all in him; through one man’s obedience, righteousness and life come to all in him. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.

Therefore, since we have been justified by faith. Key words. A completed fact. Not hoping to be, but have been. Everything that follows rests on this.

We have peace with God. Key words. Not just peace of mind, but peace with God: the war is over. We were his enemies (v. 10); now reconciled. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.” The difference is one letter in Greek. The context, a list of what we have, favours “we have.”

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. The only way.

Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. Key words. “Access” (prosagōgēn): introduction, as into a king’s presence. We stand in grace, permanently, as on firm ground.

And we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Key words. “Rejoice” (kauchōmetha): boast, exult. The same word as the boasting excluded in 3:27. Now a right boasting: in God’s glory, which we will share (8:18, 30). Hope is not wishful thinking, but confident expectation.

In a sentence. Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand, and we rejoice in the hope of God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. You have peace with God. The war is over. Live like it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

parallels.desc: the effect of righteousness will be peace

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,

Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings. Key words. Not just in spite of them, but in them. Not because suffering is good in itself, but because of what God does through it (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

Knowing that suffering produces endurance. “Suffering” (thlipsis): pressure, affliction. “Endurance” (hypomonē): staying power, steadfastness under a load.

And endurance produces character. Key words. “Character” (dokimēn): proven character, tested genuineness, like metal tested in fire. Faith that has been through trouble is proven real.

And character produces hope. Tested faith deepens hope. A chain: suffering, endurance, character, hope.

In a sentence. Not only so, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and character produces hope.

For worship. Your trials are not wasted. God is using them to forge character and hope.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

And hope does not put us to shame. Key words. Christian hope will not disappoint us. We won’t be embarrassed on the last day, like someone who trusted a false promise (Psalm 25:3; Isaiah 28:16).

Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts. Key words. “Poured” (ekkechytai): poured out lavishly, the word used of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). God’s love for us, not first our love for him, made real in our hearts. Not just believed, but experienced.

Through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Every believer has the Spirit, given at conversion (8:9). He assures us of God’s love (8:15–16).

In a sentence. And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom he has given us.

On a Tuesday. God’s love has been poured into your heart. Ask the Spirit to make you feel it today.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —

For while we were still weak. Key words. “Weak” (asthenōn): powerless, helpless. Unable to save ourselves.

At the right time Christ died for the ungodly. Key words. “The right time”: God’s appointed moment in history (Galatians 4:4). “For the ungodly”: in their place. Not for the good, but for the ungodly (4:5).

For one will scarcely die for a righteous person. A righteous person: someone just and upright. Few would die for him.

Though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die. A good person: someone kind and generous, a benefactor. Perhaps someone might die for him. But Christ died for neither: for the ungodly.

In a sentence. When we were still powerless, at just the right time Christ died for the ungodly, and very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die.

For worship. Christ died for the ungodly, the powerless. That means you. Wonder at it.

parallels.desc: when the fullness of time had come

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

But God shows his love for us. Key words. “Shows” (synistēsin): demonstrates, proves. Present tense: the cross keeps proving it. If you doubt God’s love, look at the cross. And notice: God shows his love through Christ’s death. Not the loving Son appeasing an angry Father, but the Father showing his love by giving his Son (John 3:16).

In that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Key words. Not after we improved. While we were still sinners. God’s love is not a response to our goodness; it came first. The greatest love in the universe was given to those who deserved it least.

In a sentence. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt God loves you, look at the cross. He loved you while you were still a sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood. “By his blood”: by his sacrificial death (3:25).

Much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. Key words. The argument from greater to lesser. If God did the harder thing, justifying enemies, he will surely do the easier: keep his friends safe on the day of wrath. Final salvation is certain.

For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son. Key words. “Enemies”: hostile to God (8:7). Reconciliation: the end of hostility, restored relationship. God took the initiative (2 Corinthians 5:18–20).

Much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. Key words. His death reconciled us; his risen life keeps us. He lives to intercede for us (8:34; Hebrews 7:25). A living Saviour guarantees our salvation.

Assurance and perseverance. These verses are a foundation for the perseverance of the saints. If God loved us as enemies, he will not abandon us as friends.

In a sentence. Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him, for if while we were God’s enemies we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life.

For worship. If God loved you as his enemy, how much more will he keep you as his friend. Rest secure.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

More than that, we also rejoice in God. Key words. The climax: not just in God’s gifts, but in God himself. The highest joy. The goal of salvation is God himself.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. Received: a gift.

In a sentence. Not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice not only in what God gives, but in who God is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The argument that begins in v. 12 is the most theologically ambitious in the entire letter. Paul steps back from the individual experience of justification and places it within a cosmic, historical framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose representative actions determined the status and destiny of everyone who belongs to them. This is the doctrine of federal headship — the two-Adam theology that is foundational to the Reformed understanding of both sin and salvation.

The parallel is deliberate and asymmetrical. Adam sinned; condemnation and death spread to all. Christ obeyed; righteousness and life are given to all who are in him. But the parallel is asymmetrical because grace exceeds sin in every dimension: "the free gift is not like the trespass" (v. 15). The trespass brought condemnation; the gift brings justification for many trespasses. Adam's one sin brought death; Christ's one act of righteousness brings the free gift of life. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (v. 20). The gospel is not simply the repair of the damage done by Adam; it is a new creation that surpasses Eden.

The phrase "as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 21) is the conclusion to which the whole argument has been driving. Sin had a reign — a dominion, a kingdom of death. Grace now has a counter-reign — a dominion of life and righteousness. The believer has been transferred from one kingdom to the other. Adam is no longer her representative head; Christ is. She bears the condemnation of neither Adam's sin (fully atoned) nor her own (fully forgiven). She stands under the reign of grace, heading toward the eternal life that is the gift of her new federal head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal Headship: The Solidarity of Adam and Christ

Romans 5:12–21 is the biblical foundation of the Reformed doctrine of original sin and the imputation of Adam's guilt. Paul teaches that death spread to all because all sinned in Adam — not merely by imitating his example, but by being represented by him. Adam was the covenantal head of humanity; his act was our act in the only sense that matters covenantally. This is why all die, even infants who have not sinned in the way Adam sinned (v. 14). The parallel with Christ is the point: just as we were condemned in Adam by imputation, we are justified in Christ by imputation. The same covenantal logic that makes us sinners in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. You cannot reject one side of the parallel without undermining the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Adam-Christ typology was deeply embedded in Jewish theology of Paul's day — the figure of Adam as the representative of humanity was well established. Paul takes this shared theological framework and uses it to explain both the universality of sin and the universality of the gospel's offer: as Adam's headship was universal (all who are human bear his guilt), so Christ's headship is available to all (all who are in him receive his righteousness). Now: The doctrine of original sin is the one Christian teaching that can be empirically verified by reading any newspaper. Every generation produces fresh evidence that something has gone profoundly wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names it: Adam. And then offers the only remedy: Christ. The diagnosis and the cure are inseparable.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.

Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man. Key words. “One man” is Adam (Genesis 3). Sin entered human history through him. Paul treats him as a real, historical man.

And death through sin. Death is not natural; it is the penalty of sin (Genesis 2:17; 6:23).

And so death spread to all men because all sinned. Key words. “Because” (eph’ hō). Augustine, reading the Latin translation (in quo, in whom), took it as in whom all sinned, that is, in Adam. Most scholars now agree the Greek means because, so the translation in whom cannot be pressed. But the question remains: in what sense did all sin?

Two readings of “all sinned”. The first says all die because each person sins personally, following Adam’s example. The second says all sinned in Adam, when he sinned as the representative head of the human race. Verdict: the second, for three reasons Paul gives in the passage itself. First, death reigned even over those who did not sin as Adam did (v. 14), including infants, who have committed no personal sins; so their death must come from Adam’s sin. Second, Paul says five times that condemnation and death came through one man’s one trespass (vv. 15–19), not through each person’s many sins. Third, v. 19 says that by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners. Personal sins follow, and they are real and add to our guilt; but the root is our union with Adam. This is what theologians call original sin: we inherit both Adam’s guilt, counted to us, and his corrupted nature (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3).

Is it fair to be condemned for Adam’s sin? This is the question every reader asks, and Paul does not run from it. Several things help. Representation is how God has always related to humanity: the head acts for those in him, as a nation’s leader can bind the whole nation to war or peace. Adam was the best representative humanity could ever have had, placed in a perfect world with every advantage; no one can say they would have done better. Each of us confirms Adam’s choice by our own sins, every day. And most importantly, if we reject the principle of representation, we lose the gospel, because we are saved in exactly the same way: by another man’s obedience counted to us (vv. 18–19). We cannot accept the second Adam and refuse to understand the first. The question is not whether we will be represented, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

Where Christians differ: was Adam a real person? Some Christians, seeking to harmonise Genesis with evolutionary theories of human origins, hold that Adam is a symbol of humanity rather than a real first man. Verdict: Paul’s argument requires a real, historical Adam. He sets one man against one man, one trespass against one act of righteousness, and a real history of death reigning from Adam to Moses (v. 14). If there was no real Adam whose sin brought condemnation, Paul’s parallel with the real Christ whose obedience brings justification falls apart. Jesus too treated Adam and Eve as real (Matthew 19:4–5), and Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam (Luke 3:38).

For sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law. Key words. “Counted” (ellogeitai, charged to an account, as in a ledger). Between Adam and Moses there was no written law, so people’s sins were not charged as transgressions of a stated command, in the way Adam’s was (see 4:15). Yet people still died, and death is the penalty of sin. Why? Because Adam’s sin was counted to them. This is Paul’s evidence for the point he has just made: death reigned because all sinned in Adam.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagians taught that Adam only set a bad example, and each person sins freely on their own. Verdict: Paul teaches that Adam’s sin was counted to the whole human race, so that all are born guilty and corrupt (vv. 18–19; Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). Adam was the federal head of humanity, and his fall became ours. This is hard, but it is the background of the gospel: in the same way, Christ’s righteousness is counted to all who are in him.

In a sentence. Just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death came to all people because all sinned, for sin was in the world before the law, though sin is not charged where there is no law...

For worship. You were in Adam, and fell with him. In Christ, you are raised with him. Thank God for the second Adam.
verseByVerse.note: “One man” is Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.

Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses. Key words. Death reigned like a king. Everyone died: infants, people who never broke a direct command.

Even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam. Adam broke a direct command. Those between Adam and Moses didn’t have one. They still died, because of Adam.

Who was a type of the one who was to come. Key words. A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, points to Christ, head of the new. Two men, two heads, two families. Adam is the pattern Christ reverses (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49).

In a sentence. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command as Adam did, who was a pattern of the one to come.

On a Tuesday. Death reigns in Adam. Life reigns in Christ. Which family are you in?
verseByVerse.note: A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, foreshadows Christ, head of the new.

parallels.desc: the first man Adam, the last Adam

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.

But the free gift is not like the trespass. Key words. Similar in pattern, but not equal in power. The gift is greater.

For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift... abounded for many. “Much more”: grace is stronger than sin. Grace overflows.

For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation. One sin brought condemnation.

But the free gift following many trespasses brought justification. Key words. The wonder of grace: one sin brought condemnation, but the gift deals with many sins, a mountain of them, and brings justification. Grace takes on a whole lifetime of sins.

In a sentence. But the gift is not like the trespass, for if many died through one man’s trespass, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, overflow to many; and the gift is not like the result of one man’s sin, for judgment followed one sin and brought condemnation, but the gift followed many trespasses and brought justification.

For worship. Grace is bigger than all your sins. It covers many trespasses.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.

Because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man. Death the tyrant.

Much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life. Key words. Not just “life will reign,” but “they will reign in life.” Believers become kings, sharing Christ’s rule (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). “Receive”: grace and righteousness are received as gifts. “The free gift of righteousness”: righteousness itself is a gift, credited to us.

Through the one man Jesus Christ. Through him alone.

In a sentence. If death reigned through one man’s trespass, how much more will those who receive God’s abundant grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. You were made to reign with Christ. Live today as one who will.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.

As one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. Key words. The parallel. “All men” in Adam; “all men” in Christ. Who are the “all” in Christ? Not every human being, since Paul has just said it is “those who receive” the gift (v. 17), and he teaches elsewhere that many perish (2:12). It is all who are in Christ, as all in Adam are condemned.

Where Christians differ: are all saved? Universalists read “justification and life for all men” as meaning every person will be saved. Verdict: Paul limits it to “those who receive” (v. 17), believers. As all in Adam die, so all in Christ are made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22). The “all” is all who belong to each head. Scripture clearly teaches that some perish eternally (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46).

For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners. Key words. “Made” (katestathēsan): constituted, appointed, put in the category of. Adam’s disobedience was counted to all in him.

So by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous. Key words. Christ’s obedience counted to all in him. His “obedience”: his whole life of perfect obedience to God’s law, culminating in obedience to death on the cross (Philippians 2:8). Theologians call it his active and passive obedience: he both kept the law perfectly for us, and bore its penalty for us. Both are credited to believers. This is imputed righteousness.

In a sentence. As one trespass resulted in condemnation for all people, so one righteous act resulted in justification and life for all people, for as through one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous.

For worship. Christ’s perfect obedience is credited to you. You stand before God in his righteousness.

parallels.desc: shall my servant make many to be accounted righteous

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Now the law came in to increase the trespass. Key words. “Came in” (pareisēlthen): came in alongside, as a side entrance. The law wasn’t given to save, but to show sin as sin, to make it more obvious, even to provoke it (7:7–13). It exposes our need.

But where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. Key words. One of the greatest sentences in Scripture. “Abounded all the more” (hypereperisseusen): super-abounded, overflowed beyond measure. However great your sin, grace is greater. No sinner is beyond its reach.

So that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life. Two kings: sin reigning through death, grace reigning through righteousness. Grace now rules, and leads to eternal life.

Through Jesus Christ our Lord. The refrain that ends each section of chapters 5–8 (5:11, 21; 6:23; 7:25; 8:39).

In a sentence. The law came in so that the trespass might increase, but where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that just as sin reigned in death, grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Where your sin abounds, grace abounds more. Come to Christ, whatever you have done.
