For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many.<sup>16</sup>And the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.<sup>17</sup>For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men.<sup>19</sup>For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.<sup>20</sup>Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,<sup>21</sup>so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Romans 6 opens with the most dangerous question the gospel generates: "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" If grace covers all sin, and more sin produces more grace, why not sin freely? Paul's answer — "By no means!" — is the most vehement denial in the letter. The question misunderstands both the nature of grace and the nature of the union with Christ that is the foundation of the justified life.

The answer Paul gives is not primarily ethical (you should not sin) but theological (you cannot sin in the way that question imagines, because of who you now are in Christ). Union with Christ in his death and resurrection has changed the believer's fundamental status with respect to sin. She has died to it. It no longer has jurisdiction over her. The command that follows — "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" — is not a technique for sin management but a theological reality to be reckoned with and lived from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's answer to the antinomian question is grounded in baptism — not as a magical ritual but as the enacted sign of the believer's union with Christ in his death and resurrection. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" Baptism is the visible declaration of an invisible reality: the believer has been co-crucified with Christ, co-buried with him, and co-raised with him into newness of life. These are not future aspirations; they are present realities that define who the Christian is.

The key concept is "our old self was crucified with him" (v. 6) — the person we were in Adam, defined by sin's dominion, is dead. Not sick, not weakened, not being rehabilitated — dead. Sin still exists in the believer (7:14–25 will be painfully honest about this), but sin no longer reigns. The one who is in Christ has been transferred out of sin's kingdom and into grace's kingdom. She is not a sinner desperately trying to become a saint; she is a saint who still struggles with sin. The identity has changed, even while the struggle continues.

The imperatives of vv. 11–14 flow from the indicatives of vv. 1–10. "Consider yourselves dead to sin" (v. 11) — reckon it, take it into account, live from this reality. "Let not sin therefore reign" (v. 12) — the fact that sin no longer must reign does not mean the battle is over; it means the battle is now winnable. "Present yourselves to God" (v. 13) — the person whose old self has been crucified with Christ is now free to offer herself as a living sacrifice to the God she could not truly serve before.

Two things at the edges of the section carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is that Paul grounds our security in Christ’s experience before he applies anything to ours: the death he died he died to sin once for all, and being raised from the dead he will never die again — death no longer has dominion over him (vv. 9–10). That is the anchor. Our dying and rising are real because they are participation in his, and his cannot be undone or repeated. The second is the promise the section ends on: sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (v. 14). It is stated as a fact about the future rather than a target to aim at — and the reason given is the opposite of what any moralist would expect. Sin loses its grip not because the rules have been tightened but because the government has changed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds sanctification in union with Christ, not in moral effort or spiritual discipline alone. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that justification and sanctification, though distinct, are inseparable — both are fruits of union with Christ. John Murray's landmark study Redemption Accomplished and Applied showed that union with Christ is not an add-on to the Christian life but its very foundation: every blessing of salvation flows from being in Christ. We are justified in Christ, sanctified in Christ, glorified in Christ. The call to holiness in Romans 6 is not the demand to earn what we have not yet received; it is the call to live consistently with what is already true of us in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The antinomian objection Paul addresses — "let us sin that grace may abound" — was apparently a real misreading of his gospel in his own day (v. 1 and 3:8). Some had heard his message of free grace and concluded that moral behaviour was irrelevant. Paul's reply is not to retreat into moralism but to deepen the gospel: the same grace that justifies also transforms. Grace is not a license; it is a power that liberates from the dominion of sin. Now: The same objection recurs whenever grace is preached with full biblical clarity. The person who is never accused of antinomianism by those who prefer a works-based gospel has probably not yet preached grace clearly enough. But Paul's answer stands: grace does not produce moral indifference; it produces the only genuine moral transformation available — the transformation of a person who has died and risen with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?

Meaning first. Romans 6 answers the obvious objection to grace: if grace abounds where sin increases (5:20), why not sin more? Paul’s answer: because believers have died to sin. Union with Christ means we died with him and were raised with him, so sin is no longer our master. We must reckon ourselves dead to sin and alive to God, and offer our bodies to God as instruments of righteousness. We have changed masters: once slaves of sin, now slaves of God, and the end of that slavery is eternal life. Justification never leaves a person in sin; it joins them to Christ, who breaks sin’s power.

What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited (3:8). If more sin means more grace, why not sin?

By no means! Paul’s horror.

How can we who died to sin still live in it? Key words. The answer in one question. Believers have died to sin. Not that sin has died in us, or that we no longer feel it, but that we died to its reign. Our relationship to sin has changed decisively. A dead person can’t go on living in the old way.

What “died to sin” does not mean. It does not mean that believers no longer feel the pull of sin, or that sin has been removed from them, or that they have become unable to sin. Paul goes on to command them not to let sin reign (v. 12), which would be pointless if they could no longer sin; and chapter 7 describes the believer’s real struggle with it. Nor is it a command (die to sin!); it is a past fact (we died), something that has already happened to every believer in union with Christ.

What it does mean. The key is v. 10, which says that Christ also died to sin. Christ never had sin in him, so dying to sin cannot mean sin was rooted out of him. It means he died to sin’s realm and claim: he came under the reign of sin and death for our sake, bore its penalty, and through death passed out of that realm for ever. Believers, united to him, have died with him to that same reign. Sin was once our master, ruling us and holding a legal claim on us; that relationship ended when we died with Christ. We now belong to a different realm, the reign of grace (5:21).

Then why do I still sin? Because sin’s reign has been broken, but its presence remains until the resurrection. The old regime has been overthrown, but its forces still fight in the land. Sin still lives in our mortal bodies and pulls at us (vv. 12–13; 7:20–23); but it is no longer our rightful master, and it has no right to our obedience. That is why Paul can command us to resist it: we are not slaves trying to escape, but free people refusing to go back. The fight is real, but it is fought from victory.

In a sentence. Should we go on sinning so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin keep living in it?

On a Tuesday. You have died to sin. Don’t live as if you were still its slave.
verseByVerse.note: Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. Key words. “Baptized into Christ”: united with him. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, and especially with his death. When he died, we died with him.

We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death. Key words. Baptism pictures burial: going under the water, as into the grave (Colossians 2:12). Immersion makes the picture vivid.

In order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. Key words. Rising from the water pictures rising with Christ. The purpose: a new kind of life. “Walk”: daily conduct. “Newness”: a new quality of life, the life of the resurrection.

Where Christians differ: what does baptism do? Some see baptism as the moment when union with Christ actually happens (baptismal regeneration). Verdict: Paul assumes that those he addresses are believers, for whom baptism expressed their faith. Union with Christ is by faith, wrought by the Spirit (Galatians 3:26–27; Ephesians 3:17); baptism is the visible sign and seal of it. The reality is union with Christ; baptism is its God-given picture. Credobaptists see this as strong support for believers’ baptism by immersion, picturing death, burial and resurrection.

In a sentence. Don’t you know that all who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death, buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the Father’s glory, we too may live a new life?

For worship. Remember your baptism: you died and rose with Christ. Walk in newness of life.

parallels.desc: buried with him in baptism

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.

For if we have been united with him in a death like his. “United” (symphytoi): grown together, like a graft into a tree.

We shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. Both now, in new life, and at the last day, in a resurrection body.

We know that our old self was crucified with him. Key words. The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam, before conversion (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9). Crucified, put to death, with Christ (Galatians 2:20). Not being crucified gradually, but was crucified: a completed fact.

In order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing. “Body of sin”: the person as controlled by sin. “Brought to nothing” (katargēthē): rendered powerless, put out of action. Not annihilated, but stripped of its power.

So that we would no longer be enslaved to sin. The purpose: freedom from sin’s slavery.

In a sentence. If we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his, for we know our old self was crucified with him so that the body ruled by sin might be done away with, and we would no longer be slaves to sin.

On a Tuesday. Your old self was crucified. Sin is no longer your master. Believe it, and say no to it.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.

For one who has died has been set free from sin. Key words. “Set free” (dedikaiōtai): literally “justified.” A dead man is released from all claims; the law has nothing more to say to him. Death ends obligations. Having died with Christ, sin has no more legal claim on us.

Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him. Union with his death guarantees union with his life.

In a sentence. For anyone who has died has been set free from sin, and if we died with Christ, we believe we will also live with him.

For worship. You died with Christ, so you will live with him, now and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.

We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again. Key words. Unlike Lazarus, Christ’s resurrection is permanent. He has conquered death for ever (Revelation 1:18).

Death no longer has dominion over him. Death once had him; now never.

For the death he died he died to sin, once for all. Key words. Not that Christ had sin in himself, but he died to sin’s claim, its power and penalty, which he bore for us. This is the key to the whole chapter: the same words, died to sin, are used of believers in v. 2. Since Christ had no sin, dying to sin cannot mean that sin was removed from inside him; it means that he passed out of the realm where sin and death had a claim. So it is with believers who died with him (see the note on vv. 1–2). “Once for all” (ephapax): a single, final act, never to be repeated (Hebrews 7:27; 9:12, 26; 10:10).

But the life he lives he lives to God. His risen life is wholly for God.

In a sentence. We know that since Christ was raised from the dead, he cannot die again; death no longer rules him, for the death he died, he died to sin once for all, but the life he lives, he lives to God.

On a Tuesday. Christ died to sin once for all. Your sin was dealt with completely. Live to God.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.

So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Key words. The first command in Romans. “Consider” (logizesthe): reckon, count, calculate. The bookkeeping word of chapter 4. Not pretending, but counting on what is true. You are dead to sin and alive to God, because you are in Christ. Believe it, and live from it.

Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body. Key words. Sin still lives in us, and wants to reign again. Don’t let it. “Mortal body”: still subject to death and temptation, not yet glorified.

To make you obey its passions. Sinful desires.

The pattern. First what God has done (indicative), then what we must do (imperative). Not “become what you are not,” but “be what you are.”

In a sentence. In the same way, count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus, and don’t let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its evil desires.

For worship. Reckon it true today: you are dead to sin and alive to God. Then act on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.

Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness. Key words. “Members” means the parts of the body: hands, eyes, tongue and the rest. “Instruments” (hopla): tools, or weapons. Your body parts are weapons. Don’t put them at sin’s service.

But present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life. Offer yourselves to God, as people raised from death (12:1).

And your members to God as instruments for righteousness. Your eyes, tongue, hands, used for God.

For sin will have no dominion over you. Key words. A promise, not just a command. Sin will not be your master. You will still struggle with it (7:14–25), but it won’t rule you.

Since you are not under law but under grace. Key words. Not under the law as a way of acceptance with God, with its condemnation and its inability to change the heart. Under grace: God’s favour, which both forgives and empowers.

Where Christians differ: not under law? Antinomians take this to mean believers have no obligation to God’s moral law. Verdict: the very next verse asks, “Are we to sin because we are not under law?” and answers, “By no means!” Not under law means not under its condemnation or as the means of justification. Believers are “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21) and fulfil the law by love (13:8–10).

In a sentence. Don’t offer any part of yourself to sin as a tool of wickedness, but offer yourselves to God as those brought from death to life, and your body parts to him as tools of righteousness, for sin shall no longer be your master, since you are not under law but under grace.

On a Tuesday. Give your eyes, tongue and hands to God today. Sin is not your master.
verseByVerse.note: “Members” means the parts of the body — hands, eyes, tongue — used for good or evil.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of v. 15 replays the question of v. 1 in a new key: "Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" This is the libertarian version of the antinomian objection — if the law is not our master, then surely we are free to do anything. Paul's answer is again a flat denial, followed by a theological argument: freedom from sin does not mean freedom from all master; it means a change of master. Every human being serves either sin or righteousness — there is no neutral ground, no autonomous freedom that is subject to nothing.

The language of slavery runs throughout the passage and is deliberately shocking. Sin is a slave-master. Righteousness is a slave-master. The difference is in the direction: slavery to sin leads to death; slavery to righteousness leads to life and holiness. The Christian is not more free than the unbeliever in the sense of being subject to nothing; she is more free in the sense that she now serves the master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light — the master whose service is perfect freedom.

The concluding verse is one of the most famous in the letter: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The contrast between wages and gift is the contrast between law and gospel. Death is what sin earns — a wage paid in proportion to the work done. Eternal life is what God gives — a gift, free, unearned, proportionate not to the recipient's merit but to the giver's generosity. The entire letter is in this sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 establishes that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new and deeper obedience — obedience that flows from a changed heart rather than a legal compulsion. The Reformers distinguished between the "old obedience" (driven by fear of punishment and desire for reward) and the "new obedience" (driven by love for God and gratitude for grace). Calvin was particularly insistent that the justified Christian is not released from obedience but liberated for it — the law now functions as a guide for the regenerate, not as a court that condemns. The third use of the law: the Christian, freed from condemnation, embraces the law as the expression of the will of the God she loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's slavery metaphor was immediately intelligible to a first-century audience in which slavery was the defining social institution. Every person knew what it meant to be owned by a master, to have their labour and their body subject to another's will. Paul's redeployment of this metaphor is arresting: you were a slave before, and you are a slave now — the only question is whose slave you are. The liberated Christian is not autonomous; she is re-owned, by a Master who purchased her with his own blood. Now: The modern West prizes autonomy above almost everything — the right to define oneself, to determine one's own values, to answer to no authority beyond the self. Romans 6 is a direct challenge to this: the autonomous self is a myth. Every person serves something — appetite, ambition, approval, comfort, identity. The gospel does not offer escape from all masters; it offers the only master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?

Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! A second form of the objection (v. 1). Not “keep on sinning,” but “commit acts of sin,” since we’re not under law.

If you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey. Key words. Everyone serves someone. There is no neutral freedom. You are either a slave of sin or a slave of obedience to God (Matthew 6:24; John 8:34).

Either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness. Two masters, two destinations.

In a sentence. Shall we sin because we are not under law but grace? By no means! Don’t you know that when you offer yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

For worship. Everyone serves a master. Choose to serve the one who gives life.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.

But thanks be to God. Key words. Paul thanks God, not them, for their change. Conversion is God’s work.

You who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart. Key words. “From the heart”: not outward conformity, but inner obedience. The new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27).

To the standard of teaching to which you were committed. Key words. “Standard” (typon): pattern, mould. They were handed over to the gospel’s teaching, as metal is poured into a mould, and shaped by it. Christian teaching shapes the believer.

And, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness. Freed from one master, bound to another. Christian freedom is not independence but a new, good slavery.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God that, though you used to be slaves to sin, you have come to obey from the heart the pattern of teaching that has claimed your allegiance, and having been set free from sin, you have become slaves to righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Let the gospel mould you. Obey it from the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.

I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. Key words. Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the Roman church were slaves or former slaves. Paul uses an image they knew, though it is imperfect, since serving God is not oppressive.

Just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness. Sin multiplies sin. Each sin makes the next easier.

So now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. Key words. Now put the same energy into righteousness. Righteousness leads to sanctification: growing holiness. Holiness also builds on itself.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. Free from righteousness: it had no claim on you. A grim freedom.

In a sentence. Paul uses everyday terms because of human limitations: just as they used to offer themselves as slaves to impurity and ever-increasing wickedness, so now they should offer themselves as slaves to righteousness leading to holiness, for when they were slaves to sin, they were free from the control of righteousness.

For worship. Put as much energy into holiness as you once put into sin.
verseByVerse.note: Slavery was part of everyday life across the Roman world; many in the church were slaves or former slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.

But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? Key words. A searching question. What did sin ever really give you? Shame, regret, and death.

For the end of those things is death. The destination of sin.

But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God. “Slaves of God”: the highest freedom.

The fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life. Key words. Two harvests: shame and death, or holiness and eternal life. Sanctification is the road; eternal life is the end. No one reaches the end without the road (Hebrews 12:14).

In a sentence. What benefit did they reap then from things they are now ashamed of? Those things end in death. But now, freed from sin and enslaved to God, the benefit they reap leads to holiness, and the result is eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Ask what sin has really given you. Then compare it with what God gives.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For the wages of sin is death. Key words. Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer: what is earned. Sin pays, and its pay is death: physical, spiritual, eternal. You earn it.

But the free gift of God is eternal life. Key words. Not wages, but a gift (charisma, gift of grace). Death is earned; life is given. You can’t earn eternal life, any more than you can avoid earning death apart from Christ.

In Christ Jesus our Lord. The gift comes only in him.

In a sentence. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For worship. You have earned death. God gives you life. Receive the gift with thanks.
verseByVerse.note: Wages were the regular pay of a soldier or labourer — what is earned. A gift is not.

How can we who died to sin still live in it?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?<sup>4</sup>We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.<sup>5</sup>For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.<sup>6</sup>We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.<sup>7</sup>For one who has died has been set free from sin.<sup>8</sup>Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.<sup>9</sup>We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.<sup>10</sup>For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.<sup>11</sup>So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.<sup>12</sup>Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.<sup>13</sup>Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness.<sup>14</sup>For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.<sup>15</sup>What then? 7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther and Calvin, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life. Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.

Meaning first. Romans 7 explains the believer’s relationship to the law of Moses. First, believers have died to the law through Christ, as a widow is released from her marriage, so that they belong to Christ and serve in the new way of the Spirit (vv. 1–6). Second, the law is not sin; it is holy, righteous and good, but sin used it to provoke and kill (vv. 7–13). Third, Paul describes the painful struggle of one who loves God’s law but still finds sin at work in him: I do not do the good I want. The cry “Wretched man that I am!” is answered at once: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (vv. 14–25). The law can show sin, but cannot defeat it; only Christ and the Spirit can.

For I am speaking to those who know the law. Jews, and God-fearing Gentiles familiar with Moses.

That the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives. Key words. A basic legal principle: death ends legal obligations.

For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage. An illustration from marriage.

In a sentence. Don’t you know, brothers and sisters who know the law, that the law has authority over someone only while they live? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he is alive, but if he dies, she is released from the law that bound her to him.

On a Tuesday. Death ends obligations. In Christ, you died to the law’s condemnation.

parallels.desc: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.

She will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. Marriage is binding for life.

But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress. Key words. Death frees her to remarry.

Where Christians differ: divorce and remarriage. Some use these verses to say remarriage after divorce is never allowed while a former spouse lives. Verdict: Paul is using marriage as an illustration, not giving a full teaching on divorce. Marriage is meant to be for life. Elsewhere Scripture allows divorce for adultery (Matthew 19:9) and for desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15), and in those cases the innocent party may remarry. This is the Westminster position (24.5–6). Divorce is always a tragedy, to be avoided where possible.

In a sentence. So if she has another man while her husband is alive, she is called an adulteress, but if he dies she is free from that law and not an adulteress if she marries another man.

For worship. Marriage is meant for life. Honour it, and pray for marriages around you.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.

Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ. Key words. The application. In the illustration, the husband dies; here, we die. But the point is the same: death ends the old relationship. Through Christ’s death (his body on the cross), we died to the law as a way of salvation and as a condemning master.

So that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead. Key words. A new marriage. Freed from the law, we are married to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25–32). The church is his bride.

In order that we may bear fruit for God. Fruit of a marriage: children. Fruit of union with Christ: good works, holiness.

For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death. Key words. “In the flesh”: in our unconverted state, before the Spirit. The law aroused sinful desires, like a sign saying “Don’t touch” makes you want to touch. Its fruit was death.

In a sentence. So, my brothers and sisters, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God, for when we were in the realm of the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in us, bearing fruit for death.

On a Tuesday. You are married to Christ. Bear fruit for him.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.

But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive. Key words. “But now” again (3:21). Released, like a prisoner freed. The law held us, not because it was bad, but because we were sinners under its condemnation.

So that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code. Key words. Freed not to do nothing, but to serve. In a new way: by the Spirit, from a changed heart, not by external rules written on stone (2 Corinthians 3:6). This is the new covenant: the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Chapter 8 explains it.

In a sentence. But now, by dying to what once held us captive, we have been released from the law so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, not in the old way of the written code.

For worship. You serve God now by the Spirit, from the heart. That is freedom.

parallels.desc: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.

Two things in the middle of the chapter carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is Paul’s conclusion at v. 13, which is the point of the whole autobiographical section: the law did not kill him, sin did — working death in him through what is good, so that sin might be shown to be sin and might become sinful beyond measure. That is the purpose of the exercise. The law was given partly to provoke sin into the open, where its true character could be seen; a disease that is invisible cannot be treated, and sin’s worst feature is exactly its capacity to use a holy commandment as its instrument. The second is the image at v. 23, which supplies the vocabulary for everything Christians have said since about the inner conflict: another law waging war against the law of the mind, and taking the man captive. Paul does not describe an imbalance or a tension. He describes a campaign, with two sides, prisoners, and territory — which is why the chapter can end in a cry rather than a conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in the literature of the day — Ovid's famous line, spoken by Medea: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the philosophers' solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.” But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.

That the law is sin? By no means! If the law aroused sin, is the law itself evil? No.

Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. The law reveals sin (3:20). Like an X-ray: it shows the disease, but can’t cure it.

For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.” Key words. The tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart: not an outward act but an inward desire. As a Pharisee, Paul may have thought he kept the law outwardly (Philippians 3:6). But the tenth commandment exposed his heart.

But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. “Opportunity” (aphormēn): a base of operations, a military term. Sin used the law as a launching pad. Tell a child not to touch something, and the desire grows.

For apart from the law, sin lies dead. Dormant, not yet stirred up.

In a sentence. Is the law sin? Certainly not! But Paul would not have known what sin was except through the law, for he would not have known coveting if the law had not said, “You shall not covet,” but sin, seizing the opportunity the commandment gave, produced in him every kind of covetous desire, for apart from the law, sin was dead.

On a Tuesday. Let the tenth commandment search your heart. What do you covet?
verseByVerse.note: Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.

I was once alive apart from the law. Key words. Who is the “I”? Perhaps Paul as a child before he understood the law; or Paul speaking for Adam, who lived before the command; or for Israel before Sinai. Probably Paul’s own experience, told in a way that echoes Adam and Israel. He felt alive, self-satisfied.

But when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. When the law’s demand pierced his conscience, sin revived, and he saw himself as spiritually dead, condemned.

The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me. Key words. The law promised life to those who keep it (Leviticus 18:5). But to a sinner, it brings death. Not the law’s fault, but sin’s.

In a sentence. Once Paul was alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and he died, and the very commandment that was meant to bring life brought death.

For worship. The law shows you are dead. Only Christ makes you alive.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.

For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Key words. “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve (Genesis 3:13; 2 Corinthians 11:3). Sin lies: it says the forbidden thing will satisfy, that God is holding back good. It used God’s good command to kill.

So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good. Key words. The verdict. The law is not the problem. It reflects God’s holy character. The problem is sin. We must never despise God’s law.

In a sentence. For sin, seizing the opportunity the commandment gave, deceived him and through the commandment killed him, so the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous and good.

On a Tuesday. Sin lies to you. God’s law tells you the truth. Believe God.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.

Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! The law didn’t kill; sin did.

It was sin, producing death in me through what is good. Sin used a good thing for evil. That shows how evil sin is.

In order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure. Key words. God’s purpose in the law: to unmask sin, to show it for what it truly is. “Sinful beyond measure” (kath’ hyperbolēn): utterly, hyperbolically sinful. When we see that sin twists even God’s good law into an instrument of death, we see how terrible it is.

In a sentence. Did what is good become death to him? By no means! It was sin, using what is good to bring death, so that sin might be shown for what it is, and through the commandment become utterly sinful.

For worship. Ask God to show you how sinful sin is. Only then will you treasure his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.

For we know that the law is spiritual. From the Spirit, reflecting God’s nature.

But I am of the flesh, sold under sin. Key words. “Of the flesh” (sarkinos): made of flesh, human, weak. “Sold under sin”: as a slave sold to a master. The tense changes here to the present: Paul is now describing his present experience.

For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. Key words. The universal experience of the struggling believer. Wanting to do right, failing; hating sin, doing it.

Where Christians differ: who is the “I” of verses 14–25? Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer. Some (many early Greek fathers, Wesley, and many modern scholars) see an unbeliever under the law, or Paul before conversion. Verdict: with Augustine, Luther, Calvin and the Reformed tradition, this best describes a believer. The present tense; the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), which no unbeliever has (8:7); the hatred of sin (v. 15); the cry for deliverance and thanks for it (vv. 24–25): all fit a regenerate person who still has indwelling sin. It describes the struggle, not the whole Christian life; chapter 8 shows the victory by the Spirit. Mature believers often feel this struggle most keenly, because they love God’s law most.

But how can a believer be “sold under sin”? This is the strongest objection to reading vv. 14–25 as the experience of a Christian, and it deserves an honest answer. In 6:17–18 Paul says believers have been set free from sin; here he says I am sold under sin. Three things help. First, Paul carefully limits where this is true: nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh (v. 18); with my flesh I serve the law of sin (v. 25). He is describing what remains of the old nature, not the whole person, whose inner being delights in God’s law (v. 22). Second, he is describing the believer measured against the law alone, considered apart from the Spirit’s help: as far as the law’s power goes, even a believer cannot overcome sin; the law can command but not enable. That is why chapter 8, where the Spirit is named nineteen times, follows immediately. Third, the language of captivity describes real defeats in a real war (v. 23), not surrender: a soldier can be taken prisoner in a battle without changing sides.

A mediating view. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in his great sermons on Romans, argued for a third option: that Paul describes a person awakened by the law to his sin, convinced and distressed, but not yet regenerate and not yet resting in Christ. Douglas Moo holds that Paul describes his own past experience as a Jew under the law, seen now with Christian eyes. These readings take seriously the strong language of vv. 14 and 23. But the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), the hatred of sin (v. 15), and the thanksgiving for Christ’s deliverance (v. 25) are hard to fit any but a believer. The Reformed verdict above remains the most natural reading, and the most pastorally true to what believers actually experience.

In a sentence. We know the law is spiritual, but Paul is unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin, and he does not understand what he does, for what he wants to do he does not do, but what he hates he does.

On a Tuesday. If you feel this struggle, you are not alone. It is the mark of a heart that loves God’s law.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.

Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. Key words. His very unwillingness shows he sides with the law. His deepest self agrees with God.

So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. Key words. Not an excuse, but a diagnosis. Paul’s true self, the new self, does not want sin. Sin is an intruder, a squatter in the house. “Dwells” (oikousa): lives, makes its home. Sin is still present, though no longer the master. The believer is responsible for his sins, but they don’t express who he truly is in Christ.

In a sentence. If he does what he does not want to do, he agrees that the law is good, and so it is no longer he himself who does it, but sin living in him.

For worship. Sin is an intruder in a believer’s heart, not its true master. Fight it in Christ’s strength.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.

For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. Key words. “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the physical body. In his flesh, his fallen nature, nothing good. Paul carefully qualifies it: not “in me” entirely, since the Spirit dwells in him (8:9), but in my flesh.

For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. Key words. Willing, but not able in his own strength. The flesh can’t do it. Only the Spirit can (8:4, 13).

For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing. Not that he never does good, but that he never does it as fully as he wants, and evil keeps breaking through.

In a sentence. Paul knows that good itself does not dwell in him, in his sinful nature, for he has the desire to do good but cannot carry it out, and he does not do the good he wants, but keeps doing the evil he does not want.

On a Tuesday. You can’t defeat sin in your own strength. Depend on the Spirit, every hour.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.

Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. Repeating v. 17.

So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand. Key words. “Law” here means principle, a fixed pattern. Whenever he wants to do good, evil is right there beside him. Temptation is always close (Genesis 4:7).

In a sentence. If he does what he does not want, it is no longer he who does it, but sin living in him, so he finds this law at work: when he wants to do good, evil is right there with him.

For worship. Expect temptation to stand close when you try to do good. Stand closer to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.

For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being. Key words. “Delight” (synēdomai): rejoice with, take pleasure in. Like the psalmist (Psalm 1:2; 119:97). No unbeliever delights in God’s law (8:7). This is the new heart. “Inner being”: the inner self, renewed by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).

But I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind. Key words. War. The believer is a battlefield. The flesh against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). Not peace yet, but war.

And making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members. Taken prisoner at times. Not total defeat, but painful losses.

In a sentence. In his inner being he delights in God’s law, but he sees another law at work in his body, waging war against the law of his mind and making him a prisoner of the law of sin at work within him.

On a Tuesday. The war inside you is a sign of life. Dead people don’t fight sin.

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

Wretched man that I am! Key words. A cry of anguish. Not despair, but deep longing. The more you love God, the more your sin grieves you.

Who will deliver me from this body of death? Key words. “Who,” not “what.” Not a technique, but a person. “This body of death”: this body subject to death and to sin’s pull. Some say an ancient punishment tied a corpse to a murderer. He longs for full deliverance.

Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! Key words. The answer bursts out at once. Jesus Christ delivers: now in part, by the Spirit (8:2), and fully at the resurrection, when this body of death is changed (8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:57).

So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin. Key words. A summary of the present tension. The believer, between conversion and glory, is both. Not yet sinless, but no longer sin’s slave at heart. Chapter 8 shows the Spirit’s power in this struggle.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some holiness teachers claim believers can reach a state of sinless perfection in this life. Verdict: Paul, an apostle, still struggled. John says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Believers grow in holiness and win real victories, but sinless perfection comes only at glorification (Philippians 3:12; 1 John 3:2).

In a sentence. What a wretched man he is! Who will rescue him from this body of death? Thanks be to God, who delivers him through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with his mind he serves God’s law, but in his sinful nature he serves the law of sin.

For worship. When you cry “Wretched man that I am!”, answer at once: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the mountain peak of the New Testament. Commentators across twenty centuries have reached for superlatives and still found them inadequate. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "no separation" — and between those two impossibilities of loss, it contains the fullest and most glorious account of the Christian life available in Scripture: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of redemption, and the love of God from which nothing in the universe can separate us.

The movement of the chapter is from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to eternal security (vv. 28–39). In each movement, the Spirit is central: He liberates (vv. 1–11), he adopts (vv. 14–17), he intercedes (vv. 26–27). And over all of it stands the sovereign love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will glorify — a chain that has never had a broken link and never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." One sentence — and the whole of the gospel's comfort is here. Not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. No condemnation. The verdict is absolute, unconditional, and permanent. It rests not on the quality of the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and the irreversible union with him by faith.

The reason for the "no condemnation" is the "law of the Spirit of life" which has set the believer free from "the law of sin and death" (v. 2). This is not two different legal codes but two different powers — the power of the Spirit that gives life versus the power of sin that produces death. Christ condemned sin in the flesh (v. 3) — He bore its penalty, exhausted its power, stripped it of its right to condemn — so that the Spirit-empowered believer might fulfil the righteous requirement of the law (v. 4).

The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in vv. 5–11 is not between body and soul — Paul is not a Gnostic. It is between life oriented around the self and its capacities (flesh) and life oriented around God and his Spirit (Spirit). The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. The Christian is not defined by the flesh but by the Spirit — "you, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you" (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Definitive Justification and Ongoing Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the permanent foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The condemnation that does not exist for those in Christ is not merely past (sins before conversion) but total: nothing from the past, present, or future can generate condemnation for the one who is in Christ. This is because justification is not a process but an event — a forensic declaration that has been made and cannot be unmade. The Christian may sin grievously; she is not beyond discipline, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glorification.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jewish legal system that Paul's readers knew well had a concept of condemnation — the verdict of guilty rendered by a court against one who had violated the law. Paul takes this forensic language and applies it to the ultimate court: the tribunal of God. The verdict of "no condemnation" is the legal declaration of the divine Judge that the case is closed, the penalty has been paid, and the accused walks free — permanently. Now: Countless Christians live under a cloud of functional condemnation — not doubting their doctrinal justification but unable to feel free, perpetually haunted by past sins, unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 is the word that cuts through all of this: not less condemnation, not reduced condemnation — none. Take it in. Live from it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.

Meaning first. Romans 8 is the summit of the letter, and perhaps of the whole Bible. It begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation. In between: the Holy Spirit, mentioned nineteen times, who frees us from sin’s power, gives life, makes us God’s children, assures us of adoption, helps us pray, and guarantees our future glory. Present sufferings are nothing compared to the coming glory, when creation itself will be set free. God works all things for the good of those he has called, and his purpose runs unbroken from foreknowledge to glory. If God is for us, who can be against us? Nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Key words. One of the most precious verses in Scripture. “Therefore”: because of Christ’s work (3:21–5:21) and the believer’s deliverance (7:25). “Now”: already, not someday. “No condemnation” (ouden katakrima): none at all. Not reduced, not probationary, but none. The verdict of the last day has been given now. “In Christ Jesus”: united to him. His standing is ours.

For the law of the Spirit of life. Key words. “For” (gar): v. 2 explains why there is no condemnation. “Law” (nomos). This is the pivotal phrase of the chapter, and it raises a fair question: Paul usually means the law of Moses when he says law, so how can a reader be confident that here it means a power or a principle? There are four good reasons.

Why “law” here can mean a ruling power. First, Paul has just used the word this way, several times, in the paragraph immediately before. In 7:21 he says, I find it to be a law: that is, a regular pattern, a fixed principle, that when he wants to do right, evil lies close at hand. In 7:23 he sees another law in his members waging war against the law of his mind and making him captive to the law of sin. A law that wages war and takes prisoners is not a written code; it is a power that rules. The law of sin and death in 8:2 is plainly the same law of sin of 7:23 and 7:25. Second, Paul had already stretched the word the same way in 3:27, where boasting is excluded not by a law of works but by the law of faith: the principle or order of faith. Third, ordinary Greek, like ordinary English, used law for a fixed rule of how things work, as we speak of the law of gravity. Fourth, the two laws in v. 2 are set against each other as rival masters, one freeing from the other. The law of Moses is holy, righteous and good (7:12); it cannot be the law of sin and death in the sense of something evil. So the law of sin and death is the ruling power of sin, which always ends in death; and the law of the Spirit of life is the ruling power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life.

Where Christians differ: does “law” here still mean the law of Moses? Some scholars (for example James Dunn, and in his own way N. T. Wright) argue that both laws are the Mosaic law seen two ways: the law used by sin to produce death (7:8–11), and the same law, now empowered by the Spirit, leading to life. Verdict: there is a real play on words, and Paul is aware that he is using his key word in a surprising way. But the most natural reading, and that of most careful commentators (Calvin, Murray, Moo, Schreiner among them), is that law here means the governing power or authority under which a person lives. Two regimes, two rulers: the reign of sin leading to death, and the reign of the Spirit giving life. This also fits 5:21, where sin reigned in death but grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

Has set you free in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Set free” (ēleutherōsen, aorist tense: a decisive act, done once). Not a process that may or may not succeed, but a liberation that has happened. “In Christ Jesus”: the freedom is located in him. We are free because we are joined to him.

From the law of sin and death. Key words. Sin as a ruling power, and death as its wage and its end (6:23). The two belong together: where sin rules, death follows.

How did the one power set me free from the other? Paul answers in vv. 3–4, which begin with “For”. The liberation has two sides, and both matter. First, the legal side: sin’s claim on us was cancelled. Sin rules in death because the law’s sentence against the sinner stands; God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son (v. 3), so the sentence has been carried out and sin has no legal right left to hold us. This is why v. 2 can explain v. 1: no condemnation, because sin’s grip, which rested on our guilt, has been broken. Second, the living side: the Spirit, who is life, now lives in us (vv. 9–11). By uniting us to Christ in his death and resurrection, the Spirit has ended sin’s reign over us (6:6–7, 14: sin will have no dominion over you), and has given us a new heart with new desires (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that we now want God and can resist sin. A useful picture, often used by preachers: the law of gravity is not repealed when an aircraft flies, but a stronger law, the lift of the wing, overcomes it, as long as the aircraft flies in that power. Sin still pulls; the Spirit is the stronger power.

What it does not mean. Set free from the law of sin does not mean that sin is no longer present, or that the believer no longer struggles. Romans 7:14–25 and Galatians 5:17 describe that struggle honestly. It means sin is no longer the master. We were slaves who had no choice; now we are free people who fight, and who are on the winning side. Nor does it mean freedom from God’s moral law as a guide for life (v. 4; 13:8–10).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh” to v. 1. This was probably copied from v. 4, and makes no condemnation sound conditional on our walk. The earliest manuscripts don’t have it. No condemnation rests on being in Christ, not on our performance. In v. 2, the manuscripts vary between “set you free” (singular, as in the ESV), “set me free” (as in the King James Version) and “set us free”. The singular “you” is probably original: Paul turns from the “I” of chapter 7 and speaks directly to each reader.

In a sentence. Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because through Christ Jesus the ruling power of the Spirit who gives life has set you free from the ruling power of sin that ends in death.

On a Tuesday. No condemnation. None. Whatever you did yesterday, if you are in Christ, God does not condemn you. And sin is no longer your master. When it pulls at you today, you are not a slave obeying a master but a free person resisting an enemy, with a stronger power living in you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. Key words. “Could not do” (to adynaton tou nomou, the impossibility of the law). The law couldn’t save, not because it was bad, but because we were too weak to keep it (7:14–25). It could tell us what is right and condemn us for doing wrong, but it could not give us the power to obey or the forgiveness we need. God did what the law couldn’t.

What Paul means by “the flesh”. This is the first time the word appears in Romans 8, and it runs through the whole first half of the chapter (vv. 3–13), so it is worth understanding well. “Flesh” (sarx) in Paul has a range of meanings. Sometimes it simply means the body’s tissue (2 Corinthians 12:7), or human descent (1:3, Jesus descended from David according to the flesh), or human beings in their frailty (3:20, no flesh will be justified). But in Romans 7–8 and Galatians 5 it carries a deeper, moral meaning: human nature as it is since the fall, living from itself and for itself, apart from God and turned away from him. Several things follow. It is not the body as such: Paul does not think the body is evil, or that sin lives in matter; Christ came in flesh, and our bodies will be raised (v. 11). The flesh includes the mind (v. 6, the mind of the flesh), the will and the desires.
