It is not only bodily appetites such as sex, food and drink; in Galatians 5:19–21 the works of the flesh include jealousy, rivalry, anger and divisions, which are sins of the spirit as much as of the body. It even includes religion done in our own strength: Paul calls his proud law-keeping confidence in the flesh (Philippians 3:3–6). The flesh is the whole self organised around self, trusting self, serving self and ruling self, instead of trusting and serving God. Paul also uses the word for a realm or era: the old age of Adam, under sin and death, in contrast with the new age of the Spirit that came with Christ. So to be in the flesh (vv. 8–9) is to belong to that old realm, unconverted; believers are no longer in the flesh (v. 9). Yet the flesh is still present in believers as a pull, a remaining inclination to sin, against which they fight by the Spirit (v. 13; Galatians 5:16–17). That is why the old NIV translated the word sinful nature: not a perfect translation, but it catches the point. When the flesh appears in vv. 4–13, this is what Paul means.

By sending his own Son. His own Son: pre-existent, sent from heaven.

In the likeness of sinful flesh. Key words. Carefully worded. Not in sinful flesh, since Jesus was sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Not merely in the likeness of flesh, as if his body were unreal. In the likeness of sinful flesh: truly human, subject to weakness, temptation and death, yet without sin. He entered the very realm where sin ruled, in order to defeat it there.

And for sin. The ESV notes that this can also be rendered as a sin offering, like those laid down in Leviticus 4 and foretold in Isaiah 53:10.

He condemned sin in the flesh. Key words. “Condemned” (katekrinen), the verb of the noun in v. 1. Sin was condemned, sentenced and punished, in Christ’s flesh on the cross. That is why there is no condemnation for us: it fell on him. Penal substitution.

In order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. Key words. “Righteous requirement” (to dikaiōma, singular: the just requirement, the righteous demand). Not the many commandments, but the law’s one total demand, the whole of what it requires. “Might be fulfilled” (plērōthē, passive: be fully met). Note that Paul does not say that we might fulfil it, but that it might be fulfilled in us. “In us” (en hēmin), not “by us”.

Where Christians differ: what does it mean that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in us? Readers have long wondered whether Paul means the law’s demand for punishment, carried out on Christ; or the law’s demand for a righteous life, now lived by believers; or both. There are three main views. The first is forensic: the law demanded perfect righteousness, and that demand is fully met for us in Christ, whose obedience and death are counted as ours. Calvin took it this way, and so does Douglas Moo: the passive verb, the singular “requirement”, the word “fulfilled”, and the link with no condemnation all point to something God does, completely, rather than our partial obedience. The second is ethical: the Spirit now enables believers to live the life the law always aimed at, love for God and neighbour. C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner take this view, pointing out that the verse ends by describing the walk of those in whom it is fulfilled, and that v. 4 explains why God sent his Son: not only to forgive us but to change us (Ezekiel 36:27; Jeremiah 31:33). The third holds both together. Notice that the requirement is not mainly punishment: the law’s real demand is righteousness, and the punishment falls on those who fail to give it. Christ met that demand both by his perfect obedience and by bearing the penalty for our disobedience. Verdict: the best reading holds the two together, with the forensic sense as the foundation. In Christ, the law’s whole requirement has been fully met for us, which is why Paul can say “fulfilled” without any qualification, and why it is passive and “in us”: we are in Christ, and what is true of him is counted true of us. And the same union with Christ brings the Spirit, who begins to produce in us the very righteousness the law requires. That is why the verse ends with how we walk. Justification and sanctification are never separated: no one has the first without beginning the second.

But how can it be fulfilled if my obedience is still imperfect? The forensic side answers most of this: in Christ the requirement is fully met now, and nothing can be added to it. But even the ethical side does not claim perfection. Paul says in 13:8–10 that the one who loves another has fulfilled the law, using the same verb, without suggesting that any believer loves perfectly. He means that love is the kind of life the law describes, and that a life of Spirit-produced love is genuinely, if not yet completely, the law’s fulfilment. It is real now, and growing; it will be perfect at glorification, when we are conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29; Philippians 1:6; 1 John 3:2). So Paul looks back to the cross, around at the Spirit’s present work, and forward to glory, all at once.

Who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Key words. “Walk” (peripatousin): live, conduct one’s life step by step. This is not a condition we must meet in order for the requirement to be fulfilled; it is a description of the people in whom it is fulfilled. Everyone in Christ walks by the Spirit, imperfectly but truly. For the flesh, see above.

In a sentence. What the law could not do, because our sinful nature left it powerless, God has done: by sending his own Son, as a real human being like us but without sin, to be a sin offering, he passed sentence on sin in Christ’s own body, so that everything the law rightly requires would be fully met in us, who now live not by our sinful nature but by the Spirit.

For worship. Sin was condemned in Christ’s body, so it cannot condemn you. Everything the law asks of you, Christ has given on your behalf. Now walk by the Spirit, who is making you, day by day, the kind of person the law describes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

parallels.desc: the sin offering

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.

For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh. Key words. Two kinds of people: those who live by the flesh (unconverted) and those who live by the Spirit (converted). For the meaning of the flesh, see on vv. 3–4. “Set their minds” (phronousin): think about, focus on, care about, have one’s outlook shaped by. It means more than thinking; it is the whole direction of a person’s concerns and desires. What you think about, value and pursue shows who you are.

But those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. The Spirit-led mind cares about what God cares about (Colossians 3:1–2; Philippians 4:8): Christ, his word, holiness, his people, his kingdom.

For to set the mind on the flesh is death. Key words. “Death” (thanatos). Notice that Paul does not say it leads to death, but that it is death. In the Bible, death is first of all separation: physical death separates the soul from the body; spiritual death separates the person from God, the source of life. A mind set on the flesh is already in that state now: alive in the body, but dead toward God, unable to know, love or please him (Ephesians 2:1–3, dead in trespasses and sins, while walking in them; 1 Timothy 5:6, she is dead even while she lives). It is a kind of existence, but not the life human beings were made for. And unless God intervenes, this present death ends in physical death and finally in eternal death, the second death (6:23; Revelation 20:14). Paul sees the whole of it as one reality: what begins as separation from God now becomes separation from God for ever.

But to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace. Key words. “Life” (zōē). Not mere existence, but the life of God himself, shared with us: knowing God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3). It is eternal life, begun now and completed in the resurrection (vv. 10–11). It is the life human beings were created for in Eden: life with God, from God and for God. “Peace” (eirēnē). First, peace with God: the war is over, and we are reconciled (5:1, 10), in contrast with the mind of the flesh, which is hostile to God (v. 7). Second, peace within, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, rest, harmony, a life put right, at peace with God, with oneself and with others (Philippians 4:7). Like death, life and peace are present realities that grow into an eternal future.

What it does not mean. Paul is not saying that a Christian who has a worldly thought is spiritually dead, or that our minds are always perfectly set on the Spirit. He is describing two fundamentally different orientations of a whole life. Believers still struggle, but the basic direction of their minds has been changed.

In a sentence. Those who live by the sinful nature have their minds set on what it desires, but those who live by the Spirit have their minds set on what the Spirit desires; for a mind ruled by the sinful nature is already death, cut off from God, while a mind ruled by the Spirit is life with God and peace.

On a Tuesday. What do you think about most, and what do you want most? Set your mind on the things of the Spirit today. Life and peace are not only the reward of heaven; they are what a Spirit-set mind begins to taste now.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God. Key words. For the meaning of the flesh, see on vv. 3–4. Not neutral, but hostile. The unconverted mind is at war with God (5:10; Colossians 1:21).

For it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot. Key words. Not only does not, but cannot. Total inability. The natural person has no power to submit to God (1 Corinthians 2:14; John 6:44).

Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. Key words. Nothing an unconverted person does pleases God, because it doesn’t come from faith and love for him (Hebrews 11:6). Even their good deeds are not done for God’s glory.

Where Christians differ: free will. Arminians hold that God gives everyone enough grace (prevenient grace) to choose to believe. Verdict: Paul says the fleshly mind cannot submit to God. Only the Spirit’s regenerating work makes faith possible (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). This is why salvation is entirely God’s work: he must give new life before we can respond.

In a sentence. The mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God; it does not submit to God’s law, nor can it, and those in the realm of the flesh cannot please God.

For worship. If you love God’s law, it is because the Spirit changed you. You couldn’t have done it yourself. Thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Key words. Believers are no longer in the realm of the flesh (see on vv. 3–4), but in the realm of the Spirit, because the Spirit dwells in them. “Dwells” (oikei): lives at home, permanently. “If in fact” (eiper): not a doubt, but a reminder: since, as is the case.

Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Key words. Every Christian has the Spirit. There is no Christian without the Spirit. No two classes of believers. Note: the Spirit of God (v. 9a) is the Spirit of Christ (v. 9b). The Spirit proceeds from both. Christ is God.

But if Christ is in you. The Spirit in you is Christ in you (Colossians 1:27). The Trinity dwells in the believer (John 14:23).

Although the body is dead because of sin. Key words. “Dead” (nekron). Not a corpse, but mortal: under the sentence of death, as good as dead, certain to die. Death entered the world through sin (5:12), and even the believer’s body still carries that sentence. Christians still grow old, fall ill and die.

The Spirit is life because of righteousness. Key words. “The Spirit is life” (to pneuma zōē). Many readers find this phrase difficult, and translations differ. The King James Version and the 1984 NIV read it as the human spirit: “the spirit is life”, or “your spirit is alive”. The ESV, the 2011 NIV (“the Spirit gives life”) and the CSB read it as the Holy Spirit. Which is right?

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or the human spirit? The case for the human spirit: Paul contrasts body and spirit, two parts of the person, and the believer’s body is dead while their inner self is alive. Verdict: Paul means the Holy Spirit, for four reasons. First, he does not say the spirit is alive (zōn), which would suit the human spirit, but that the Spirit is life (zōē), a noun: the Spirit is life itself, its source. Second, the Spirit has just been called the Spirit of life (v. 2). Third, every other use of spirit in vv. 9–11 means the Holy Spirit, and v. 11, which continues the thought, says that the same Spirit will give life to your mortal bodies. Fourth, Paul’s contrast is not between two parts of a person, but between two powers: sin brings death, the Spirit brings life. So the meaning is: your body is still marked for death because of sin, but the Spirit who lives in you is life, and he gives you life now, which will reach even your body at the resurrection. The result is that the believer, as a whole person, is alive to God already (6:11). So the two readings meet in experience: we are alive inwardly because the Holy Spirit, who is life, lives in us.

Because of righteousness. Key words. “Because of righteousness” (dia dikaiosynēn), set in parallel with “because of sin”. As sin brought death, so righteousness brings life. Here this is mainly the righteousness of justification, God’s verdict that we are righteous in Christ (5:17–21: grace reigns through righteousness leading to eternal life). Because we are justified, the Spirit gives us life. The righteous life he then produces in us follows from this.

In a sentence. You, however, belong not to the realm of the sinful nature but to the realm of the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God lives in you, and anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ; but if Christ is in you, then although your body is still subject to death because of sin, the Spirit, who is life itself, gives you life because you have been made righteous.

On a Tuesday. When your body is weak, ill or ageing, remember both halves of this verse. Your body is mortal because of sin; but the Spirit of life lives in you, and you are already alive to God. The decay is real, but it is not the end of the story (v. 11).

verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.

If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you. Key words. The same Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you. Resurrection power, inside you.

He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies. Key words. The promise of bodily resurrection. As Jesus rose bodily, so will we. Salvation includes the body (v. 23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Matter matters to God.

Through his Spirit who dwells in you. The indwelling Spirit is the guarantee (Ephesians 1:14).

In a sentence. If the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who lives in you.

For worship. Your body will rise. The Spirit in you guarantees it. Treat your body with honour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Heirs with Christ: The Spirit of Adoption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit does not merely set us free from condemnation; he establishes our identity as children of God. "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (v. 15). The word Abba is the intimate Aramaic term for father — the word a child uses at the family table, in the moment of fear, in the unselfconscious familiarity of the parental relationship. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). His Spirit now enables his adopted brothers and sisters to use it too.

The adoption of which Paul speaks is not merely a legal status (though it is that — full legal rights as sons and daughters, co-heirs with Christ). It is a relational reality experienced in the present: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. This inner witness — not our feelings but the Spirit's testimony — is the ground of Christian assurance at the deepest level. When we doubt our standing, when darkness presses in, when God feels distant — the Spirit within is still crying "Abba!" on our behalf.

"Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (v. 17) — the inheritance is nothing less than God himself, shared with the Son. Everything that belongs to Christ by right of his eternal sonship is ours by right of our adoption. This is the logic behind Paul's bewildering statement in 1 Corinthians 3:21 — "all things are yours." The adopted child of God is heir to a universe, co-inheritor of a new creation. The suffering of the present age (v. 17 — "provided we suffer with him") is the path to that glory, not its obstacle.

The section does not begin there, however, and the two verses that open it are the hinge on which the rest turns. Paul first cancels an obligation: we are debtors — but not to the flesh. The old master has no further claim, which means every demand it still makes is made without authority. Then comes the one command in the passage, and it is not gentle: by the Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body (v. 13). This is the letter’s answer to the defeat of chapter 7, and it holds two things together that we habitually separate — the killing is genuinely ours to do, and the power to do it is not ours at all. And verse 14 then supplies the link to everything that follows: those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. The mortification of sin is not the price of sonship. It is the evidence of it, and the family likeness of people who are being led.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and Assurance

The doctrine of adoption (huiothesia) is one of J.I. Packer's great themes in Knowing God: he argues that adoption is a higher privilege than justification, because justification changes our status before the court while adoption brings us into the family. Reformed writing on the Holy Spirit develops the same insight: the Spirit's primary work in the believer is to mediate the Trinitarian relationship — drawing the child into the love that the Father and the Son share, enabling her to cry "Abba" with the same intimacy that the eternal Son has always known. Assurance, at its deepest level, is not confidence in our own faith or our own experience; it is the Spirit-given knowledge that we are beloved children of the Father.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman adoption law in the first century was clear: an adopted son received full legal rights, the old debts were cancelled, the new family name was his, and the inheritance was secured. Paul's readers would have understood immediately the thoroughness of what adoption meant. No second-class status, no probationary period — full sonship, full inheritance, from the moment of adoption. Now: The "spirit of slavery" (v. 15) that produces fear is the functional religion of much nominal Christianity — the haunting sense that God is primarily a demanding judge to be appeased, that our standing depends on our performance, that we must earn our place at the table. Romans 8:15 is the antidote: not slaves, sons. Not fear, Abba. Not earning, inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. — Romans 8:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh. Key words. “Debtors” (opheiletai, people under obligation). We owe the flesh nothing (see on vv. 3–4 for its meaning). It has no claim on us. We owe everything to God, who has given us life by his Spirit.

For if you live according to the flesh you will die. A warning. A life ruled by the flesh shows a person is not truly in Christ, and leads to eternal death.

But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. Key words. “Put to death” (thanatoute, present tense: keep on putting to death). The old word for this is mortification, from the Latin for killing. “The deeds of the body” (tas praxeis tou sōmatos): the sinful practices carried out through the body, under the flesh’s rule, not the body itself. “By the Spirit” (pneumati): by means of the Spirit, as the power by which it is done. “You will live”: this is the life of v. 6, life with God now and eternal life.

What does it mean to put sin to death by the Spirit? Many readers are unsure, and a common view is something like this: the Spirit shows me through God’s word that something is wrong; since the Spirit lives in me, it is now my job to say no; and by saying no I put the deed to death. That is right as far as it goes. There is real, active effort involved: Paul says you put to death, not that you wait for the Spirit to do it while you do nothing. And the Spirit does use his word to show us sin. But the great teachers on this verse add some important things.

John Owen. The fullest treatment of this verse in English is John Owen’s Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656), a short book written entirely on Romans 8:13. Owen made several points. Mortification is not merely stopping an outward act, hiding a sin, or exchanging one sin for another; it is a lifelong weakening of sin’s root, its inner desires, so that it loses its strength and its hold on the heart. It is not achieved by our own vows, rules and resolutions alone, which he said only drive sin underground. It is the Spirit’s work, and the Spirit does it by showing us the guilt and danger of the sin, by setting Christ crucified before us, by giving us faith to rely on Christ’s death and power, and by strengthening us with grace. Yet the Spirit does not do it without us: in Owen’s words, he works in us and with us, not against us or without us. So we must be active: hating the sin, watching for its approach, refusing its first motions, and above all, as Owen put it, setting faith to work on Christ for the killing of your sin. His most quoted line sums it up: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

Other voices. Thomas Chalmers, in his famous sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection, argued that the heart cannot simply be emptied of a love; it can only be freed from one love by a greater love taking its place. Tim Keller often drew on Chalmers: since sin is at root idolatry, loving something more than God, it is put to death most deeply not by gritted teeth alone but by seeing and rejoicing in the greater beauty of Christ, so that the idol loses its attraction. Modern Reformed preachers in Owen’s line, such as John MacArthur and Alistair Begg, likewise stress that the Spirit’s main instrument is the word of God, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and that mortification is daily, practical and never finished in this life.

The means the Spirit uses. Putting it together, the New Testament points to these means. Scripture: knowing God’s word, so that the Spirit can use it to expose and resist sin (Psalm 119:11; Hebrews 4:12). Faith in Christ’s death: reckoning yourself dead to sin and alive to God because you are united to him (6:6, 11). Prayer: asking for the Spirit’s strength, and confessing sin honestly (1 John 1:9). Refusing early: saying no to the first thought, not the last (James 1:14–15). Cutting off opportunities: make no provision for the flesh (13:14; Matthew 5:29–30). Replacing, not only removing: putting on the new self, its love, gratitude and service (Colossians 3:5–14; Ephesians 4:22–32). And fellowship: other believers who know your struggle and pray for you (Hebrews 3:13; James 5:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by our success in killing sin; Paul is describing the life of those already justified, and those who belong to Christ will do this, imperfectly but truly. Nor does it mean harming the body, or rigid self-denial for its own sake (Colossians 2:20–23). And it does not mean waiting passively for the Spirit to take temptation away; by the Spirit, you put to death.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, we have an obligation, but not to our sinful nature, to live as it dictates; for if you live by the sinful nature you will die, but if, by the power of the Spirit, you keep putting to death the sinful practices of the body, you will live.

On a Tuesday. Name the sin you most need to put to death. Then do three things: ask the Spirit for strength, look at Christ crucified for that very sin, and take one concrete step to cut off its opportunities. Don’t negotiate with it.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”

For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. Key words. “For” (gar): v. 14 explains v. 13. Those who by the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body are those who are led by the Spirit. “Led” (agontai, present passive: are being led, continually). The Spirit is the one who leads; we are led. “All”: every believer, not a spiritual elite. In context, being led by the Spirit means being led in holiness: away from the flesh, toward obedience to God and the putting to death of sin. The same is true in Galatians 5:16–25, where being led by the Spirit is set against the works of the flesh and shows itself in the fruit of the Spirit. This is the mark of God’s children.

What it does not mean. Being led by the Spirit here does not mean receiving detailed inner guidance for life’s decisions: which job to take, which house to buy, which person to marry. Many believers read it that way, and then worry that they are not hearing the Spirit, or treat their feelings and impressions as the Spirit’s voice. But that is not Paul’s subject. He is describing what every child of God already experiences: the Spirit drawing them, through his word, to trust Christ, to hate sin, to fight it, and to live for God. God does guide our lives, by his providence, and he gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5; Proverbs 3:5–6). But the way Scripture teaches us to make decisions is by knowing and obeying his revealed word, praying for wisdom, seeking good counsel, and then choosing freely within his will, trusting him with the outcome. A believer who is unsure which car to buy is not therefore unsure whether he is a child of God. Nor does being led mean that the Spirit bypasses Scripture with new revelations; the Spirit leads by the word he inspired, applying it to our hearts, convicting, encouraging and changing our desires.

For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear. Not the fear of a slave before a master, or of a criminal before a judge, which is how people relate to God under the law without grace.

But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons. Key words. “Adoption” (huiothesia). In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, his old debts cancelled, his status changed for ever. Adopted by God: brought into his family, given his name, made his heirs. “Sons”: in the ancient world, sons inherited. Women believers too are “sons” in this sense: full heirs (Galatians 3:26–28).

By whom we cry, Abba! Father! Key words. “Cry” (krazomen, call out, often with deep feeling). “Abba”: Aramaic for Father, the intimate word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Not formal, but warm and close. The Spirit enables us to call God what Jesus called him. The cry of a child running to its father.

In a sentence. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God is a child of God, for the Spirit you received does not make you slaves who live in fear again; he is the Spirit who makes you God’s adopted children, and by him we cry, Abba, Father.

For worship. You are adopted. Call God Abba, Father today, and mean it. And if you are fighting sin and longing to please him, take that as the sign that his Spirit is leading you.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, as if born into the family. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

parallels.desc: sons of the living God

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,

Setting and background. In Roman law, adoption was a formal legal act performed before witnesses, so that if the adoption were ever challenged, for example after the father’s death, the witnesses could testify that it had really taken place. Paul has just spoken of the Spirit of adoption (v. 15), and in the law of Moses a matter was established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). So here are two witnesses to our adoption.

The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit. Key words. “Bears witness with” (symmartyrei, testifies together with). Two witnesses: the Holy Spirit, and our own spirit, our inner self. “Himself” (auto): the Spirit in person.

That we are children of God. Key words. “Children” (tekna). This is the content of the testimony.

Where Christians differ: to whom does the Spirit testify? Many Christians struggle with this verse because they are not sure they hear or feel anything, and wonder whether they lack the Spirit’s witness. One suggested way out is to read it as the Spirit testifying to God the Father that we are his children, rather than testifying to us. It is a thoughtful suggestion, and it has a real foothold: a few verses later the Spirit does speak to the Father on our behalf, interceding for us (vv. 26–27). Verdict: in this verse, though, the witness is given to us. First, the verb means to testify together with: the Spirit’s testimony joins our spirit’s testimony, which only makes sense if our own spirit is also hearing and confessing the truth. Even if the Greek is read as the Spirit testifying to our spirit, the hearer is still us, not the Father. Second, the Father does not need to be told who his children are; the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), since he chose them (v. 29). Third, the context is about our fear and assurance: the Spirit of slavery led to fear, but the Spirit of adoption leads us to cry Abba (v. 15). The witness is for our sake.

How does the Spirit’s witness work? This is the most helpful answer for those who struggle. The witness is not usually a voice, a vision or a special feeling. Look at v. 15: by the Spirit we cry, Abba, Father. Galatians 4:6 says the same: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. The Spirit’s witness is mainly the cry he produces in us: a real, if sometimes weak, trust in God as our Father, a desire to come to him, and confidence that he will receive us for Christ’s sake. When you pray, Father, forgive me for Jesus’ sake, and you mean it, the Spirit is bearing witness with your spirit. He works through the gospel promises, giving us faith to believe them (1 John 5:10–13), and through the new life he produces: love for God’s people (1 John 3:14), obedience (1 John 2:3), and hatred of sin (v. 13). The Westminster Confession (18.2) puts it this way: assurance rests on the divine truth of the promises of salvation, the inward evidence of the graces those promises speak of, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God.

Where Christians differ: a direct witness? Some teachers, including the Puritan Thomas Goodwin, John Wesley and Martyn Lloyd-Jones, held that besides this ordinary witness the Spirit sometimes gives a direct, immediate assurance, an overwhelming sense of God’s love, and they encouraged believers to seek it. Verdict: God may give seasons of special joy and assurance, and believers may thank him for them. But the verse does not make such experiences the test of whether we are God’s children. The normal witness of the Spirit is the one every believer has: faith in Christ’s promises, the cry of Abba, and the fruit of the new life. Do not wait for a feeling before you believe you are God’s child; believe God’s promise, and the Spirit will witness through it.

Where Christians differ: can we be sure? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent) holds that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of being in grace. Verdict: the Spirit himself testifies that we are God’s children. Assurance is the birthright of believers (1 John 5:13; Westminster Confession 18). It may be shaken or weak at times, but it is God’s will that his children know they are his.

In a sentence. The Spirit himself joins his testimony to the testimony of our own hearts that we are God’s children.

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure whether you hear the Spirit’s witness, ask a simpler question: do I, however weakly, turn to God as my Father, trusting Jesus to bring me to him? If you do, that cry is the Spirit’s own witness in you. Believe it.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. — Romans 8:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.

And if children, then heirs. Children inherit.

Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Key words. Heirs of God: we inherit God himself, and all he has. Fellow heirs with Christ: we share his inheritance, the whole world (4:13), the new creation. Everything that belongs to Christ is ours (1 Corinthians 3:21–23).

Provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. Key words. “Provided” (eiper, if indeed, since). “Suffer with him” (sympaschomen). The road to glory goes through suffering, as it did for Christ (Luke 24:26; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 4:13). Does this make the inheritance depend on how much we suffer? No. Paul is not setting a price, but describing the family path: the children share their brother’s road. Suffering with him does not mean that every believer will be martyred, or that suffering earns anything. It covers all that comes to believers because they belong to Christ: opposition, the cost of obedience, and the groaning of living in a fallen world while waiting for glory (vv. 18–23). Every true child of God shares in it in some measure; it is a mark of belonging, not a payment for the inheritance.

In a sentence. If we are children, then we are heirs, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we share in his sufferings so that we may also share in his glory.

For worship. You are a fellow heir with Christ. Your suffering now is the road to sharing his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Future Glory: Groaning, Intercession, and the Golden Chain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The present sufferings are real — Paul does not minimise them — but they are not worth comparing to the glory that is to be revealed (v. 18). The entire creation groans, longing for the liberation that the resurrection of the children of God will bring. The believer groans too, in the Spirit, longing for the full redemption of the body. And the Spirit himself groans on behalf of believers with groanings too deep for words, interceding according to the will of God. Three levels of groaning: creation, believer, Spirit — all pointed toward the same consummation: the full glory of the children of God in the new creation.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (v. 28). This verse has comforted more afflicted souls than almost any other in Scripture — and it has been more abused by careless application than almost any other. Paul is not promising that everything that happens to Christians will feel good or produce obvious benefit. He is promising that the God who is sovereign over all things is working in all things — the good and the bad, the joyful and the painful — toward a single end: the good of those he has called. The suffering is not outside his purposes; it is within them.

The "golden chain" of vv. 29–30 is the most concise summary of the Reformed ordo salutis in Scripture: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, each leading inevitably to the next, with no link missing and none reversible. The glorification is in the past tense — "he also glorified" — because it is as certain as if it had already happened. The God who foreknew in eternity past will glorify in eternity future, and nothing can interrupt the chain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Effectual Calling and the Golden Chain

Romans 8:29–30 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine of election and effectual calling. Foreknowledge here is not merely prior knowledge but prior relational knowing — the same sense in which God "knew" Israel (Amos 3:2) or the Shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:14). Those whom God foreknew with this special, electing love he predestined; those he predestined he called (effectually, inwardly, irresistibly); those he called he justified; those he justified he glorified. The chain is unbreakable. Every link is divine. The reason no one finally falls from grace is not that believers are strong enough to hold on, but that the God who foreknew and called them is powerful enough to keep what he has started.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The groaning of creation in vv. 19–22 draws on the Jewish understanding that the natural world was affected by human sin (Genesis 3:17–18) and will be renewed in the messianic age. Paul extends this vision: not just Israel but the whole creation waits for the redemption of God's children. The gospel is not merely the rescue of souls; it is the renewal of all things. Now: Romans 8:28 is one of the most misused verses in the Christian repertoire — invoked as a quick comfort for minor inconveniences and sometimes grotesquely applied to genuine catastrophe. Used rightly, it is not a promise that things will work out the way we hope; it is the promise of a sovereign God who is working toward his purpose in all things — and his purpose is better than our preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.

For I consider. Key words. “Consider” (logizomai): calculate, the bookkeeping word again. Paul did the sums. He knew suffering well (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).

That the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. Key words. Put them on the scales: sufferings on one side, glory on the other. The glory far outweighs. An eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). “Revealed to us”: or “in us.” We will share it.

In a sentence. Paul considers that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you suffer today, weigh it against the glory to come. It is light by comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope

For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. Key words. “Eager longing” (apokaradokia): watching with outstretched neck, craning to see. The whole universe is waiting on tiptoe for the day when God’s children are revealed in glory.

Does creation really long for anything? No. Rocks, rivers and stars do not have minds or feelings. Paul is using personification: a figure of speech that speaks of non-human things as if they were people, to help us feel a truth. The Bible does this often. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). The earth mourns (Isaiah 24:4). The mountains and hills break into singing, and the trees clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12). The sea roars and the fields exult because the Lord is coming to judge the earth (Psalm 96:11–13), which is the very hope Paul has in view here. And Jesus said that if his disciples were silent, the stones would cry out (Luke 19:40).

Poetic, but not unreal. The picture describes something true. Creation really is not yet what God means it to be. It is in bondage to decay (v. 21): things wear out, die and break down. And its future is really tied to ours: it will be set free when God’s children are revealed in glory. We say a dry field is crying out for rain; the field feels nothing, but the need is real. So here: the whole created order is unfinished, pointing beyond itself. Paul lends it human longing so that we will feel how much is at stake, and so that we will long too (v. 23).

What it does not mean. Not that nature has a soul, or that the earth is a goddess to be honoured; that is the error Paul condemned in 1:25, worshipping the creature rather than the Creator. But also not that the physical world does not matter. God will not scrap his creation; he will renew it and set it free (v. 21; Revelation 21:1–5).

For the creation was subjected to futility. Key words. The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–19). “Futility” (mataiotēti): frustration, emptiness, the word of Ecclesiastes (“vanity of vanities”). Creation can’t fulfil its purpose: decay, disaster, death.

Not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope. Key words. Who is him who subjected it? Not Adam, who had no power to subject creation to anything, nor Satan, who could not do it in hope. It is God, who pronounced the curse on the ground because of Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–19). Creation did not choose its frustration; it was bound up with humanity’s fall, because humanity was meant to rule it. And God subjected it in hope, with its liberation already planned. The curse was never meant to be final.

In a sentence. The creation waits in eager expectation for God’s children to be revealed, for creation was subjected to frustration, not by its own choice, but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope...

For worship. The whole world is waiting for what God will do. So should you.
verseByVerse.note: The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin.

parallels.desc: cursed is the ground because of you

verseByVerse.quote: that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

That the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption. Key words. Creation itself will be liberated. Not destroyed and replaced, but renewed (Acts 3:21; Revelation 21:1–5; Isaiah 65:17). Decay, death and disorder will end.

And obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Creation’s destiny is tied to ours. When God’s children are glorified, creation will be set free with them. This will happen when Christ returns, at the same time as the resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:23, 51–54). Then God will make the new heavens and the new earth (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1).

What are the new heavens and the new earth? The phrase comes from Isaiah (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22) and is taken up by Peter and John (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). “The heavens and the earth” is the Bible’s way of saying the whole universe, as in Genesis 1:1: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. So the promise is a whole renewed creation, not just a better place for souls.

New in what sense? The Greek word for “new” here (kainos) usually means new in kind or quality, rather than brand-new from nothing. Our resurrection bodies are the best guide. They will be our bodies, raised and transformed: sown perishable, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The risen Jesus still bore the marks of the nails (John 20:27). In the same way, the new creation will be this creation, set free (v. 21), and yet so changed that it is truly new. Peter speaks of fire (2 Peter 3:10–12), but he also compares it with the flood, when the world of that time perished (2 Peter 3:6), yet the earth itself remained. The fire purifies and remakes; it does not simply erase.

What will it be like? Scripture gives us glimpses, not a map. God himself will dwell with his people: heaven and earth joined (Revelation 21:3). There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4), and no more curse (Revelation 22:3). It will be a home of righteousness (2 Peter 3:13). We will have real, resurrected bodies, and eat at the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:11; 26:29). God’s servants will serve him and reign (Revelation 22:3–5). The river and the tree of life are there (Revelation 22:1–2): Eden restored, and more than restored, because it is now a city full of the nations, who bring their glory into it (Revelation 21:24–26).

What it does not mean. Not that our final hope is to float on clouds as spirits for ever. When believers die, they go to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), but that is not the end of the story. The final hope is the resurrection of the body in a renewed creation. Nor do we know the details: Revelation’s gold and jewels are pictures of glory, not a building plan. And it is not something we build by our own efforts. God says, I am making all things new (Revelation 21:5). Yet nothing done in the Lord is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Where Christians differ: the future of creation. Some believe the earth will be annihilated and believers will live in a purely spiritual heaven; others (premillennialists) expect a renewed earth in a thousand-year kingdom before the final state. Verdict: Scripture promises that this creation will be set free and renewed at Christ’s return: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Not escape from the material world, but its redemption. The amillennial view sees this as the final state, following Christ’s single return.

In a sentence. ...that the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom and glory of the children of God.

On a Tuesday. God will renew this world. Care for it now, as a sign of what he will do.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.

For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. Key words. Not death throes, but birth pains. The groaning of creation, earthquakes, storms, disease, is not meaningless. It is labour, leading to new birth (Matthew 24:8).

Does creation really groan? Not literally. Creation is not a person: the earth has no mind, and it does not feel pain as a mother in labour does. As in verse 19, Paul is using poetic language, personification, speaking of creation as if it were a person to help us feel a truth (see the note on v. 19). The picture of childbirth says two true things at once. The pain is real: creation really is broken, subject to decay, disease and disaster. And the pain is not pointless: like labour, it is leading somewhere, to the birth of a new creation (v. 21). Then the poetry turns to us: we, who really do feel, groan too (v. 23).

And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly. Key words. The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10). The Spirit is the first instalment of our full salvation (Ephesians 1:14). We groan too: not in despair, but longing.

As we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. Key words. We are adopted now (v. 15), but the full adoption awaits: the resurrection of our bodies. Already, and not yet. The body will be redeemed, bought back from decay.

In a sentence. We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to now, and not only creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our bodies.

For worship. Your groaning is not hopeless. It is labour pains before the birth of a new world.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come.

verseByVerse.quote: For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.

For in this hope we were saved. Key words. Salvation has a future dimension. We were saved, and saved with a hope of what is still to come.

Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? Hope by definition is about what we don’t yet have.

But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. Key words. “Patience” (hypomonēs): endurance, steadfastness. Christian hope produces patient endurance. Not passive waiting, but steadfast living (5:3–4).

In a sentence. In this hope we were saved, but hope that is seen is no hope at all, for who hopes for what they already have? But if we hope for what we do not yet have, we wait for it patiently.

On a Tuesday. What you hope for is not yet seen. Wait for it with patience; it is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. Key words. “Helps” (synantilambanetai): takes hold together with, shares the load. Like someone grabbing the other end of a heavy log.

For we do not know what to pray for as we ought. Key words. An honest admission. Even Paul didn’t always know what to pray. In suffering especially, we don’t know what is best.

But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Key words. The Spirit prays for us, from within. Creation groans (v. 22), we groan (v. 23), and now the Spirit is said to groan too.

What does “too deep for words” mean? The Greek is two words: stenagmois alalētois, “groanings” that are alalētos, literally “not spoken”. It can mean wordless, never put into speech, or unutterable, too deep to be put into speech. Either way, the point is not that God cannot understand them, or that the Spirit is short of words. The point is that this praying happens below the level of our words. Our words fail; his intercession does not. And it is perfectly understood: the Father, who searches hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit (v. 27).

Whose groanings are they? Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes. But he has just said that we groan inwardly (v. 23), and the Spirit is the Spirit who lives in us (vv. 9–11). So many, including Calvin, understand it this way: the Spirit stirs up in our hearts the deep, wordless longings that we cannot express, and takes them up as his own intercession before the Father. Others stress that the Spirit intercedes for us in a way hidden from us altogether. Both agree on the heart of it: the Spirit is praying for us, within us, in line with God’s will. Groaning is also a word borrowed from our experience. It speaks of deep, earnest desire, not of the Spirit being in distress or unable to cope.

What it means in real life. You sit by a hospital bed and cannot find a single sentence to pray. You wake at night with a weight you cannot name, and all you can say is, O God. Your grief over a child, a marriage or your own sin comes out as a sigh or tears. That is not failed prayer. The Spirit takes that wordless longing, and before the Father it becomes a prayer that is exactly right, because the Spirit always asks according to the will of God. You do not have to find the right words to be heard.

What it does not mean. Not that words in prayer do not matter: Jesus gave us words to pray (Matthew 6:9–13), and the Psalms are full of them. Not a secret prayer language that only some believers have (see below). And not that we can stop praying because the Spirit prays instead. He helps us in our weakness (v. 26): he takes the other end of the load, and we keep carrying it with him.

And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit. God the Father knows what the Spirit means. Perfect communication within the Trinity.

Because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God. His prayers are always in line with God’s will, so they are always answered. Two intercessors: Christ at God’s right hand (v. 34), and the Spirit in our hearts.

Where Christians differ: are these groanings tongues? Some see these groanings as speaking in tongues. Verdict: no. They are “too deep for words”, not spoken in any language, and they belong to every believer, since Paul is speaking of all who have the Spirit (vv. 9, 14). Tongues were a spoken gift given to some, not to all (1 Corinthians 12:30). This is the Spirit’s hidden intercession for all God’s children.

In a sentence. In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans, and he who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for God’s people in accordance with God’s will.

For worship. When you don’t know how to pray, the Spirit prays for you. You are never alone in prayer.

parallels.desc: you have searched me and known me

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. — Romans 8:28
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

And we know. Key words. Not hope or guess, but knowledge. Certain.

That for those who love God all things work together for good. Key words. All things: not just good things, but suffering, loss, failure, even sin. Not that all things are good, but that God works them together for good. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.” Either way, God is the one at work. “Good”: defined by v. 29, being made like Christ. Not necessarily comfort, but Christlikeness.

For those who are called according to his purpose. Key words. The promise is for those who love God, and they love him because he called them. His purpose comes first. God’s calling here is effectual: it brings people to faith (v. 30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean everything will turn out the way we want, or that bad things aren’t truly bad. It means that God, in his wisdom, weaves even the worst things into his good purpose for his people. Joseph said it: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

In a sentence. We know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.

On a Tuesday. Whatever is happening to you, God is working it for good, the good of making you like Christ. Trust him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.”

parallels.desc: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good

verseByVerse.quote: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. — Romans 8:29–30
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.

For those whom he foreknew. Key words. “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand. In Scripture, “know” often means to love, to choose (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5; Matthew 7:23). Notice: “those whom” he foreknew, not “what” he foreknew. He foreknew persons, not their faith.

He also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Key words. The goal of predestination: likeness to Christ. God’s plan is to make his children like his Son.

In order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Christ the eldest brother, with a vast family like him.

And those whom he predestined he also called. Effectual calling: the call that brings people to faith.

And those whom he called he also justified. Declared righteous, by faith.

And those whom he justified he also glorified. Key words. The golden chain: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, unbroken. Every person in the first link is in the last. No one drops out. And “glorified” is in the past tense, though future for us: so certain that God speaks of it as done.

Where Christians differ: foreknowledge and predestination. Arminians teach that God foreknew who would believe and predestined them on that basis. Verdict: Paul says God foreknew persons, not their choices; “foreknew” in biblical usage means to set one’s love on beforehand. And the chain is unbroken: all who are called are justified, so the call must be effectual, not merely an invitation many refuse. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (Ephesians 1:4–5; 2 Timothy 1:9). This is unconditional election, and it is the ground of perfect assurance: if God began it in eternity, he will finish it in glory.

In a sentence. Those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters, and those he predestined he also called, those he called he also justified, and those he justified he also glorified.

For worship. From eternity past to eternity future, God holds your salvation in an unbreakable chain. Worship him.
verseByVerse.note: “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — Nothing Can Separate Us from the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a doxology of certainty — a sustained rhetorical climax in which Paul asks a rapid series of questions, answers each in triumph, and then piles up a list of everything in the universe that might be imagined to separate the Christian from the love of God — only to declare that none of it can. This is not wishful thinking; it is the logical conclusion of everything Paul has argued since 1:16. The gospel that justifies the ungodly will not ultimately abandon the justified; the God who did not spare his own Son will certainly spare those for whom his Son died.

"If God is for us, who can be against us?" (v. 31). The answer is not that no one will be against us — Paul has just described tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword (v. 35). The enemies are real. But no enemy, however powerful, can ultimately prevail against those for whom God himself has declared himself as advocate and champion. The "who" of the question is not answered with "no one" but with "it doesn't matter" — because God's being for us outweighs any opposition.

The concluding list — death, life, angels, rulers, things present, things to come, powers, height, depth, anything else in all creation — is Paul's way of saying: I have tried to think of everything, and I cannot think of anything that can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. The love of God is not a feeling that fluctuates with our spiritual temperature; it is the settled, sovereign, covenant commitment of the God who gave his Son for us. That love will not let us go — because it has never been dependent on us to begin with.

Two of the questions in between deserve naming, because they are the ones a troubled conscience actually asks. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? and Who is to condemn? (vv. 33–34). Paul does not answer by denying that there is anything to charge — the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet. He answers by naming who occupies the two seats that matter: it is God who justifies, and the one who might condemn is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is at this moment interceding. The prosecution may say what it likes; the bench and the counsel for the defence are already taken. And then v. 37, which is not a claim that the hardships are avoided: in all these things — the tribulation, the famine, the sword — we are more than conquerors, which means the victory is won inside the trouble rather than by escaping it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Perseverance of the Saints

Romans 8:31–39 is the biblical anchor of the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance (or preservation) of the saints. The saints do not persevere because they are strong; they persevere because God keeps them. The question is not whether we can hold on to God but whether God will hold on to us — and Paul's answer is thunderous. The God who predestined, called, and justified will glorify. Nothing in the universe — not even our own faithlessness — can sever the love that chose us before we existed and purchased us at the cost of the Son. Perseverance is not a human achievement; it is a divine gift, the last link in the golden chain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's list of hardships in v. 35 — tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword — was not hypothetical for his original readers. The Roman church would face Nero's persecution within a decade. Some of them would be burned as torches in Nero's gardens; some would be torn by dogs. Paul writes these verses for people who will need them when the persecution comes. Now: The Christian in the comfortable West reads Romans 8:35–39 as comfort for ordinary difficulties. The Christian in the persecuted church reads it as the word they need to die well. Both readings are valid, and the comfortable Christian is unwise to forget that what sustained the martyrs is the same grace that sustains her — and the same grace may yet be tested in ways she has not anticipated.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?

What then shall we say to these things? Paul draws the conclusion of everything he has said.

If God is for us, who can be against us? Key words. Not that no one opposes us, since many do, but that no opposition can succeed against those God is for.

He who did not spare his own Son. Key words. An echo of Abraham, who did not withhold Isaac (Genesis 22:12, 16). But God went further: he did not spare his Son.

But gave him up for us all. “Gave him up” (paredōken): handed over, to death. “For us all”: all God’s people, those foreknown and called (vv. 29–30).

How will he not also with him graciously give us all things? Key words. The argument from greater to lesser. If God gave the greatest gift, his Son, he will not withhold anything lesser that we need. Every good thing comes with Christ.

In a sentence. What then shall we say in response? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things?

On a Tuesday. God gave you his Son. He will not hold back anything you truly need.

parallels.desc: the LORD is on my side; I will not fear
you have not withheld your son

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.

Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? Key words. A courtroom scene. “God’s elect”: those chosen by God. Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), conscience accuses, others accuse. Can any charge stand?

It is God who justifies. The judge himself has declared them righteous. Who can overturn the Supreme Court?

Who is to condemn? No one, because:

Christ Jesus is the one who died. He paid the penalty.

More than that, who was raised. Proof the payment was accepted.

Who is at the right hand of God. Reigning, in the place of power.

Who indeed is interceding for us. Key words. Four reasons no one can condemn us: his death, resurrection, exaltation, intercession. He pleads his finished work for us continually (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1). Our defence attorney is the judge’s Son, and the one who paid our fine.

In a sentence. Who will bring any charge against those God has chosen? It is God who justifies. Who then can condemn? No one, for Christ Jesus who died, and more than that, was raised to life, is at the right hand of God interceding for us.

For worship. When Satan or your conscience accuses you, point to Christ: he died, rose, reigns and prays for you.

parallels.desc: he who vindicates me is near; who will contend with me?

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, "For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.”

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Key words. The final question. Can anything break Christ’s love for us?

Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? Seven trials, most of which Paul himself endured (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The sword: Paul was later beheaded.

For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. Key words. From Psalm 44:22. Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned us. It has always been the lot of God’s people. Believers are not spared suffering, but they are never separated from Christ’s love in it.

In a sentence. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger or sword? As Scripture says: for your sake we face death all day long; we are considered sheep to be slaughtered.

On a Tuesday. Suffering doesn’t mean Christ has stopped loving you. Nothing can separate you from him.

parallels.desc: for your sake we are killed all the day long

verseByVerse.quote: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

No, in all these things we are more than conquerors. Key words. “More than conquerors” (hypernikōmen): super-conquerors, overwhelmingly victorious. Not by escaping trials, but in them. The trials themselves become servants of our good (v. 28).

Through him who loved us. Key words. Past tense: who loved us, at the cross. The victory is his, shared with us.

What do we conquer? Not people. Paul will soon tell us to bless those who persecute us (12:14), and our enemies are to be loved, not defeated (12:20–21). What we conquer are “all these things”: the list in verse 35 (tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword) and the list in verses 38–39 (death and life, angels and rulers, present and future, powers, height and depth). Behind them stands the accusation of verses 33–34: who shall bring any charge, who is to condemn? Each of these threatens to do one thing: to separate us from the love of Christ, to break our faith, or to prove that God has abandoned us. To conquer them is for them to fail at that.

In what way do we conquer? Not in the way the world means. Verse 36 has just quoted Psalm 44: for your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. Sheep led to slaughter do not look like conquerors. Yet that is exactly who Paul calls conquerors. We win, not by escaping these things, but in them. Three things happen.

1. They cannot separate us from God’s love. A persecutor can take your freedom, your health or your life, but not your Saviour (vv. 38–39). The thing these enemies were trying to do, they cannot do.

2. They are made to serve us. God works all things together for good (v. 28). Suffering produces endurance, character and hope (5:3–5), and our light, momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). The enemy is turned into a servant.

3. Even death becomes gain. For Paul, to die was to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:21–23). The last enemy, which seems to win, opens the door home (1 Corinthians 15:54–57).

Why “more than” conquerors? An ordinary conqueror wins the battle but is often wounded by it, and loses something. The believer loses nothing that finally matters, and gains from the very battle: the enemy ends up serving him. And the victory is secure before the battle even starts, because Christ has already won it: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33; Colossians 2:15). Revelation gives the same picture: the saints conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (Revelation 12:11). They conquered by dying faithful.

What it looks like. A Christian with cancer whose body weakens while her trust in Christ grows deeper. Believers in prison for their faith who sing, as Paul and Silas did at midnight (Acts 16:25). A grieving father who still says, the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord (Job 1:21). Paul himself, chained in Rome, writing the most joyful of his letters. None of them escaped. All of them conquered.

What it does not mean. Not triumphalism: that Christians will be healthy, wealthy and successful, or that the church will win every battle in society. Not that we will always feel victorious: Paul once despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Our feelings may say defeat while the fact is victory. And not that the victory is our own strength or courage. It is through him who loved us. Christ’s love holds us; we do not hold ourselves.

In a sentence. In every hardship we do more than survive: through Christ, who loved us, none of these things can separate us from him, and God turns them to our good.

For worship. In your trials, you are more than a conqueror through Christ who loved you.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For I am sure. Key words. “Sure” (pepeismai): persuaded, convinced. A settled conviction.

That neither death nor life. Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen. Death can’t; it brings us to Christ. Life can’t, with all its trials and temptations.

Nor angels nor rulers. Spiritual powers, good or evil.

Nor things present nor things to come. Nothing in the present or the future.

Nor powers, nor height nor depth. Perhaps astrological terms, the stars thought to rule human fate. Or simply: nothing above, nothing below.

Nor anything else in all creation. Key words. Everything that is not God is created. Nothing created can overpower the Creator’s love. Including ourselves: we are part of creation too.

Will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Key words. The love of God is found in Christ. As long as we are in him, we are in that love, for ever.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Some hold that, though nothing outside us can separate us, we can separate ourselves by turning away. Verdict: “nor anything else in all creation” includes us. And the chain of vv. 29–30 ensures that all who are justified are glorified. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his own, and they persevere because he keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). It is not a licence for carelessness, but the ground of joyful, confident obedience.

In a sentence. For Paul is convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Nothing in all creation can separate you from the love of God in Christ. Nothing. Rest in it.
verseByVerse.note: Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen.

By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,<sup>4</sup>in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.<sup>5</sup>For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.<sup>6</sup>For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.<sup>7</sup>For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot.<sup>8</sup>Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.<sup>9</sup>You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. 9.title: The Sovereignty of God in Election
9.overview:
Romans 9 is one of the most contested chapters in the Bible — and one of the most important. Having concluded chapter 8 with the ringing assurance that nothing can separate the called from the love of God, Paul faces an obvious and agonising question: what about Israel? If God's purposes cannot fail, why has the covenant people largely rejected their Messiah? Has the word of God failed (v. 6)? The question is not merely theological; it is personal — Paul carries a great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen (v. 2).

Paul's answer operates at two levels.
