At the level of Israel's history, he demonstrates that God has always worked through election within the covenant community — not all of Abraham's descendants, but Isaac; not both of Isaac's sons, but Jacob. The principle of sovereign election is not new to the new covenant; it has always been God's method. At the level of theological principle, Paul defends the justice and freedom of God in election with arguments from Exodus and from the potter-and-clay image of Jeremiah — arguments that have made comfortable readers deeply uncomfortable for twenty centuries, and that are meant to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before Paul addresses the theological question, he opens his heart. "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." This is not rhetoric; this is the visceral grief of a man who loves his people with a love that has been intensified, not diminished, by his encounter with Jesus Christ. The apostle who will argue the sovereignty of divine election without flinching is also the apostle who weeps for the lost.

The catalogue of Israel's privileges in vv. 4–5 is breathtaking in its scope: adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises, patriarchs, and — the climax — the Christ himself, who is God over all, blessed forever. Israel's advantages are not nothing; they are everything. The tragedy Paul mourns is not that Israel never had the gospel; it is that the Messiah came from Israel and was rejected by Israel. The most profound privilege in history became the most profound irony in history.

The emotional weight of this opening is deliberate. Paul is not a cold Calvinist dispensing doctrinal tablets from a safe distance. He is a broken-hearted evangelist who would, if it were possible, exchange his own eternal security for the salvation of his kinsmen. That passion drives the theological argument that follows — the question is not academic but is drenched in tears.
verseByVerse.theology:
Evangelistic Passion and Doctrinal Conviction

Romans 9:1–3 demonstrates that a robust doctrine of divine sovereignty in election does not produce indifference toward the lost. Paul believed in unconditional election (v. 11) and still ached for the salvation of those he loved. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that election is the encouragement of mission, not its enemy: we preach because God has people everywhere (Acts 18:10), and because the means he uses to call the elect is the preaching of the gospel. Paul's tears and Paul's theology belong together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's list of Israel's covenant privileges was designed to prevent any glib dismissal of Jewish unbelief — as though Israel had simply missed something obvious. The privileges were real, the access was extraordinary, and the rejection of the Messiah was therefore the greater tragedy. Now: The Christian who has grown up in a church family, heard the gospel from childhood, been surrounded by every means of grace, and yet has never personally trusted Christ is in a position analogous to the Israel Paul mourns. Privilege does not save; it only deepens accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit— — Romans 9:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—

Meaning first. Romans 9–11 answers the question that chapter 8 raises. If nothing can separate God’s elect from his love, what about Israel? God made promises to Israel, yet most Jews have rejected their Messiah. Has God’s word failed? If it failed for them, how can we trust it for us? Paul answers in three steps. In chapter 9, God’s word has not failed, because his promise was never to every physical descendant of Abraham but to the children of promise, chosen by his free mercy: Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau (vv. 6–13). God is not unjust in choosing, for mercy is his to give, and no one has a claim on it (vv. 14–24). The Old Testament itself foretold both the calling of Gentiles and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 25–29). In chapter 10, Israel is responsible for its unbelief: it sought righteousness by works and stumbled over Christ, the stumbling stone (9:30–10:21). In chapter 11, God has not rejected his people: there is a remnant now, and a future fullness, and all of it ends in praise of the unsearchable wisdom of God. Chapter 9 is the Bible’s fullest teaching on God’s sovereign election, and Paul writes it with tears.

Setting and background. Paul was a Jew, a Pharisee, and the apostle to the Gentiles. Some Jews accused him of abandoning his people (Acts 21:21, 28). The Roman church had Jewish and Gentile believers, and Gentiles were tempted to look down on Jews (11:18–20). So Paul opens with a solemn oath of love for Israel before he says hard things.

I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying. Key words. A double oath, positive and negative. “In Christ”: as one united to Christ, speaking in his presence. Paul is not exaggerating for effect.

My conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit. Key words. Conscience (Greek syneidēsis, co-knowledge, the inner witness) is a second witness, and it speaks under the Spirit’s guidance. The law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Paul brings them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul turned against his people when he preached to Gentiles. The doctrine of election that follows is not spoken coldly; it comes from a heart breaking for the lost.

In a sentence. Paul solemnly swears in Christ, with his conscience confirming it by the Holy Spirit, that what he is about to say about his love for Israel is true.

On a Tuesday. Hard truths should be spoken by people who love those they speak to. Before you correct, make sure your heart is grieved, not proud.

verseByVerse.quote: that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.

That I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. Key words. Sorrow (lypē) and anguish (odynē, pain like a wound) that never stop. The man who has just sung that nothing can separate him from God’s love (8:39) carries a constant grief. Joy in God and grief for the lost live together in a healthy Christian heart.

For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ. Key words. “Accursed” is anathema, something devoted to God for destruction (the Old Testament ḥerem, Joshua 6:17). “I could wish” is a carefully chosen form in Greek: it expresses a wish that he knows cannot be granted, since he has just said nothing can separate him from Christ. But if it were possible, he would be willing.

For the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. Key words. Fellow Jews, his own flesh and blood. Paul echoes Moses, who prayed that God would blot him out of his book rather than destroy Israel (Exodus 32:32). Both men show the heart of Christ, who actually was made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that one person can be damned in place of another, or that Paul’s salvation was uncertain. Only Christ could bear the curse for others, and he did. Paul is expressing the depth of his love, not offering a real exchange.

In a sentence. Paul has great sorrow and constant pain in his heart, so much that, if it were possible, he would be willing to be cursed and cut off from Christ if it would save his fellow Jews.

For worship. Ask God for a heart like this for those you love who do not know Christ. Then pray for them by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — devoted to destruction.

parallels.desc: Moses: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.

They are Israelites. Key words. Not just Jews but Israelites, the honoured covenant name, from Jacob, renamed Israel when he wrestled with God (Genesis 32:28). Paul lists eight privileges (vv. 4–5), which make their unbelief all the more tragic.

The adoption. Key words. Israel was God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1). This national sonship was a privilege and a picture, pointing to the full adoption of all believers in Christ (8:15).

The glory. Key words. The Shekinah, God’s visible glorious presence, in the cloud and fire, the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11).

The covenants. Key words. Plural: with Abraham, at Sinai, with David, and the promised new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Some early manuscripts read the singular, the covenant, but the plural is well supported and fits the list.

The giving of the law. Key words. One Greek word, nomothesia: the event at Sinai when God spoke his law to them. No other nation had laws so righteous (Deuteronomy 4:8).

The worship. Key words. Latreia: the priestly service of tabernacle and temple, the sacrifices God himself had appointed.

And the promises. Key words. Above all, the promises of the Messiah and of salvation.

In a sentence. They are Israelites; theirs were the sonship as God’s people, the glory of his presence, the covenants, the law given at Sinai, the temple worship and the promises.

On a Tuesday. Privileges do not save. Being raised in a Christian home or church is a great gift, but it is not the same as faith. Do not trust in your privileges; trust in the Christ they point to.
verseByVerse.note: “The glory” is God’s glorious presence among his people, as in the tabernacle and temple.

parallels.desc: Israel is my firstborn son

verseByVerse.quote: To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. — Romans 9:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

To them belong the patriarchs. Key words. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers to whom God made the promises.

And from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ. Key words. The greatest privilege. The Messiah was a Jew. “According to the flesh”: by his human descent (1:3). The phrase implies there is more to him than his human descent, which Paul now says.

Who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. Key words. A clear statement that Christ is God. Having said what Christ is according to the flesh, Paul says what he is beyond the flesh: God over all.

Textual note: the punctuation. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so the sentence can be divided in more than one way. The ESV text reads it as referring to Christ. Its footnote gives alternatives that make it a separate praise of God the Father, such as: Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever. Verdict: The ESV text is right. The natural flow of the Greek joins “who is” to the Christ just named; “according to the flesh” calls for a contrast; and Paul’s separate blessings of God normally put “blessed” first, which here it does not. Most of the church fathers read it this way. It fits the New Testament’s plain teaching that Jesus is God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Son replaces the Father, or that the Father and the Son are the same person. The Son is God over all together with the Father and the Spirit, one God in three persons.

In a sentence. Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them, as far as his human descent goes, comes the Messiah, who is God over all, forever praised. Amen.

For worship. The Jesus who was a Jewish man is God over all. Bless him forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes alternative punctuations, such as “Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever”; the ESV text calls Christ God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–29 — God's Sovereign Choice: Election and the Potter's Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But it is not as though the word of God has failed" (v. 6). Paul's answer to the crisis of Israel's unbelief begins here, and it begins with a bold reframing: the apparent failure of Israel is not evidence that God's word has failed, but evidence that God's word always operated by election within the covenant people. "Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." Physical descent never automatically conferred covenant membership; God's sovereign choice always determined the true Israel within the physical Israel.

The examples cascade: Isaac, not Ishmael. Jacob, not Esau — chosen before either had done anything, "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (vv. 11–12). The principle is starkly stated: election is unconditional — it precedes any human act or merit. It rests on God's sovereign call, not on human lineage, religious achievement, or anticipated faithfulness. The citation of Malachi 1:2–3 — "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" — is the Old Testament's own statement of the unconditional nature of God's electing love.

The potter-and-clay image of vv. 19–23 (drawn from Jeremiah 18 and Isaiah 29, 45) is Paul's defence of God's sovereign right to do as he wills with his own creation. The objection — "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?" — is met not with a philosophical solution to the problem of compatibilism but with a reminder of creaturely status: who are you, O man, to answer back to God? This is not a retreat from argument; it is the recognition that the creature's moral expectations of the Creator reveal a confusion about the fundamental relationship between the two. God does not owe explanation to clay.

Between the patriarchs and the potter stand two verses this section cannot be understood without. Paul raises the objection himself — Is there injustice on God’s part? (v. 14) — and answers it not with a theory but with a quotation: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (v. 15, from Exodus 33:19). Those words were spoken to Moses at the golden calf, when Israel had just forfeited everything and Moses asked to see God’s glory. What God showed him was his freedom to be merciful. So the sentence that sounds coldest here was originally God’s answer to a plea for a nation that deserved destruction, and it was good news.

Then Pharaoh (vv. 17–18), who cannot be passed over. God tells him, For this very purpose I have raised you up, and Paul draws the conclusion at its hardest: he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. Two things must be said and both are in the text. Exodus says God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Exodus also says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, repeatedly and deliberately, and Paul is not unaware of either.

And v. 16 has already ruled out the comfortable escape: it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. Nobody is saved by wanting it hard enough or trying hard enough. That sentence closes a door on self-salvation, which is the only door it was ever meant to close.

The vessels of vv. 22–23 repay close reading, because Paul breaks the symmetry on purpose. The vessels of mercy he has prepared beforehand for glory — God is named as the one who did it. The vessels of wrath are simply prepared for destruction, with no agent named at all. Paul had the grammar available to say God prepared them, and he did not use it. Alongside that stands the strangest word in the sentence: God has endured with much patience the vessels of wrath. Whatever else this passage teaches, it does not describe a God impatient to destroy.

And the section does not end with the potter; it ends with four quotations, which is where its whole emotional direction turns. Verse 24 finally names the point of the argument — even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles. Then Hosea, twice (vv. 25–26): those called not my people will be called sons of the living God — words originally spoken about Israel’s own rejection and restoration, now stretched to take in outsiders.

Then Isaiah, on the remnant (vv. 27–28). And finally Isaiah 1:9 (v. 29), which does not say what a modern reader expects: not only a remnant was left, as though God were rationing, but that if the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom. The survival of anyone at all is the mercy. Read the chapter from that last verse backwards and the question changes shape — it stops being why are some passed over, and becomes why is anybody here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unconditional Election

Romans 9:6–29 is the primary New Testament text for the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election — God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation, made before the foundation of the world, based not on foreseen faith or merit but on his own good pleasure and purpose. Calvin devoted extensive treatment to this chapter in the Institutes (III.21–24), arguing that to make election conditional on foreseen faith is to make the grace of God a reward for human initiative, which contradicts the very nature of grace. The alternative — that God elects on the basis of his own sovereign love, working through human responsibility — is the only framework that gives glory entirely to God and hope entirely from God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The examples of Isaac/Ishmael and Jacob/Esau were drawn from Israel's founding narratives — stories every Jewish reader knew by heart. Paul was not importing foreign principles; he was showing that the principle of sovereign election was embedded in Israel's own origin story. The God who chose Jacob over Esau before either was born is the same God who has, in Christ, gathered a people from both Jews and Gentiles by the same sovereign grace. Now: The doctrine of unconditional election produces, in those who receive it, either rebellion ("that's not fair") or worship ("why me, Lord?"). The second response is the correct one. The person who asks "Why was I chosen?" and finds no answer in herself has understood the doctrine — and is on her knees.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”

But it is not as though the word of God has failed. Key words. The theme of chapters 9–11. “Failed” (ekpiptō) means fallen down, like a flower dropping or a ship running aground. God’s promise has not fallen short.

For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel. Key words. The answer. There are two Israels: the physical nation descended from Jacob, and within it the true Israel, those chosen and called by God. The promise was always to the second. Paul said something similar in 2:28–29: a true Jew is one inwardly.

And not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring. Key words. Physical descent from Abraham did not make someone a child of the promise. Abraham had two sons in Genesis, Ishmael and Isaac (and later more by Keturah), but only one carried the promise.

But “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” Key words. Paul quotes Genesis 21:12. God told Abraham that the line of promise would come through Isaac, not Ishmael. Ishmael was Abraham’s son and was blessed, but he was not the heir of the covenant.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s promise to Israel was a trick. It does not mean that being a physical Jew counts for nothing (3:1–2; 11:28–29). It means that God never promised to save every descendant of Abraham, and so the unbelief of many Jews does not cancel his word.

In a sentence. It is not that God’s word has failed: not everyone descended from Israel is true Israel, and not all Abraham’s descendants are his true children; rather, as God said, his offspring would be counted through Isaac.

On a Tuesday. When it looks as if God’s promises have failed, look again at what he actually promised. He always keeps his word, though not always in the way we expected.

parallels.desc: through Isaac shall your offspring be named

verseByVerse.quote: This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: "About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”

This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God. Key words. Ishmael was a child of the flesh: born by ordinary human means, when Abraham and Sarah tried to get the promised son by their own plan through Hagar (Genesis 16). Natural birth does not make a child of God.

But the children of the promise are counted as offspring. Key words. Isaac was born by God’s promise and power, to a barren woman past age (Galatians 4:23, 28). “Counted” (logizomai, the same word used for righteousness being counted in chapter 4) means reckoned by God’s decision. Being God’s child depends on God’s word, not human descent or effort.

For this is what the promise said. Key words. Paul quotes from Genesis 18:10 and 14. God named the time and the son before Isaac was conceived.

What it does not mean. Someone might object: Ishmael was the son of a slave, so of course Isaac was chosen; the difference lay in the mothers. Paul answers that in the next example, where the sons have the same mother and father, and are even twins.

In a sentence. So it is not the children born naturally who are God’s children, but the children born by God’s promise who are counted as Abraham’s offspring, for God’s promise was, “At this time next year I will come back, and Sarah will have a son.”

For worship. If you are a child of God, you were born by his promise and power, not by your own effort. Thank him for his word that made you his.

parallels.desc: Sarah shall have a son

verseByVerse.quote: And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls —
verseByVerse.commentary:
And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—

And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac. Key words. A stronger example. Same father, same mother, conceived together: twins (Genesis 25:21–26). Nothing about their birth made a difference between them.

Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad. Key words. God spoke before their birth, before either had done anything. So his choice cannot have been based on their deeds.

In order that God’s purpose of election might continue. Key words. “Purpose” (prothesis, as in 8:28) and “election” (eklogē, choosing out) together: God’s purpose that works by choosing. “Might continue” (menō, remain, stand): God timed his word so that it would be plain that his choice stands on his purpose alone.

Not because of works but because of him who calls. Key words. The basis of election is not anything in the person, but God who calls. Calling here is God’s effective summons, as in 8:30.

Where Christians differ: election based on foreseen faith. Arminian teachers say God chose people because he foresaw that they would believe; others say election here is only about nations or roles in history, not individual salvation. Verdict: Paul’s point excludes foreseen faith. If God had chosen Jacob because he foresaw Jacob’s faith, Paul would simply say so, and the objection of verse 14 (is God unjust?) would never arise. Paul says the choice was made before they had done anything, good or bad, and not by works but by him who calls. Faith is not the cause of election but its fruit (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). And though Jacob and Esau stand at the head of nations, Paul uses them to answer a question about individual salvation: why some Jews are saved and others are not (vv. 1–6, 24, 27). This is unconditional election (Westminster 3.5; Canons of Dort 1.7–10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is arbitrary or that his choice is random. His reasons are hidden in his own wisdom and love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). It does not mean human choices do not matter; Esau truly despised his birthright (Hebrews 12:16).

In a sentence. And there is more: Rebekah’s twins had the same father, our ancestor Isaac, yet before they were born or had done anything good or bad, so that God’s purpose in choosing might stand, based not on works but on God who calls,

On a Tuesday. Your salvation does not rest on your record. It rests on God’s purpose, which was settled before you did anything. That is humbling, and it is a firm place to stand.

verseByVerse.quote: she was told, "The older will serve the younger." As it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
she was told, “The older will serve the younger.” As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

She was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Key words. From Genesis 25:23. God reversed the normal order, in which the firstborn has the leading place. Esau was born first, but Jacob received the blessing.

As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Key words. Paul quotes Malachi 1:2–3, written centuries later, when God pointed to his covenant love for Israel (Jacob’s descendants) and his judgement on Edom (Esau’s descendants). Paul uses it to confirm that God’s choice of Jacob over Esau was his free, sovereign love.

Hated. Key words. In Hebrew idiom, “love” and “hate” in a comparison can mean choosing one and not the other, loving one and loving the other less (Genesis 29:30–31; Luke 14:26). The ESV note says so. So “hated” here means first of all that God did not choose Esau for covenant love. But it is not merely neutral: in Malachi, Edom is under God’s just anger for its wickedness (Malachi 1:4).

Where Christians differ: individuals or nations. Some say verses 10–13 speak only of nations (Israel and Edom) and earthly roles, not eternal salvation. Verdict: The original prophecies did concern the nations that came from the two brothers. But Paul applies the principle to individuals and to salvation, because that is his question: why some Israelites are saved and others are not (vv. 3, 6, 22–24). And nations are made up of individuals. Jacob and Esau themselves illustrate God’s choice of persons. The objection that follows (v. 14) only makes sense if Paul is teaching unconditional individual election.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God hates people as a cruel tyrant, or that Esau was condemned for no reason. All are sinners, and none deserve mercy. God’s choosing of some is pure grace; his passing over of others leaves them to their own just deserts.

In a sentence. Rebekah was told the older would serve the younger, just as Scripture says, “I loved Jacob, but I rejected Esau.”

For worship. If God has set his love on you, it was not because you were better than others. Bow, and thank him for his free love.
verseByVerse.note: “Hated” in Hebrew idiom can mean “loved less” or “passed over” — here, not chosen.

parallels.desc: the older shall serve the younger
I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! For he says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means! For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”

What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? Key words. The natural objection. If God chooses one twin and not the other, before either has done anything, isn’t that unfair? The fact that Paul raises this objection shows he is teaching unconditional election. No one would accuse God of injustice for choosing those he foresaw would believe.

By no means! Key words. Mē genoito, Paul’s strongest denial (as in 3:4; 6:2). God cannot be unjust.

For he says to Moses. Key words. Paul answers from God’s own words in Exodus 33:19, spoken when Moses asked to see God’s glory, right after Israel’s sin with the golden calf. Israel deserved destruction. God spared them by mercy.

“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Key words. God’s mercy is his to give freely. Mercy by its nature is undeserved. If it were owed, it would be justice, not mercy. So God is not unjust when he gives mercy to some and not to others. No one is treated worse than they deserve; some are treated far better.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has no reasons, or that he enjoys the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). It means the reason for his mercy lies in himself, not in us.

In a sentence. What should we say then? Is God unjust? Absolutely not! For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whoever I choose to have mercy on, and compassion on whoever I choose to have compassion on.”

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to say God is unfair, remember: you do not want fairness. Fairness is judgement. You need mercy, and it is his to give.

parallels.desc: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious

verseByVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

So then it depends not on human will or exertion. Key words. The conclusion. “Will” (thelō, desire, choice) and “exertion” (trechō, running, the image of a race): salvation does not finally rest on human choosing or striving. Esau wanted the blessing and ran to hunt game for it (Genesis 27), but did not get it.

But on God, who has mercy. Key words. Salvation rests finally on God’s mercy. We do will and run, but only because God has first worked in us to will and to work (Philippians 2:13).

For the Scripture says to Pharaoh. Key words. The other side: hardening. Paul quotes Exodus 9:16. Notice “the Scripture says”: what Scripture says, God says.

For this very purpose I have raised you up. Key words. God brought Pharaoh onto the stage of history, made him king, and kept him standing through the plagues.

That I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. Key words. God’s purpose was to display his power and glory through Pharaoh’s defeat. It worked: Rahab in Jericho had heard of it forty years later (Joshua 2:10), and so did the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean human choices are fake or that we should not repent and believe. The gospel commands everyone to believe (10:9–13). It means that when anyone does believe, the credit goes to God’s mercy, not their own wisdom.

In a sentence. So it does not depend on human desire or effort, but on God’s mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh, “I raised you up for this purpose: to show my power through you and to make my name known throughout the world.”

For worship. If you have run to Christ, praise the mercy that made you run.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”

So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. Key words. The two sides of God’s sovereignty, drawn from the two quotations: mercy (Moses) and hardening (Pharaoh). To harden (sklērynō) is to make stubborn, unresponsive.

How God hardens. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12; 10:20), and God foretold it before any plague (Exodus 4:21). Both are true. God does not put evil into a good heart. He hardens by withholding the softening grace that would melt the heart, and by giving sinners over to the sin they already love (1:24, 26, 28). Pharaoh freely chose his stubbornness and was fully guilty; God judicially confirmed him in it. The Westminster Confession says that God, for sinners already sinful, withholds his grace and gives them over to their own lusts (5.6).

You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” Key words. The second objection. If God decides who is hardened, how can he blame anyone? Again, the objection only arises because Paul really is teaching that God decides. No one asks this of an election based on foreseen faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God makes people sin against their will or forces innocent people to reject him. No one who wants God is turned away (John 6:37). The hardened are sinners who do what they want.

In a sentence. So God has mercy on whom he chooses and hardens whom he chooses. Then someone will say to Paul, “Why does God still blame us? Who can resist what he wills?”

On a Tuesday. Do not play with sin, thinking you can repent later. Repeatedly refusing God hardens the heart, and God may give you over to it. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15).
verseByVerse.note: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it.

verseByVerse.quote: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, "Why have you made me like this?" Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?

But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Key words. Paul does not give a philosophical answer. He rebukes the attitude behind the question. “Answer back” (antapokrinomai) means talking back, arguing with God as if he owed us an account. Job learned the same lesson (Job 38–42; 40:2).

Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” Key words. From Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9. A clay pot has no rights against its potter. We are creatures; God is the Creator. He is not answerable to us.

Has the potter no right over the clay. Key words. “Right” is exousia, authority. The image comes from Jeremiah 18:1–6, where God reshapes Israel as he wills.

To make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use. Key words. The same lump: all humanity, all alike sinful in Adam (5:12). From it God makes some vessels for honour (salvation) and leaves others for dishonour (judgement). The lump is not innocent clay; it is fallen humanity, already deserving wrath. God wrongs no one by showing mercy to some.

Where Christians differ: double predestination. Some say God chooses only to save, and the lost simply choose damnation without any decree. Others (hyper-Calvinists) say God creates people in order to damn them and causes their sin in the same way he causes faith. Verdict: Scripture teaches that God decrees both: he elects some to life, and he passes by the rest and ordains them to wrath for their sin (Westminster 3.3, 3.7). But the two are not symmetrical. God works faith in the elect by his Spirit; he does not work sin in the reprobate. The saved owe everything to grace; the lost owe their condemnation entirely to their own sin. Hold the mystery with humility, as Paul does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is a tyrant who enjoys destruction, or that we should not ask God honest questions. The psalms are full of honest questions. Paul forbids not the question but the accusation: the creature putting the Creator on trial.

In a sentence. But who are you, a mere human, to talk back to God? Should a clay pot say to its maker, “Why did you make me like this?” Doesn’t the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one pot for honourable use and another for common use?

For worship. Bow before God’s right to rule. He is the potter; you are the clay. And remember: the hands that shape you were pierced for you.

parallels.desc: shall the potter be regarded as the clay?

verseByVerse.quote: What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory —
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—

What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power. Key words. God has good purposes in permitting evil and judging it. He wants his holy wrath against sin and his power to be seen, as with Pharaoh.

Has endured with much patience vessels of wrath. Key words. Yet he puts up with sinners for a long time. He did with Pharaoh through ten plagues, and with the Canaanites for four hundred years (Genesis 15:16). His patience gives time for repentance (2:4; 2 Peter 3:9).

Prepared for destruction. Key words. Notice the grammar. The Greek participle (katērtismena) is passive, and Paul does not say who prepared them. They are ripe for destruction, fitted for it by their own sin. Contrast the next phrase, where Paul says God prepared the vessels of mercy.

In order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy. Key words. The ultimate goal. God’s patience with the wicked and his judgement of them show the vessels of mercy what they were saved from, and so make his grace shine brighter.

Which he has prepared beforehand for glory. Key words. Here the verb is active, and God is the subject: he prepared them beforehand (proētoimasen), as in Ephesians 2:10. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish. The difference in grammar is deliberate: God is the author of salvation, but not the author of sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the cause of sin. It does not mean we can know who the vessels of wrath are, or that anyone who wants to repent is barred. We do not know who is elect; we preach to all.

In a sentence. What if God, wanting to show his anger and make his power known, has been very patient with the objects of his wrath, ready for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory to the objects of his mercy, whom he prepared in advance for glory?

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a vessel of mercy, prepared for glory. Live like it, and be patient with sinners, as God was with you.

verseByVerse.quote: even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
verseByVerse.commentary:
even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?

Even us whom he has called. Key words. The vessels of mercy are identified: we, whom God has effectually called (8:30). Election is not abstract. It shows in a real church, made of real people who were called by the gospel and came.

Not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles? Key words. God’s choice crosses the boundary of race. This brings Paul back to his question about Israel: God’s purpose never was to save every Jew, but to call out a people from Jews and Gentiles alike.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has abandoned the Jews. Paul himself is a Jew who was called. Chapter 11 will show there is still a remnant, and a future for Israel.

In a sentence. Those objects of mercy include us, whom he called, not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles.

For worship. Look around your church at the different backgrounds and races. Each one was called by the same God. Praise him for his wide mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: As indeed he says in Hosea, "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" "And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved.’” “And in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’”

As indeed he says in Hosea. Key words. Paul now shows that the Old Testament foretold both the calling of Gentiles (vv. 25–26) and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 27–29). He quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10.

Those who were not my people I will call “my people.” Key words. Hosea’s children were given names of judgement: Lo-ammi, not my people, and Lo-ruhamah, not loved (Hosea 1:6, 9). God promised to reverse those names.

How Paul uses Hosea. Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel, who by their idolatry had become like pagans. Paul applies the words to Gentiles. This is not misuse. Israel had become like the nations, and so the principle is the same: God can make a people out of those who are not a people, by sheer grace. Peter applies the same words to Gentile believers (1 Peter 2:10).

And in the very place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they will be called “sons of the living God.” Key words. God’s grace reaches the very place of rejection and makes outsiders sons. This is adoption.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the northern tribes have no part in the promise; Hosea’s words are fulfilled in the church made up of Jews and Gentiles.

In a sentence. As God says in Hosea, “I will call those who were not my people ‘my people,’ and her who was not loved ‘my loved one’”; and “in the very place where they were told, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘children of the living God.’”

For worship. You were once “not my people.” Now you are called a child of the living God. Thank him for your new name.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel; Paul applies the words to the Gentiles too.

parallels.desc: I will say to Not My People, “You are my people”

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”

And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel. Key words. “Cries out”: urgent, prophetic proclamation. Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22–23, mainly from the Greek translation.

Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea. Key words. An echo of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Israel became numerous, as promised.

Only a remnant of them will be saved. Key words. The remnant (hypoleimma): a small number preserved through judgement. In Isaiah, only a remnant returned from the Assyrian disaster. The principle runs through the Old Testament, from Noah to Elijah’s seven thousand (11:4). So the fact that most Jews have rejected Christ is not a surprise; the prophets foretold it.

For the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay. Key words. God will do what he has said, decisively. His word of judgement and of salvation will be accomplished.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the remnant were saved because they were better. Chapter 11 says it is a remnant chosen by grace (11:5).

In a sentence. And Isaiah cries out about Israel: “Even if the Israelites are as many as the sand on the seashore, only a remnant will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence on the earth with speed and finality.”

On a Tuesday. Do not measure God’s faithfulness by numbers. Even when the faithful are few, God is keeping his word.

parallels.desc: only a remnant will return

verseByVerse.quote: And as Isaiah predicted, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”

And as Isaiah predicted. Key words. Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9.

If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring. Key words. “Lord of hosts” (Greek Sabaōth, from the Hebrew): the Lord of the armies of heaven, all-powerful. “Offspring” (sperma, seed): a few survivors, like seed from which a new crop grows.

We would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah. Key words. The cities wiped out completely for their sin (Genesis 19). Israel deserved the same. That any survived at all was God’s mercy alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the remnant is a reason for pride. The point is the opposite: without God’s mercy, no one would be left.

In a sentence. As Isaiah said before, “Unless the Lord Almighty had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah.”

For worship. Without God’s mercy, we would all be Sodom. Thank him that he leaves a seed, and that you are part of it.

parallels.desc: if the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–33 — The Stumbling Stone: Israel's Pursuit and Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a turn from theology to history. The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have attained it — by faith. Israel, which pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain it — because they pursued it as if it were by works rather than by faith. They stumbled over the stumbling stone: Christ. The stone God laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) was meant to be the foundation of Israel's hope; it became the obstacle over which they fell.

The irony is complete. The people who had every advantage — every covenant privilege, the law, the promises, the patriarchs — failed to reach what the people with no advantage attained. The reason is not their lack of zeal (Paul will say in 10:2 that they have zeal, but not according to knowledge) but their misdirection: seeking a righteousness of their own rather than the righteousness of God. The stumbling stone is not a surprise or a trap; it is the very cornerstone that God announced. But it requires faith to receive it as such.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Stone and the Two Ways

The stone of Romans 9:33 is used in the New Testament as a central Christological image (cf. 1 Peter 2:6–8, Matthew 21:42–44). Christ is simultaneously the cornerstone (the secure foundation for all who believe) and the stumbling stone (the cause of fall for all who refuse). The same Christ who is salvation to the one who believes is judgment to the one who will not. The gospel is never neutral; it is always either the savour of life or the savour of death (2 Corinthians 2:16). There is no third option.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's pursuit of righteousness by works was not insincere. It was zealous and disciplined. But zeal misdirected is more dangerous than apathy, because it produces a confidence in one's own religious achievement that closes the hand against the gift of grace. Now: The same dynamic plays out in every religious context. The most difficult people to bring to genuine faith are often the most religious — those who have so much invested in their own righteousness that they cannot bring themselves to stand before God empty-handed and receive what only grace can give.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.

What shall we say, then? Key words. Paul now turns from God’s sovereignty to human responsibility. Both are true. Election explains why some believe; unbelief explains why others are lost. This section runs to the end of chapter 10.

That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it. Key words. A paradox. “Pursue” (diōkō) is a hunting or racing word. The Gentiles were not chasing a right standing with God, yet they caught it.

That is, a righteousness that is by faith. Key words. The righteousness of chapters 3–4: God’s gift of a right standing, received by faith in Christ.

But that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Key words. Israel ran hard after righteousness through the law, and failed to reach it. The irony: the ones who tried hardest missed, because they ran on the wrong track.

What it does not mean. It does not mean effort is bad, or that the law was a bad goal. The law itself pointed to Christ (10:4). The problem was the way they pursued it.

In a sentence. What then shall we conclude? That Gentiles, who were not seeking righteousness, have received it, the righteousness that comes by faith; but Israel, who chased a law that would bring righteousness, did not attain it.

On a Tuesday. Religious effort cannot win God’s approval. Stop running on the wrong track. Receive Christ’s righteousness as a gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. Key words. The reason. Israel treated the law as a ladder of works to climb up to God, rather than receiving his promise by faith. “As if”: works were never the true way. Even in the Old Testament, people were justified by faith (4:1–8).

They have stumbled over the stumbling stone. Key words. The stumbling stone is Christ. A crucified Messiah offended them (1 Corinthians 1:23). He tells them their works cannot save; that is the offence.

As it is written. Key words. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion) with Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling). The same stone is a foundation for those who trust it and a stumbling block for those who do not. Peter uses the same combination (1 Peter 2:6–8).

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Key words. Believing in him is the way. Not put to shame: never disappointed or disgraced at the judgement. “Whoever” opens the door to anyone, Jew or Gentile. This leads into chapter 10, where everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved.

Where Christians differ: sovereignty and responsibility. Some think that if God elects, human responsibility vanishes; others think that if humans are responsible, God cannot be fully sovereign. Verdict: Paul holds both in the same chapter without apology. Israel’s unbelief is truly their fault (vv. 30–33; 10:21), and salvation is truly God’s sovereign mercy (vv. 6–24). We cannot fully reconcile them in our minds, but Scripture teaches both, and we must too (Westminster 3.1; Acts 2:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ is a trap. He is offered as a foundation to all. Only those who refuse him stumble over him.

In a sentence. Why? Because they sought it by works, not by faith. They tripped over the stumbling stone, as Scripture says: “Look, I am placing in Zion a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall, and the one who believes in him will never be put to shame.”

For worship. Build on Christ the cornerstone. Whoever trusts him will never be put to shame.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 moves from the theology of election (chapter 9) to the human experience of faith and the missionary imperative of proclamation. Paul's pastoral heart is again on display: his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is their salvation. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but a misdirection of it — a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, a pursuit of their own righteousness that refuses to submit to the righteousness of God.

The great passage of vv. 9–15 moves from confession and faith to calling on the name of the Lord to preachers sent with good news — a chain that runs from individual conversion back to the sovereign act of apostolic commissioning. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through preachers who are sent, who go, who speak. The chapter ends with the sobering testimony of Israel's own scriptures: they have heard, they have understood, and they have not believed. The tragedy of unbelief is complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's pastoral longing for Israel's salvation (v. 1) is the emotional key to the chapter. He is not writing as a detached analyst of Israel's religious failure; he is writing as a broken-hearted brother who knows exactly what his people are missing and cannot stop praying for them. The diagnosis is precise: "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Zeal without knowledge is not a small problem; it is perhaps the most dangerous religious condition possible, because it generates confident misdirection.

The contrast between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith (vv. 5–8) draws on Deuteronomy 30, where Moses speaks of God's word as near to the people — not beyond the sea, not in the heights of heaven, but in their mouths and in their hearts. Paul identifies this nearness with the gospel: "the word of faith that we proclaim." The righteousness of God is not a distant achievement to be scaled by heroic effort; it is a near word to be received by confession and faith.

Two verses stand between the diagnosis and that contrast, and they should not be passed over. They are the hinge of the chapter. Israel, Paul says, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, did not submit to God’s righteousness (v. 3).

Watch the sequence, because it is a clinical description of how a religious life goes wrong. First not knowing what God was offering; then setting about producing a version of it themselves; and finally — the word that makes it a moral matter rather than a misunderstanding — refusing to submit.

That verb is the surprise. One does not expect righteousness to be something a person submits to. But a righteousness that arrives as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is precisely what a competent, disciplined, self-respecting person finds hardest. The offence of the gospel is not that it asks too much. It is that it will not let you contribute.

Then v. 4, which the chapter cannot do without: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The word is telos, and it carries both senses at once — the terminus and the goal, where a road stops and what it was built to reach.

Both are true here and neither should be dropped. As a route to righteousness the law has come to its end, because the destination has arrived. And it was always heading there; Christ is not an alternative to the law but the thing it was pointing at, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that he does not overthrow the law but upholds it (3:31).

Note also the last clause, because it is the one that opens the door: to everyone who believes. The universal that will ring three times in vv. 11-13 has already sounded here, before the famous verses begin.

Verses 9–13 are among the most frequently memorised in Paul's letters — "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." The simplicity is staggering. Two things: confession of lordship, belief in resurrection. Both are the expression of the same faith. And the word "all" rings three times: everyone who believes (v. 11), everyone who calls (v. 13), for he is Lord of all and bestows riches on all who call (v. 12). The gospel has no ethnic or social exclusion clause.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Confession of Lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession "Jesus is Lord" (Kyrios Iēsous) the central act of Christian profession. In the first-century Roman world, "Kyrios" was the title of Caesar — the one to whom ultimate allegiance was owed. To confess "Jesus is Lord" was therefore not merely a theological statement but a political one: Jesus, not Caesar, holds ultimate authority over my life. The early church was often persecuted for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord" — because they had already given that title to another. Every true Christian confession has this political dimension: it declares a transfer of ultimate allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses's vision of the nearness of God's word (Deuteronomy 30) had originally been given to Israel on the plains of Moab, just before they entered the land — as a word of covenant accessibility. God was not hiding himself; he had given his word and it was near. Paul's application to the gospel makes the same point: the righteousness of God is not a distant achievement but a near word, proclaimed by apostles, received by faith. Now: The simplicity of Romans 10:9 is the permanent rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. Salvation does not require a theology degree, a track record of spiritual achievement, or a passage through elaborate ritual. It requires the honest confession of a changed allegiance and the genuine belief in a historical resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Meaning first. Romans 10 continues the explanation of Israel’s unbelief that began in 9:30, now from the human side. Chapter 9 showed God’s sovereign choice; chapter 10 shows Israel’s responsibility. Israel was zealous, but sought to establish its own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s righteousness, which comes in Christ, the end of the law (vv. 1–4). The righteousness of faith is not a hard climb to heaven or a deep dive into the grave: Christ has already come down and risen up. It is near, in the gospel word: confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him, and you will be saved, whether Jew or Greek, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (vv. 5–13). But calling requires believing, believing requires hearing, and hearing requires preachers who are sent (vv. 14–17). Israel has heard, and has understood enough to be guilty, while Gentiles who were not looking have found God, who still stretches out his hands all day long to his stubborn people (vv. 18–21). Election never makes preaching unnecessary; it makes it hopeful.

Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. Key words. “Heart’s desire” is eudokia, good pleasure, longing. Right after the strongest teaching on election in the Bible, Paul prays for the salvation of unbelieving Jews. Election does not make prayer pointless. God ordains the means as well as the end, and prayer is one of his means.

For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God. Key words. Paul speaks from experience. He had been zealous himself, so zealous that he persecuted the church (Acts 22:3–4; Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6).

But not according to knowledge. Key words. Knowledge here is epignōsis, true, full understanding. Sincerity is not enough. Zeal without truth can drive people hard in the wrong direction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is wrong, or that sincere people are saved because they are sincere. Paul’s point is that sincere, zealous people can be lost if they reject God’s way of righteousness.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul’s deepest longing and prayer to God for the Jews is that they be saved, for he can testify that they are zealous for God, but their zeal is not based on true knowledge.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the salvation of those you know, even when you believe God is sovereign. Especially then: he is able to answer.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God. Key words. Not ignorant that God is righteous, but of the righteousness that God gives, the gift of right standing revealed in the gospel (1:17; 3:21–22). They did not understand that God himself provides the righteousness he demands.

And seeking to establish their own. Key words. “Establish” (histēmi) means set up, make stand, like building a monument. Their own righteousness: a record of law-keeping that they hoped would stand before God (Philippians 3:9).

They did not submit to God’s righteousness. Key words. Receiving a gift requires humility. To accept God’s righteousness, you must admit you have none of your own. Pride refuses.

For Christ is the end of the law. Key words. “End” is telos, which can mean the termination, or the goal and fulfilment. The ESV note mentions that it can mean the goal.

For righteousness to everyone who believes. Key words. The law as a way of earning righteousness ends at Christ. Everyone who believes receives righteousness in him.

Where Christians differ: end or goal. Some take telos to mean that the law is entirely finished for Christians, with no ongoing role. Others take it to mean only that the law pointed to Christ. Verdict: Both senses are present, and they belong together. Christ is the goal the law aimed at: its sacrifices, promises and demands all pointed to him (3:21; Galatians 3:24). And so he is the end of the law as a way to gain righteousness: for everyone who believes, the attempt to be justified by law-keeping is over. But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains the rule of life for the believer, fulfilled by those who walk by the Spirit (8:4; 13:8–10; Westminster 19.5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may live lawlessly (6:15). The law no longer condemns believers, but it still shows them how to love.

In a sentence. Because they did not know the righteousness that comes from God and tried to set up their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the culmination of the law, so that there is righteousness for everyone who believes.

For worship. Give up building your own monument. Christ is your righteousness. Rest in him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law. Key words. Paul contrasts two ways of righteousness, both described by Moses.

That the person who does the commandments shall live by them. Key words. From Leviticus 18:5. Paul quotes it also in Galatians 3:12. The principle of law: do, and live. If you kept the law perfectly, you would live. But no sinner can (3:20; Galatians 3:10). So as a way to life, the law brings only death to sinners.

But the righteousness based on faith says. Key words. Paul personifies the righteousness of faith, letting it speak. It speaks words from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, where Moses told Israel that God’s word was not far off or too hard: it was near, in their mouth and heart.

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down). Key words. “Do not say in your heart” echoes Deuteronomy 9:4, where Moses warned Israel not to think God gave them the land because of their righteousness. No one needs to climb to heaven to fetch Christ. He has already come down, in the incarnation. You do not have to make salvation happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses contradicted himself, or that the law was a mistake. Leviticus 18:5 states what the law demands; Deuteronomy 30 speaks of the grace that would circumcise hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6). Both were in Moses, and both point to Christ.

In a sentence. Moses describes the righteousness of the law this way: the one who does these things will live by them. But the righteousness of faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down).

On a Tuesday. You cannot climb up to God. Christ has come down to you.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
“or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);

“Or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). Key words. In Deuteronomy, the image was crossing the sea; Paul uses the abyss (abyssos, the deep, the realm of the dead), a related Old Testament idea (Psalm 107:26; Jonah 2). No one needs to go down to the grave to bring Christ up. He has already risen. The great work is done.

But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 30:14. Salvation is not far away. It is as close as the word you hear and speak.

(That is, the word of faith that we proclaim). Key words. Paul explains: the near word is the gospel message, the word that calls for faith. Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the gospel, because the gospel is what the law always pointed to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation requires no response. The near word must be believed and confessed, as Paul says next.

In a sentence. “Or ‘Who will go down into the deep?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the message about faith that we preach.

For worship. The word of salvation is not far away. It is in your mouth and heart. Speak it and believe it today.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.

Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord. Key words. “Confess” (homologeō) means agree, declare openly. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name, the LORD. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God and to bow to his rule. In Rome, where people were expected to say Caesar is Lord, it was costly.

And believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead. Key words. Believing the resurrection is not just accepting a historical fact. It is trusting in the living Christ whom God vindicated (4:24–25). The heart in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will and affections.

You will be saved. Key words. A promise, firm and simple.

For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. Key words. Paul reverses the order: heart first, then mouth. Faith in the heart is what receives righteousness; confession with the mouth is its outward expression. They are not two separate conditions but one response, inside and outside. True faith does not stay silent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that saying the words is a magic formula, or that someone who cannot speak cannot be saved. It does not mean faith is a work that earns salvation. Faith receives; Christ saves.

In a sentence. If you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved.

On a Tuesday. Say it out loud, at work, at home, among friends: Jesus is Lord. Believe it in your heart, and live as one who belongs to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.

For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” Key words. Isaiah 28:16 again (9:33), now with “everyone” added to stress its universal reach. The Greek Old Testament says “whoever believes,” which implies everyone.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Key words. In 3:22–23 there was no distinction in sin; here there is no distinction in salvation. Same need, same remedy.

For the same Lord is Lord of all. Key words. One Lord, Jesus, over Jews and Gentiles alike (3:29–30; Acts 10:36).

Bestowing his riches on all who call on him. Key words. “Riches”: the riches of his grace and glory (2:4; 9:23; 11:33). To call on him is to pray to him for salvation, trusting him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone will in fact be saved. The riches are for all who call on him.

In a sentence. As Scripture says, “Anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame.” For there is no difference between Jew and Gentile: the same Lord is Lord of all and richly blesses all who call on him.

For worship. The Lord is rich, and generous to all who call. Call on him today, with confidence.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Key words. Paul quotes Joel 2:32, which Peter also quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). In Joel, the Lord is the LORD, Yahweh. Paul applies it to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (v. 9). This is a strong testimony that Jesus is God: to call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh.

To call on the name of the Lord. To pray to him, appeal to him, trust in him, worship him (Genesis 4:26; 12:8; 1 Corinthians 1:2). It is faith speaking.

Everyone. The door is open to all without exception. No sinner who calls will be turned away. This free offer of the gospel is real, and it fits with God’s sovereign election: the elect are those who are brought to call, and none who call are turned away (John 6:37).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people can call on him without believing, as Paul says next.

In a sentence. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

On a Tuesday. Tell people plainly: anyone who calls on the Lord Jesus will be saved. Then call on him yourself.
