verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 demolishes the sacred-secular distinction that has plagued Christian thinking since the patristic era. The body — presented to God as a living sacrifice — is itself the site of worship. This means that the Christian's daily work, physical rest, sexual life, eating and drinking, financial decisions, and embodied relationships are all, in principle, acts of worship when offered to God in faith and obedience. The Reformers' insistence on the holiness of ordinary life is grounded here. John Calvin saw the entire creation as the theatre of God's glory; Paul grounds that vision in the consecrated body of the believer. Your body is not a vehicle for your soul; it is the instrument of your worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of sacrifice was immediately understood by both Jewish and Gentile readers. In the Jewish tradition, sacrifice was the central act of worship — the presentation of an offering to God. Paul is saying that the entire life of the Christian is now the sacrifice: not an animal brought to an altar, but a person brought to God in the totality of their daily existence. The temple has been interiorised; the altar is everywhere; the offering is ongoing. Now: The call to "not be conformed to this world" is perpetually urgent because the world perpetually presses in. Every culture — including Christian subculture — has its conforming pressures, its assumed values, its default ways of measuring worth, success, and meaning. The renewal of the mind is the counter-pressure: learning to see all of life through the lens of Scripture, of the gospel, of the mercies of God, until the world's categories no longer have automatic authority over us.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.

Meaning first. Romans 12 begins the practical part of the letter (chapters 12–16): how people who have received God’s mercy should live. Paul does not leave doctrine and then turn to ethics as a separate subject; the “therefore” of verse 1 ties the whole Christian life to the mercies of chapters 1–11. First, the foundation: give your whole self to God as a living sacrifice, and be transformed by a renewed mind, not squeezed into the world’s shape (vv. 1–2). Second, life in the church: think of yourself soberly, for we are one body with many members, and each must use the gift God’s grace has given (vv. 3–8). Third, a string of short commands describing genuine love: love within the church, love toward outsiders, and love toward enemies, ending with the call to overcome evil with good (vv. 9–21). Gospel grace produces a new kind of person and a new kind of community.

I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God. Key words. “Appeal” (parakaleō, urge, exhort, encourage) is a pastor’s pleading, not a cold order. “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, and obedience follows as a response, never as a way to earn them. “Mercies” (oiktirmoi, compassions): all that God has done in Christ: justification, adoption, the Spirit, election, his faithfulness to Israel.

To present your bodies as a living sacrifice. Key words. “Present” (paristēmi), the word used in 6:13, 19 for offering your members to God. “Bodies”: not just your soul, but your whole self as you live in the world, with your eyes, hands, tongue and time. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were killed. Christ made the one atoning sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10:10–14). Now believers offer themselves as living sacrifices, not to atone, but in thanksgiving.

Holy and acceptable to God. Key words. Holy: set apart for God, like an offering without blemish. Acceptable: well-pleasing to him. Through Christ, our imperfect offerings please God (1 Peter 2:5).

Which is your spiritual worship. Key words. “Spiritual” is logikos, which can mean rational, reasonable, fitting; the ESV note mentions the rendering rational. “Worship” is latreia, the priestly service of the temple (9:4). In view of God’s mercies, this is the only reasonable response. Worship is not just what we do on Sunday; it is the whole of life given to God.

Do not be conformed to this world. Key words. “Conformed” (syschēmatizō, pressed into the shape of). “This world” is literally this age (aiōn), the present evil age with its values, opposed to God (Galatians 1:4). Do not let it mould you.

But be transformed by the renewal of your mind. Key words. “Transformed” (metamorphoō, the word used of Jesus’ transfiguration, Matthew 17:2, and of believers being changed into Christ’s image, 2 Corinthians 3:18). Both verbs are present tense and passive: keep on being transformed, by God’s work in you. The means is the renewing of the mind, a new way of thinking shaped by God’s word.

That by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. Key words. “Testing” (dokimazō, to prove, approve after testing). A renewed mind learns to recognise God’s will in daily decisions. The will of God here is his moral will, revealed in Scripture, not secret guidance. It is good (morally right), acceptable (pleasing to God) and perfect (complete, lacking nothing).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must withdraw from the world (John 17:15). It does not mean the body is bad. It means the believer’s whole life belongs to God and is being changed from the inside.

In a sentence. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, Paul urges you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; this is your true and fitting worship. Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is: his good, pleasing and perfect will.

On a Tuesday. Start the day by offering yourself to God: your body, your work, your words. Then feed your mind on his word, so that the world does not shape your thinking more than Scripture does.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The renewed mind produces, first, a sober assessment of oneself — neither inflated pride nor false modesty, but honest recognition of the measure of faith God has given and the gifts he has distributed. The image Paul uses is the body: one body, many members, each with a different function. No member of the body of Christ is the whole body; no gift given to one member is given to all; the diversity is not a deficiency but the design.

Paul's list of gifts in vv. 6–8 — prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, showing mercy — is not exhaustive but representative. Each gift comes with a manner: prophesy in proportion to your faith, serve in your serving, teach in your teaching, exhort in your exhorting, give with generosity, lead with zeal, show mercy with cheerfulness. The gifts are not to be displayed but exercised — put to work in the service of the body for the benefit of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts listed in Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata — graces, gifts of the Spirit. The Reformed tradition has emphasised that every gift is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not for the personal spiritual enhancement of the recipient. The gift of teaching is not given so that the teacher can be admired; it is given so that the body can be built up. The gift of mercy is not given as an ornament of personal piety; it is given to be exercised toward those in need. Gift and function are inseparable; the gift that is not exercised in service is a lamp hidden under a bowl.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church was a remarkable mixture of social classes, ethnic backgrounds, and educational levels. The gifts distributed by the Spirit crossed every human boundary: the slave might have the gift of teaching; the educated Greek might have the gift of service. The body-of-Christ framework was the theological revolution that made sense of this diversity. Now: The contemporary church regularly struggles with two opposite errors in the theology of gifts: the inflation of spectacular gifts (leading to unhealthy spiritual hierarchy and competition) and the dismissal of ordinary gifts (leading to the impression that only the "up-front" gifts matter). Romans 12:6–8 keeps the balance: every gift, faithfully exercised in its proper sphere, is a grace from God and a service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.

For by the grace given to me. Key words. Paul speaks with apostolic authority, which itself was a gift of grace (1:5; 15:15). He speaks humbly as he calls them to humility.

I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think. Key words. A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphroneō), but to think soberly (sōphroneō). The first fruit of a renewed mind is a right view of yourself. Pride divides the body; humility builds it.

But to think with sober judgment. Key words. Sober: sensible, realistic, neither inflated nor falsely humble. Humility is not pretending you have no gifts; it is seeing your gifts as God’s gifts.

Each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. Key words. “Measure” (metron): portion, allotment. God gives each believer faith and gifts in varying measure. Some take the measure of faith as the standard of faith, the same for all: the gospel itself. Others take it as the amount of faith or gifting given to each. Either way, what you have was given, so there is no room for boasting (1 Corinthians 4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean self-hatred or refusing to serve. Sober thinking includes recognising your gifts so that you can use them.

In a sentence. For by the grace given to Paul, he says to every one of you: do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgement, in keeping with the faith God has distributed to each of you.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself by what God has given you, not by comparison with others. That cures both pride and envy.
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

For as in one body we have many members. Key words. Paul’s favourite picture of the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:15–16). A human body is one, yet has many parts.

And the members do not all have the same function. Key words. “Function” (praxis, activity, work). An eye sees; a hand works. Difference is not a problem but the design.

So we, though many, are one body in Christ. Key words. Our unity is “in Christ”: we are joined to him, and so to one another. The church is not a club of individuals but an organism.

And individually members one of another. Key words. Each believer belongs to every other believer. You need them, and they need you. A Christian without a local church is like a hand cut off from the body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone must be the same. Nor does it mean that differences in gifts mean differences in worth.

In a sentence. Just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others.

For worship. Thank God for the other members of your church, even the ones very different from you. You belong to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;

Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. Key words. “Gifts” (charismata) come from “grace” (charis). A spiritual gift is grace in action, an ability given by God for building up the body. Not earned, not chosen by us (1 Corinthians 12:11).

Let us use them. Key words. The Greek has no verb, but the sense is clear. Gifts are for using, not admiring.

If prophecy, in proportion to our faith. Key words. Prophecy (prophēteia) in the New Testament was speaking a message revealed by God for the church (1 Corinthians 14:3, 29–31). “In proportion to our faith” is literally according to the analogy (analogia) of the faith. It may mean according to the measure of faith given to the prophet (v. 3), or in agreement with the faith, the body of truth already revealed. Reformed interpreters drew from this the principle of the analogy of faith: Scripture interprets Scripture, and no teaching may contradict the rest of God’s word.

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Continuationists believe the gift of prophecy continues in the church, giving new messages from God. Verdict: The gift of prophecy, in the sense of new revelation from God, belonged to the foundation period of the church, laid by apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). With the completion of Scripture, the canon is closed, and no new revelation is to be added (Hebrews 1:1–2; Westminster 1.1, 1.6). Today the prophetic function continues in a secondary sense through faithful preaching, which applies Scripture to the church. This view is held charitably: many continuationist brothers and sisters love Christ, and everyone agrees that any claimed word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that only some Christians have gifts. Every believer has been given grace to serve.

In a sentence. We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with the faith;

On a Tuesday. Ask: what has God given me to serve others with? Then use it this week, in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: ...if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. — Romans 12:7–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.

If service, in our serving. Key words. “Service” (diakonia): practical help, the root of deacon. Whoever has this gift should give themselves to it.

The one who teaches, in his teaching. Key words. Explaining and applying God’s truth (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 2:2).

The one who exhorts, in his exhortation. Key words. “Exhorts” (parakaleō, the same word as v. 1): urging, encouraging, comforting. Teaching informs the mind; exhortation moves the will.

The one who contributes, in generosity. Key words. Giving to others’ needs. “Generosity” (haplotēs) means simplicity, single-mindedness: giving without hidden motives or holding back (2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11).

The one who leads, with zeal. Key words. “Leads” (proistēmi, stands before, presides) is used of elders (1 Thessalonians 5:12; 1 Timothy 5:17). Lead with diligence and earnestness, not laziness.

The one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. Key words. Caring for the sick, poor and suffering. “Cheerfulness” (hilarotēs, from which we get hilarity): a glad heart, not grudging. God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts (compare 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Nor does it mean that those without a particular gift are excused from the duty. All must serve, give and show mercy. The gifted do so in a special way.

In a sentence. If it is serving, then serve; if it is teaching, then teach; if it is encouraging, then encourage; if it is giving, give generously; if it is leading, lead diligently; if it is showing mercy, do it cheerfully.

For worship. Every gift in your church comes from the same grace. Thank God for your teachers, servers, givers, leaders and those who show mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — Love in Action: The Ethics of the Transformed Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–21 form a rapid-fire sequence of practical exhortations that read almost like headings from a sermon on the Christian life — compressed, vivid, and comprehensive. Love without hypocrisy. Abhorring evil, holding fast to what is good. Outdoing one another in showing honour. Fervent in spirit. Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer. Contributing to the needs of the saints. Blessing those who persecute. Weeping with those who weep. Not being haughty. Repaying no one evil for evil. Living at peace with everyone. Not taking revenge. Overcoming evil with good.

The section begins and ends with love: "Let love be genuine" (v. 9) and "overcome evil with good" (v. 21). Everything between is the anatomy of genuine love in practice. Paul is not describing an achievable moral programme; he is describing the shape of a Spirit-renewed life — what grace looks like when it has taken hold of a person and begun the long work of conforming her to Christ.

The command to bless persecutors (v. 14) and to overcome evil with good (v. 21) are among the most demanding in the entire New Testament. They presuppose a radical reorientation of the instinct for self-protection and retaliation — an instinct that the Spirit does not suppress but redirects. The Christian who blesses her persecutor is not pretending the persecution is acceptable; she is entrusting the righting of wrongs to the God who says "vengeance is mine" (v. 19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35) and acting from the love that wishes even the enemy's good.

Two things in the section deserve naming. The first is a piece of wordplay in v. 13. The command is not merely to show hospitality but to pursue it — and the verb is the one Paul uses in the very next line of those who persecute you. The same word, one sentence apart, running in opposite directions: some people are chasing you, and you are to go chasing after strangers.

The second is v. 20, which is the sharpest instruction here and the most misread: if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. Paul takes it from Proverbs 25:21–22, and the burning coals are not a promise that your kindness will make him suffer in some superior way. The image is most naturally read as the burning of shame that leads to repentance. The aim of the exercise is not a defeated enemy. It is an enemy who has stopped being one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ethic of the Cross in Daily Life

The ethics of Romans 12:9–21 are the daily practical form of the theology of the cross. The crucified Christ did not retaliate; he blessed those who cursed him; he overcame evil with the supreme good of his self-offering. The Christian who lives by this ethic is not simply following rules but is embodying the pattern of the One who died for his enemies. This is why Paul can ground the command to bless persecutors in the experience of God's mercy (v. 1): the person who knows she was God's enemy and has been loved into sonship has the deepest possible motivation for loving her enemies. She is doing to them what was done to her.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman church included people from across the social spectrum — slaves, freedmen, members of Caesar's household (Philippians 4:22), wealthy patrons, poor migrants. The potential for social friction, hierarchy, and mutual contempt was enormous. Paul's commands — "outdo one another in showing honour" (v. 10), "do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly" (v. 16) — were written for a community in which these things were concrete daily challenges, not abstract ethical principles. Now: The contemporary church is no less stratified by income, education, race, and social status. Romans 12:9–21 is still the practical charter of a community that crosses every human division by the power of a love that is genuinely without hypocrisy. The test is not whether the church affirms diversity in principle but whether its members weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice — across every line that the world uses to divide.

verseByVerse.quote: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. — Romans 12:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.

Let love be genuine. Key words. The heading of verses 9–21. “Love” is agapē, self-giving love. “Genuine” (anypokritos, without hypocrisy, unhypocritical: no actor’s mask). Love that is not play-acting.

Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Key words. Love is not soft on evil. “Abhor” (apostygeō) is a strong word: loathe, shudder at. “Hold fast” (kollaō, to glue, cling to). Real love hates what harms the beloved.

Love one another with brotherly affection. Key words. Two family words: philadelphia (love of brothers and sisters) and philostorgos (tender family affection). The church is a family, and its love should be warm.

Outdo one another in showing honor. Key words. A competition in honouring others: try to be first to show respect. Some take it as “prefer one another in honour”: put others ahead of yourself (Philippians 2:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is just a feeling. It means active, sincere goodwill that shows itself in actions.

In a sentence. Love must be sincere. Hate what is evil; cling to what is good. Be devoted to one another in love. Honour one another above yourselves.

On a Tuesday. Find someone in your church today and honour them: a word of thanks, a note, a meal, a real compliment. Try to get there first.

parallels.desc: hate evil, and love good

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.

Do not be slothful in zeal. Key words. Do not be lazy (oknēros, hesitant, sluggish) when it comes to eagerness (spoudē, diligence). Christian love works hard.

Be fervent in spirit. Key words. “Fervent” (zeō, to boil, be hot). The ESV notes that this can also be read as fervent in the Spirit, that is, set on fire by the Holy Spirit. Both are true: a warm spirit comes from the Spirit (Acts 18:25).

Serve the Lord. Key words. As slaves (douleuō) of the Lord Jesus. All our zeal must be directed to him, not to our own projects. A few manuscripts read “serve the time,” but “serve the Lord” is the better reading.

Rejoice in hope. Key words. The hope of glory (5:2; 8:24–25). Joy now, because of what is coming.

Be patient in tribulation. Key words. “Patient” (hypomenō, endure, remain under the load). Tribulation (thlipsis, pressure, affliction) is expected (5:3).

Be constant in prayer. Key words. “Constant” (proskartereō, persist, devote yourself to). Prayer is how hope and patience are kept alive (Acts 2:42; Colossians 4:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean frantic busyness. Zeal is directed toward the Lord and sustained by prayer.

In a sentence. Never be lacking in zeal, but keep your spiritual fervour, serving the Lord. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer.

For worship. Pray now. Ask the Spirit to set your heart on fire again, to fill you with hope, and to give you patience in what you are going through.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “fervent in spirit” can also be read “fervent in the Spirit.”

verseByVerse.quote: Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.

Contribute to the needs of the saints. Key words. “Contribute” (koinōneō, share, have fellowship). The saints: fellow believers, God’s holy people. Christians share their goods with Christians in need (Acts 2:44–45; Galatians 6:10). Paul himself was collecting for the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25–26).

And seek to show hospitality. Key words. “Seek” (diōkō, pursue, chase). Hospitality (philoxenia, love of strangers): opening your home. Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor and dangerous inns (Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5–8). Do not just wait for chances; go after them.

Bless those who persecute you. Key words. A turn toward outsiders. This echoes Jesus’ words (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28). To bless is to speak well of, and to ask God’s good for.

Bless and do not curse them. Key words. Paul repeats it for emphasis. Do not call down harm on enemies. Jesus prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34); Stephen did the same (Acts 7:60).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring injustice or refusing to seek legal protection. It means our hearts and words toward persecutors are filled with goodwill, not revenge.

In a sentence. Share with the Lord’s people who are in need. Practise hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.

On a Tuesday. Invite someone into your home this week. And pray by name for someone who has treated you badly.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor, unsafe inns.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Key words. Sympathy: feeling with others. It can be harder to rejoice with the successful than to weep with the sad, because envy gets in the way. Love does both (1 Corinthians 12:26).

Live in harmony with one another. Key words. Literally, think the same thing toward one another: be of one mind, not in every opinion, but in shared purpose and care.

Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Key words. “Haughty”: thinking high things. “Associate with” (synapagō, to be carried along with). “The lowly” can mean lowly people or lowly tasks. Spend time with ordinary, poor, unimportant people. Jesus did.

Never be wise in your own sight. Key words. From Proverbs 3:7 (as in 11:25). Do not be conceited about your own opinions.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faking emotion. It means caring enough to enter into others’ lives.

In a sentence. Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but be willing to associate with people of low position. Do not be conceited.

For worship. Thank God for someone else’s blessing today, sincerely. And sit with someone who is grieving.

parallels.desc: be not wise in your own eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.

Repay no one evil for evil. Key words. The instinct to pay back is strong. The Christian breaks the cycle (Matthew 5:38–39; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9).

But give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. Key words. “Give thought” (pronoeō, plan ahead, take care). Honourable: what even unbelievers recognise as good and noble (Proverbs 3:4; 2 Corinthians 8:21). Our conduct should commend the gospel.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Key words. Two realistic qualifications. If possible: sometimes peace is impossible without betraying truth. So far as it depends on you: you cannot control others, only yourself. Make sure that, if there is no peace, it is not your fault.

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace at any price. We do not give up the truth of the gospel to keep peace.

In a sentence. Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everyone. If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you are at odds with? Do your part to make peace. Apologise for your share. Leave the rest to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”

Beloved, never avenge yourselves. Key words. A tender address as he gives a hard command. Personal revenge is forbidden.

But leave it to the wrath of God. Key words. Literally, give place to wrath: step aside and let God deal with it. This is not because evil does not matter, but because justice belongs to God, and he will do it perfectly. He also acts through the governing authorities (13:4).

For it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:35. God will judge all evil, either at the cross or at the last judgement. So we can let go.

To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink.” Key words. From Proverbs 25:21–22. Not just refrain from revenge: actively do good to your enemy.

For by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head. Key words. Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and repentance through unexpected kindness: the burning pain of conscience. Some connect it with an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried a pan of coals on his head as a sign of remorse. It does not mean kindness is a clever way to hurt your enemy more.

What it does not mean. It does not mean crime should go unpunished, or that victims may not report wrongs to the authorities. Chapter 13 gives the state the sword. What is forbidden is personal revenge.

In a sentence. Do not take revenge, dear friends, but leave room for God’s wrath, for it is written, “It is mine to avenge; I will repay,” says the Lord. On the contrary: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head.”

For worship. Hand your desire for revenge to God. He is just. Then do something kind for the person who wronged you.
verseByVerse.note: Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and a change of heart through kindness.

parallels.desc: vengeance is mine
if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

Do not be overcome by evil. Key words. “Overcome” (nikaō, conquer, win the victory). If evil makes you bitter and vengeful, it has won. Being wronged is not defeat; becoming like the wrongdoer is.

But overcome evil with good. Key words. Goodness is the weapon that defeats evil. This is how Christ conquered: by suffering, forgiving, and doing good to his enemies. The cross is the supreme example (5:8, 10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean being passive or naive. It is active, strategic goodness.

In a sentence. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

On a Tuesday. When someone does you wrong today, ask: what good can I do in return? That is how you win.

Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.<sup>17</sup>Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.<sup>18</sup>If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.<sup>19</sup>Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”<sup>20</sup>To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”<sup>21</sup>Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Romans 13 addresses two dimensions of the Christian's life in the world that might seem unrelated but are theologically connected: the relationship to governing authorities (vv. 1–7) and the debt of love that fulfils the whole law (vv. 8–14). Both passages apply the gospel-transformed mind of 12:2 to concrete social realities. The Christian is not a free agent owing nothing to anyone; she is embedded in a created order (civil government) and a moral order (the law of love) that place real obligations on her life.

The passage on governing authorities is one of the most important and most abused in the New Testament — used to justify passive submission to every form of political power, and also to justify every form of political resistance. Paul's point is neither absolutist submission nor automatic resistance; it is the theological grounding of civil authority in God's own ordering of human society, combined with the practical obligation to honour, obey, and pay taxes to those who wield legitimate authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (v. 1). The theological foundation is clear: civil government is not a human invention that God tolerates; it is an ordering of human society that God has established for the good of human beings. The magistrate, the soldier, the tax official — in their legitimate exercise of authority, they are God's servants (diakonos — the same word used for church deacons) for the maintenance of order, the punishment of evil, and the commendation of good.

The context matters: Paul is writing to Rome under the early Nero, before the persecutions of the 60s. The Roman state, for all its paganism, provided the remarkable infrastructure of law, roads, and relative peace (the Pax Romana) that enabled the gospel to spread across the empire. Paul is not asking the Roman Christians to endorse every policy of the emperor; he is asking them not to be revolutionaries — not to treat their citizenship in the kingdom of God as a license to ignore or undermine the civil order that God has established.

The limits of this submission are implied by the rest of Scripture (Acts 5:29 — "We must obey God rather than men") and by Paul's own record of civil disobedience. When the governing authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must obey God. But the default posture is submission, because the default function of civil government — even imperfect civil government — is the ordering of human life in a fallen world for the common good.

Three things in the passage should not be passed over. The first is v. 2, which supplies the sanction: whoever resists the authority resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment. Paul is not merely recommending civic good manners. He is saying that the ordering itself has God behind it, so that contempt for it is not a neutral act.

The second is the second half of v. 4, and it is the hinge on which the previous chapter turns. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain; he is an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. A few verses earlier Paul forbade the Christian to avenge himself and told him to give place to the wrath (12:19). He now names the office through which some of that wrath is administered in the present. Vengeance was not abolished when it was taken out of your hands. It was relocated.

The third is v. 5, which gives the motive: submission is owed not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience. That distinguishes the Christian citizen from the merely prudent one. Fear of penalty produces compliance wherever penalties are likely; conscience produces the same behaviour where no one is watching and nothing would follow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformation developed the doctrine of the two kingdoms — the kingdom of God's left hand (civil government) and the kingdom of his right hand (the church) — as the theological framework for understanding passages like Romans 13. God governs the civil sphere through natural law and common grace, using even unbelieving rulers to maintain order and restrain evil. God governs the church through Word and Spirit. The two kingdoms are distinct but not separate; the Christian citizen participates in both, with different modes of loyalty appropriate to each. Luther and Calvin both insisted on the legitimacy and dignity of civil authority while limiting its scope: Caesar has his domain; Christ has his; and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians were tempted, for obvious reasons, to view the imperial state with suspicion or hostility — an institution that had crucified their Lord and would eventually persecute them. Paul's command to submit was not politically naive; it was theologically grounded. God uses even imperfect and eventually hostile governments to structure human life. The Christian who refuses all civil order in the name of heavenly citizenship has not understood the two-kingdom distinction. Now: In democracies, Romans 13 applies to the obligation of citizens to participate in civil society — paying taxes, respecting legitimate authority, working through legal channels to promote justice. It does not require silent compliance with injustice; the Christian who uses the legitimate tools of civil society to oppose evil is not violating v. 1 but fulfilling v. 4's vision of government as a servant of good.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.

Meaning first. Romans 13 carries on the theme of how believers live in the world. Chapter 12 forbade personal revenge and said to leave it to God’s wrath; chapter 13 shows one way God carries out that wrath in this age: through the governing authorities. First, Christians submit to the government, because God appointed it to reward good and punish evil, and so they pay taxes and give honour where due (vv. 1–7). Second, the only debt Christians should always carry is love, for love fulfils the law (vv. 8–10). Third, the hour is late; the day of Christ’s return is near. So believers should wake up, throw off the deeds of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ (vv. 11–14). The Christian is a good citizen, a loving neighbour, and a person living for the coming day.

Setting and background. Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his reign, before his persecution of Christians in AD 64. A few years earlier, Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome after disturbances (Acts 18:2). There was unrest over taxes in Rome around this time. Christians, who confessed Jesus as Lord, could easily be seen as rebels. Paul makes clear that the gospel does not make Christians revolutionaries.

Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. Key words. “Every person” (literally every soul): no exceptions, apostles included. “Be subject” (hypotassō, place yourself under, in an ordered rank). “Governing authorities” (exousiai hyperechousai, authorities that are over you): the rulers of the state, from emperor to local magistrates.

For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Key words. “Instituted” (tassō, appointed, ordered). Government is God’s idea. Human authority derives from his authority. Jesus told Pilate that he would have no authority unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11; Daniel 4:17; Proverbs 8:15).

Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed. Key words. “Resists” (antitassō, set oneself against, in battle array). To rebel against lawful authority is to rebel against God’s order.

And those who resist will incur judgment. Key words. Judgement (krima): from God, and through the state’s own punishment.

Where Christians differ: obedience and resistance. Some say Christians must obey the state in everything. Others say Christians may overthrow any unjust government. Verdict: Christians must submit to the governing authorities in all lawful things, even when rulers are unbelievers or unjust (1 Peter 2:13–18). But no human authority can command what God forbids or forbid what God commands. Then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Such disobedience should be open, peaceful, and willing to accept the consequences. Reformed tradition has also taught that when rulers become tyrants who destroy the purpose for which God gave them authority, lesser lawful magistrates may lead lawful resistance; this is a grave matter, a last resort, and never a private person’s revenge (Westminster 23.4). Paul’s point here is the normal duty: submission.

Even wicked rulers? A reader naturally asks: was Nero instituted by God? Was a tyrant? Paul is speaking of two things at once. First, the office: government as such is God’s ordinance, his gift to restrain evil in a fallen world; anarchy is never his will. Second, God’s providence: no ruler comes to power apart from God’s sovereign rule, which sets up kings and removes them (Daniel 2:21; 4:17). Sometimes he gives a nation a wicked ruler as a judgement, as he used Assyria and Babylon (Isaiah 10:5; Jeremiah 27:6). That a ruler holds power by God’s providence does not mean God approves of what he does with it, any more than God approved of Pilate condemning Jesus (John 19:11). The ruler is accountable to God for every abuse, and will answer for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every action of a government is approved by God, or that rulers are above God’s law. It does not mean Christians cannot vote, speak out, protest lawfully, or seek to change laws.

In a sentence. Let everyone submit to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except what God has established; the authorities that exist have been established by God. So whoever rebels against the authority is rebelling against what God has instituted, and those who do so will bring judgement on themselves.

On a Tuesday. Obey the speed limit, file your taxes honestly, and speak respectfully of your leaders. Your citizenship is part of your worship.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

parallels.desc: by me kings reign

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.

For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Key words. The purpose of government: to restrain evil and protect good. Paul describes what rulers are meant to be, and what they generally are, even when imperfect.

Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval. Key words. The way to live without fear of the police is to do right. Approval (epainos, praise): rulers commend good citizens.

For he is God’s servant for your good. Key words. “Servant” is diakonos, minister, the same word used of church deacons. The ruler is God’s minister, whether he knows it or not, as Cyrus was (Isaiah 45:1). His job is the good of the people: peace, order and justice.

But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. Key words. The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including the power of death (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). In vain: for no purpose. God gave it real authority to use force.

For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. Key words. “Avenger” (ekdikos): the one who carries out justice. Here is the link to 12:19. Individuals must not take revenge; God carries out his wrath partly through the state. So the state may do what the individual may not.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong. Verdict: Scripture gives the state the right to use the sword, including the death penalty for the gravest crimes such as murder (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). This rests on the dignity of the human made in God’s image. Christians may disagree on whether, in a given country with its legal system, the death penalty should be used, given the risk of error and injustice. But it is not wrong in principle. This is not personal revenge, which is forbidden; it is God’s justice carried out by lawful authority.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the state may use the sword to compel faith or punish true worship. Its sphere is civil justice, not the conscience before God.

In a sentence. For rulers hold no terror for those who do right, but for those who do wrong. Do you want to be free from fear of the one in authority? Then do what is right and you will be commended. For the one in authority is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for rulers do not bear the sword for no reason. They are God’s servants, agents of wrath to bring punishment on the wrongdoer.

For worship. Thank God for the order and protection your government provides, imperfect as it is. Pray for those who serve in law and justice.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience.

Therefore one must be in subjection. Key words. “Must” (anankē, necessity): it is required.

Not only to avoid God’s wrath. Key words. Wrath here is the punishment the state carries out on God’s behalf. One reason to obey is fear of consequences.

But also for the sake of conscience. Key words. A higher reason. Conscience (syneidēsis) knows that government is God’s ordinance. So believers obey the law even when no one is watching and they could get away with breaking it. Obedience comes from inside, not just fear.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conscience must obey a law that requires sin. Conscience bound to God may need to disobey such a law (Acts 5:29).

In a sentence. Therefore it is necessary to submit to the authorities, not only because of possible punishment but also as a matter of conscience.

On a Tuesday. Obey the law when no one is checking. A good conscience before God is worth more than getting away with it.

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.

For because of this you also pay taxes. Key words. Because government is God’s servant, it has a right to be funded. Jesus said to give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s (Mark 12:17).

For the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Key words. “Ministers” here is leitourgoi, a word often used of priestly service. Public officials are, in their sphere, doing God’s service. “Attending to” (proskartereō, devoting themselves to): governing is their full-time work.

Pay to all what is owed to them. Key words. “Pay” (apodidōmi, give back, render what is due). Not a gift but a debt.

Taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed. Key words. “Taxes” (phoros) were direct taxes, on land and persons; “revenue” (telos) meant customs and tolls on goods. Pay both honestly.

Respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. Key words. “Respect” (phobos, literally fear, reverence) and “honour” (timē). We owe our leaders not only money but respect, even when we disagree with them (1 Peter 2:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean tax money is always spent well, or that we cannot argue for lower or fairer taxes. It means we pay what the law requires.

In a sentence. This is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, who give their full time to governing. Give to everyone what you owe them: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honour, then honour.

On a Tuesday. Be honest on your tax return, even with the small things. And when you speak of politicians, speak with respect.
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (v. 8). The transition from taxes and respect to love is sudden but logical: both are obligations owed to those among whom we live. But the debt of love is unique — it is a debt that is perpetually owed and perpetually paid but never fully discharged. You can pay a tax and be done with it; you can never be done with the obligation to love, because the opportunities to love are inexhaustible and the command is perpetual.

Paul's claim is audacious: love fulfils the entire law. The specific commandments — do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not covet — are all "summed up" in this word: love your neighbour as yourself (quoting Leviticus 19:18). This does not make the specific commandments irrelevant; it establishes their theological root. Love is the soil from which all the particular expressions of right conduct grow. The person who truly loves her neighbour will not steal from him, will not lie to him, will not commit adultery against him. Love is not a substitute for the law's specific demands; it is the power that fulfils them from within.

The passage closes with the urgency of eschatological time: "the night is far gone; the day is at hand" (v. 12). The Christian lives in the interim between the first coming of Christ (which inaugurated the day of salvation) and his return (which will complete it). This is not time to sleep; it is time to wake, to lay aside the works of darkness, to put on the armour of light — and supremely to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 14). The Christian life is not moral self-improvement; it is the clothing of oneself in Christ, day by day, until the transformation is complete.

Between the dawn and the clothing stands v. 13, which supplies the specifics: let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. Three pairs, and the order of them is the sting. The list begins where anyone would expect a vice list to begin and ends somewhere entirely respectable — with arguing and envy, which are set down in the same sentence, under the same heading, as the drunken procession through the streets.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

Romans 13:8–10 gives the summary of the second table of the law: love your neighbour as yourself. This is not a replacement of the law with an undefined sentiment; it is the identification of the animating principle from which all the law's specific demands flow. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites — love is the motive; the law is the guide. The renewed person who loves God supremely and her neighbour genuinely will want to know concretely what that love requires in specific situations, and the law provides exactly that: the concrete shape of love in action.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's command to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh" (v. 14) was the verse that Augustine read in the garden in Milan in 386 AD, at the moment of his conversion. He had been struggling with the inability to break free from sexual sin; these words fell on him with the weight of divine command and divine grace simultaneously. The verse is still doing what it did to Augustine: convicting, commanding, and empowering. Now: The urgency of vv. 11–14 is the urgency of the gospel in every age: the window of this life is short; the return of Christ is certain; the works of darkness are not appropriate wear for people who are children of light. Every day lived in unrepentant sin is a wasted day; every day lived in Christ is a day that will outlast the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Owe no one anything. Key words. Leave no debt unpaid. Following verse 7, it means pay what you owe: taxes, respect, money.

Except to love each other. Key words. The one debt that can never be fully paid. We always owe more love, because Christ loved us so much (1 John 4:11). Augustine called it the debt we always pay and always owe.

For the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. Key words. Love fulfils (plēroō) the law: it does what the law requires toward others.

For the commandments. Key words. Paul lists the second table of the Ten Commandments, our duties to neighbour: the seventh, sixth, eighth and tenth (Exodus 20:13–17; Deuteronomy 5:17–21).

And any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Key words. “Summed up” (anakephalaioō, brought together under one head, as in Ephesians 1:10). From Leviticus 19:18. Jesus called it the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39–40; Galatians 5:14).

Where Christians differ: is borrowing wrong? Some take “owe no one anything” to forbid all borrowing, including mortgages or loans. Verdict: Scripture does not forbid borrowing as such; it regulates it (Exodus 22:25; Psalm 37:21; Matthew 5:42). The command is to pay what you owe when it is due and not leave debts unpaid. But Scripture warns that the borrower is slave to the lender (Proverbs 22:7), so wisdom avoids unnecessary debt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we can decide for ourselves what love requires. Love is defined by the commandments; it fulfils them, not ignores them.

In a sentence. Let no debt remain outstanding, except the continuing debt to love one another, for whoever loves others has fulfilled the law. The commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other command there may be, are summed up in this one command: “Love your neighbour as yourself.”

On a Tuesday. Pay your bills on time. Then pay the debt you can never pay off: love the people around you today.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.

Love does no wrong to a neighbor. Key words. The commandments listed in verse 9 are negative: do not harm. Love never harms. It does not steal a neighbour’s spouse, life, goods or reputation.

Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. Key words. “Fulfilling” (plērōma, fullness, complete expression). Love is what the law looks like when it is lived from the heart. Love does far more than avoid harm; it actively seeks the neighbour’s good (1 Corinthians 13:4–7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a feeling of love is enough. Love shows itself in keeping God’s commandments (John 14:15).

In a sentence. Love does no harm to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law.

For worship. Thank Christ, who loved perfectly and fulfilled the law for you. Ask his Spirit to fill you with that love.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.

Besides this you know the time. Key words. “Time” (kairos): the significant season, the age between Christ’s first coming and his return.

That the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. Key words. Sleep here is spiritual drowsiness, carelessness, being at ease in the world (1 Thessalonians 5:6–7; Ephesians 5:14).

For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. Key words. Salvation here is its completion: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and final glory (8:23–24). Every day brings it closer.

The night is far gone; the day is at hand. Key words. The night is this present evil age; the day is the day of the Lord, Christ’s return. The night is nearly over. “At hand” (engizō, has drawn near).

So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Key words. Like taking off night clothes and putting on day clothes, or like a soldier putting on armour for the day’s battle (Ephesians 6:11–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). The works of darkness are listed next.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong about the timing? Some say Paul expected Christ to return within his lifetime and was mistaken. Verdict: Paul taught that the day is near, meaning that it is the next great event in God’s plan and could come at any time, not that he knew the date (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). Since Christ’s first coming, we have been in the last days (Hebrews 1:2). The time is short whether Christ returns tomorrow or in a thousand years, since with the Lord a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8). His return will be one visible, public event, not a secret rapture, followed by the resurrection and judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should set dates, or stop working and wait. It means live every day ready.

What “salvation is nearer” does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved, or that their salvation is still in doubt. Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses: we have been saved from sin’s penalty (justified, 5:1; Ephesians 2:8); we are being saved from sin’s power (sanctified, 6:22); and we shall be saved from sin’s presence, when Christ returns and our bodies are raised (8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). Here Paul means the third. Every day brings that final rescue a day nearer. It is as certain as the first, since those he justified he also glorified (8:30).

In a sentence. And do this, understanding the present time: the hour has already come for you to wake up from your slumber, because our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. The night is nearly over; the day is almost here. So let us put aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armour of light.

On a Tuesday. Live today as if Christ could return tonight. What would you stop doing? What would you start?

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

Let us walk properly as in the daytime. Key words. “Properly” (euschēmonōs, decently, becomingly). Live in a way that is fit to be seen in daylight, with nothing to hide.

Not in orgies and drunkenness. Key words. Three pairs of night sins. First, sins of excess. “Orgies” (kōmoi, revelling, wild parties); drunkenness.

Not in sexual immorality and sensuality. Key words. Sexual sins. “Sexual immorality” (koitai, literally beds, sexual sin). “Sensuality” (aselgeia, unrestrained lust, shamelessness).

Not in quarreling and jealousy. Key words. Sins of relationship: strife and envy. Notice Paul puts these alongside drunkenness and immorality. Church people who would never get drunk can be guilty of quarrelling and jealousy.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Believers have already put on Christ at their conversion and baptism (Galatians 3:27). Now they must put him on daily: take on his character, live in union with him, let him be the clothing others see (Colossians 3:10–14).

And make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. Key words. “Provision” (pronoia, forethought, planning ahead). Do not plan for sin. Do not leave the door open. Remove the temptations you know you are weak toward. “The flesh” here is not the body as such, but our fallen human nature with its sinful desires, which still pulls at the believer (for the fuller explanation, see the note on 8:3–4).

Augustine. Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386, after hearing a child’s voice chanting, take up and read. He wrote that at the end of the sentence, a light of certainty flooded his heart, and the darkness of doubt vanished.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all celebration or wine is sinful (John 2:1–11). It forbids excess and the loss of self-control.

In a sentence. Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not think about how to gratify the desires of the flesh.

On a Tuesday. Identify one way you make provision for the flesh: an app, a habit, a place, a route home. Remove it today. Then put on Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.
