14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14–15 address a specific pastoral conflict in the Roman church: tension between Jewish Christians who maintained food laws and Sabbath observances ("the weak in faith") and Gentile Christians who felt free from such regulations ("the strong"). But Paul's treatment of this specific conflict generates principles that apply to every generation's version of the same tension: the conflict between Christian liberty and Christian love, between what I am free to do and what love requires me to do for the sake of my brother.

The governing principle is not the extension of legal restriction to those who are free, nor the dismissal of sensitive consciences as mere scrupulosity. It is love — the willingness to limit one's own legitimate freedom for the sake of the weaker brother's conscience and the unity of the body. Paul himself is clearly among "the strong" (15:1 — "we who are strong"), but his pastoral concern is to protect the weak while educating them toward greater freedom, without allowing either group to destroy the other with contempt or judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions" (v. 1). The command is striking in both its positive and its negative dimensions. Positively: welcome him — bring him into the full fellowship of the community, do not treat his scruples as a reason for exclusion. Negatively: not to quarrel over opinions — do not make his welcome the occasion for pressuring him to adopt your view or defend your freedom. The welcome is genuine; the agenda of the welcome is his good, not your point-scoring.

The specific examples Paul uses — one person eats only vegetables, another observes certain days as special — are illustrations of a broader principle. The particulars may be first-century Jewish food laws and Sabbath observances; the principle is the obligation of both the strong and the weak to refrain from the two characteristic sins their positions generate: the strong's temptation to despise the scrupulous (treating their sensitivity as weakness or intellectual failure), and the weak's temptation to judge the free (condemning as sinful what God has declared clean).

"Each of us will give an account of himself to God" (v. 12) — the eschatological horizon is the great leveller. Neither the strong nor the weak will stand before God and be assessed on the basis of whether they were free in matters of food and days. They will give an account of themselves — whether they served Christ, whether they loved their brother, whether they built up the body. The things that divide them now will be irrelevant then; what will matter then should be what governs them now.

Four things in the section are worth adding, because the ground between the opening command and v. 12 is where the argument is actually made. The first is v. 4, which supplies the reason judging is out of order: Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The picture is a domestic household. You do not discipline another man’s staff, however sure you are that they are doing it wrong, because they were not hired by you and do not answer to you.

And that verse ends in a promise rather than a rebuke — he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Paul’s confidence is not that the disputed practice does not matter but that the disputed brother is being personally held up by someone competent. God is already at work on the person you were about to correct.

The second is v. 6, and it is the criterion the whole section turns on. Both parties — the one who observes the day and the one who does not, the one who eats and the one who abstains — are described as acting in honour of the Lord, and both are said to give thanks to God. Paul is not calling the difference trivial. He is pointing out that the same thanksgiving is going up from both sides of the table.

The third is v. 9, which grounds the whole thing in the gospel rather than in tolerance: to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. The purpose of the cross and resurrection is stated here as lordship — which settles who is entitled to rule another believer’s conscience, and the answer is the one who paid for it. And the fourth is vv. 10–11, where the argument is sealed with Isaiah 45:23: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing, the strong and the weak side by side at the same tribunal, neither of them presiding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adiaphora and the Conscience

The Reformed tradition uses the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor prohibits — the territory of Romans 14. In these matters, Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean; what the gospel has freed the conscience from need not be re-enslaved. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that in matters of adiaphora, the strong must exercise their freedom with sensitivity to the weaker conscience — not capitulating to every scruple indefinitely, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific tensions in Rome were between Jewish and Gentile believers over Torah food laws and calendar observances — real, living issues that threatened the unity of a church in which both groups worshipped together. Paul does not resolve the tension by declaring one group right and the other wrong; he transcends it by pointing both groups to a standard higher than their own position: the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation of the church has its equivalent of the Romans 14 debate: alcohol, entertainment, dress, worship style, political engagement. The principles are the same: welcome the brother with differing scruples; do not quarrel over opinions; do not despise; do not judge; remember that each will give account to God and not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.

Meaning first. Romans 14:1–15:13 deals with a problem in the Roman church: believers disagreed over matters that Scripture leaves free, such as foods and special days. Paul calls those with tender scruples the weak and those who are free in conscience the strong, and he counts himself among the strong (15:1). He gives each side its duty. The strong must not despise the weak; the weak must not judge the strong; God has welcomed both, and each answers to the Lord, before whose judgement seat we will all stand (vv. 1–12). Then he presses the strong especially: do not use your freedom in a way that makes a brother stumble or destroys him, for the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–21). Finally: keep your faith between you and God, and do not act against your conscience, for whatever does not come from faith is sin (vv. 22–23). The chapter teaches Christian liberty and Christian love together.

Setting and background. The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws and holy days of the law of Moses, and perhaps some Gentiles who avoided meat for fear it had been offered to idols (as in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). Meat sold in the markets of Rome often came from pagan temples. Some, unable to be sure, ate only vegetables (as Daniel did in Babylon, Daniel 1:8–12).

As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him. Key words. “Weak in faith”: not weak in trusting Christ for salvation, but not yet fully persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in such matters. “Welcome” (proslambanō, receive, take to oneself) means accept fully into fellowship, not just tolerate.

But not to quarrel over opinions. Key words. “Opinions” (dialogismoi, reasonings, debatable thoughts). Do not welcome someone in order to argue them out of their scruples.

One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables. Key words. The strong believe all foods are clean (v. 14; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The weak avoid meat altogether to be safe.

Where Christians differ: what counts as a disputable matter? Some apply this chapter to every disagreement, including doctrine and morality. Verdict: Romans 14 concerns things that Scripture does not command or forbid, matters indifferent in themselves (Greek adiaphora). It does not cover the gospel itself, which Paul defends fiercely (Galatians 1:8–9), or clear moral commands, such as sexual purity (13:13). Where God has spoken plainly, we do not treat it as an opinion. Where he has not, we give liberty (Westminster 20.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak are second-class Christians. It does not mean that strong opinions are always wrong. It means that in matters God has left free, love must rule.

In a sentence. Accept the one whose faith is weak, without quarrelling over disputable matters. One person’s faith allows them to eat anything, but another, whose faith is weak, eats only vegetables.

On a Tuesday. Think of a fellow Christian who has scruples you do not share. Welcome them warmly. Do not try to argue them out of it.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains. Key words. The temptation of the strong: to look down on the weak as narrow and legalistic. “Despise” (exoutheneō, treat as nothing).

And let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats. Key words. The temptation of the weak: to condemn the strong as worldly or compromising. “Pass judgement” (krinō, condemn).

For God has welcomed him. Key words. If God has accepted him in Christ, who are you to reject him? Our fellowship must be as wide as God’s welcome.

Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? Key words. “Servant” (oiketēs, a household servant). You would not judge another family’s servant; he answers to his own master. Every believer is Christ’s servant.

It is before his own master that he stands or falls. Key words. His master decides whether his service pleases him.

And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Key words. The strong person you think is falling will in fact stand, because the Lord holds him up. A word of assurance in the middle of an ethical argument: Christ keeps his servants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can never correct a brother in sin (Galatians 6:1; Matthew 18:15). It means we do not condemn others over matters God has left free.

In a sentence. The one who eats everything must not treat with contempt the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted them. Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To their own master they stand or fall. And they will stand, for the Lord is able to make them stand.

For worship. Thank God that he welcomed you. Then ask him to help you welcome others as freely.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.

One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Key words. The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish feasts and fasts (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16). Some believers still kept them as special; others considered all days alike.

Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. Key words. “Fully convinced” (plērophoreō, fully assured). Act from conviction, not from pressure or confusion.

The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. Key words. Both sides can act for Christ. The motive matters.

The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God. Key words. The test: can you thank God for it? The eater thanks God for the food; the abstainer thanks God too. Both honour the Lord.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day. Some say this verse proves no day is special for Christians. Others hold that the fourth commandment binds Christians to a strict Sabbath observance, now on Sunday, and that this verse speaks only of Jewish ceremonial days. Verdict: The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ, who is our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10; Matthew 11:28). Christians are not bound by the Sabbath laws of Moses, and Paul here leaves Jewish days to conscience. But the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, the day of Christ’s resurrection, was the day the early church gathered for worship (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Gathering with God’s people on that day, resting from ordinary work where possible, and giving it to worship, is a great privilege and a wise rhythm, not a heavy burden. Those who keep a stricter Sunday observance, as in the Westminster tradition, do so in honour of the Lord, and should be welcomed, not despised.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular gathering for worship is optional (Hebrews 10:25).

In a sentence. One person considers one day more sacred than another; another considers every day alike. Each of them should be fully convinced in their own mind. Whoever regards one day as special does so to the Lord. Whoever eats meat does so to the Lord, for they give thanks to God; and whoever abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.

On a Tuesday. Before any choice in a disputed area, ask: can I do this for the Lord, and thank God for it? If so, go ahead with a clear conscience.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.

For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. Key words. The principle beneath all of this. No Christian is his own master. We are not self-owned.

For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. Key words. All of life, and death itself, is lived toward Christ, for him, in his service, under his eye.

So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. Key words. We belong to him. This is our great comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism begins with this verse and its truth: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ (Q. 1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we have no responsibility to others. Because we belong to the Lord, we must care for those who are also his (v. 15).

In a sentence. For none of us lives for ourselves alone, and none of us dies for ourselves alone. If we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

For worship. Say it slowly: whether I live or die, I am the Lord’s. Rest in that today, whatever you face.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.

For to this end Christ died and lived again. Key words. The death and resurrection of Christ had this purpose among others: to establish his lordship over his people.

That he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. Key words. Christ’s rule reaches beyond the grave. Believers who have died are still his (1 Thessalonians 4:14–16), and believers alive now are his. Death cannot remove us from his ownership. By dying and rising he won the right to rule over all (Philippians 2:8–11; Acts 2:36).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ became Lord only at his resurrection, as if he were not God before. He was always God the Son. But as the God-man and Redeemer, he received the lordship he won by his death and resurrection.

In a sentence. For this very reason, Christ died and returned to life so that he might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.

On a Tuesday. When someone you love dies in Christ, remember: he is still their Lord. They are safe with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”

Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? Key words. To the weak: why judge? To the strong: why despise? Note the word “brother”: you are family.

For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God. Key words. The judgement seat (bēma): the raised platform where a judge sat (Acts 18:12). In 2 Corinthians 5:10 Paul calls it the judgement seat of Christ, for God judges through Christ (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). We will not be judges there; we will be judged. So we should not take the judge’s seat now.

For it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.” Key words. From Isaiah 45:23 (with “as I live” from Isaiah 49:18). Everyone will bow before God. In Philippians 2:10–11 Paul applies the same verse to Jesus: further proof that Jesus is God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned at the judgement. There is no condemnation for those in Christ (8:1). But believers will give account of their lives, and their works will be assessed and rewarded (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

In a sentence. You, then, why do you judge your brother or sister? Or why do you treat them with contempt? For we will all stand before God’s judgement seat. It is written: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before me; every tongue will acknowledge God.”

For worship. One day you will bow before the throne. Bow now, gladly, and leave the judging to him.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.

So then each of us will give an account of himself to God. Key words. “Account” (logos, a reckoning, like an account book). Each of us: personally, individually. Of himself: not of others. You will not be asked to account for your brother’s choices in matters of conscience, but for your own life (Matthew 12:36; Hebrews 4:13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must fear the judgement as unbelievers do. In Christ we are justified. But it gives a sober seriousness to how we live.

In a sentence. So then, each of us will give an account of ourselves to God.

On a Tuesday. Spend less time evaluating other Christians, and more time preparing your own account.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (v. 13). The second half of chapter 14 moves from the mutual prohibition of judging and despising to the positive obligation of the strong: limit your freedom in cases where exercising it would damage your brother's conscience and lead him into sin. The governing concern is his welfare, not your rights.

Paul's theological grounding of this obligation is striking: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (v. 15). Christ died for the weak brother. The price paid for his soul is the blood of the Son of God. The strong believer who uses her freedom to demolish someone Christ purchased at infinite cost has committed something far more serious than poor table manners. She has treated as worthless what God treated as worth his Son.

The kingdom of God principle of v. 17 is the positive vision behind the self-limitation: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." The things that matter most — right standing before God, harmony in the body, Spirit-given joy — are not determined by what we eat. The strong person who surrenders her food freedom for the sake of a brother's peace and joy has not lost anything that matters; she has demonstrated something that matters supremely: she cares more about his joy in the Holy Spirit than about her right to eat what she pleases.

Verses 13, 15 and 17 carry the section, and the rest of it carries the argument. Verse 14 is the pivot, and it is the boldest sentence in the chapter: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Both halves are asserted. The thing really is clean, and it really is defiling for the man whose conscience says otherwise — which is why the answer to his scruple is teaching rather than pressure.

Verses 16 and 19–21 then supply the working rules. Do not let the good thing you possess — your liberty — get itself a bad name (v. 16). Pursue what makes for peace and for building up (v. 19). And the counterpart: do not, for the sake of food, demolish the work of God (v. 20). Paul is running a construction metaphor across these verses, and the choice he puts to the strong is whether their freedom is putting walls up or taking them down.

Verse 22 turns to the free man personally: the faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Not conceal your convictions, but stop parading a liberty — and then a beatitude for the man who can act without a backward glance at himself.

And v. 23 closes the chapter with the sentence that has travelled furthest from it: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. In context it is about a specific man doing a specific thing while divided in his own mind. It has been made to carry a great deal more than that.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian Liberty and the Law of Love

Romans 14:13–23 establishes the fundamental principle of Christian ethics in matters of liberty: freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is not a license to do everything the law permits without regard to others; it is the freedom to serve. The one who is free in Christ is freed from the bondage of sin and law — freed for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother's conscience is a misuse of freedom as fundamental as legalism; it is just as self-centred, only differently oriented.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific issue of meat offered to idols (closely related to the Romans 14 situation, developed more fully in 1 Corinthians 8–10) was a genuine and daily challenge in the first-century city. Much of the meat available in the marketplace had passed through a pagan temple. The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul's principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother's conscience. Now: The strong Christian in every age is tempted to treat her freedom as a badge of theological maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be managed with care. The test of genuine maturity is not the willingness to exercise freedom but the willingness to limit it out of love — to choose the brother's conscience over personal preference, his joy over your rights.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.

Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer. Key words. The conclusion of verses 1–12.

But rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. Key words. A wordplay: do not judge (krinō) others; judge (krinō, decide) this instead. A stumbling block (proskomma, something you trip over) and hindrance (skandalon, a trap, snare). Do not put anything in a brother’s path that would cause him to fall into sin.

I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. Key words. Paul sides with the strong. “In the Lord Jesus”: by Jesus’ authority and teaching. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). The food laws were fulfilled in Christ. “Unclean” (koinos, common, ritually impure).

But it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Key words. If someone believes something is wrong, it is wrong for them to do it, because they would be going against their conscience. The object is not unclean, but acting against conscience is sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sin is whatever someone thinks it is, so that morality is relative. Paul speaks only of matters indifferent, like food. Murder is unclean whatever anyone thinks.

In a sentence. Therefore let us stop passing judgement on one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in the way of a brother or sister. Paul is convinced, being fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for that person it is unclean.

On a Tuesday. Before you use your freedom in front of someone, ask: could this trip them up? Love may mean holding back.

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.

For if your brother is grieved by what you eat. Key words. “Grieved” (lypeō, pained, hurt). This is more than being annoyed. It means his conscience is wounded, perhaps because he is drawn into doing what he thinks is wrong.

You are no longer walking in love. Key words. You may be right about food, but you are wrong about love. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died. Key words. A shocking contrast. Christ gave his life for this brother; will you not give up a meal for him? “Destroy” (apollymi, ruin).

Where Christians differ: can someone for whom Christ died be destroyed? Some use this verse to argue that Christ died for people who will finally perish, and that a true believer can be lost. Verdict: Paul is warning the strong about the real tendency of their actions: what they do could lead a brother into sin and spiritual ruin. The warning is real and must be taken seriously. But God uses such warnings to keep his people. Elsewhere Paul is clear that those for whom Christ died will certainly be saved (5:8–10; 8:32–34). Christ died effectively for his sheep, and none of them will be snatched from his hand (John 10:11, 28). This is definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints. The point here is ethical: treat your brother as someone precious to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak can control the strong by complaining about everything. The concern is a brother who might be led to sin against his conscience, not one who simply disapproves.

In a sentence. If your brother or sister is distressed because of what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy someone for whom Christ died.

For worship. Christ died for that difficult brother. Let that change how you see him today.

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. Key words. “What you regard as good”: your Christian liberty. If you use it carelessly, it will be criticised (literally, blasphemed). A good freedom gets a bad name.

For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking. Key words. The kingdom of God is his rule, present now in Christ and coming in fullness. Its heart is not food. To fight over food is to miss what really matters.

But of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Key words. Righteousness: right standing with God and right living. Peace: with God and with one another. Joy: delight in God. All three are given and produced by the Holy Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean bodily things do not matter to God. It means the kingdom’s essence lies in spiritual realities, not external rules.

In a sentence. Therefore do not let what you know is good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. If you are arguing with a Christian about something that is not central, stop and ask: is this serving righteousness, peace and joy?

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.

Whoever thus serves Christ. Key words. Thus: by living for righteousness, peace and joy rather than for food. This is how we serve (douleuō, as slaves) Christ.

Is acceptable to God and approved by men. Key words. Pleasing to God, and recognised as good even by people (12:17). “Approved” (dokimos, tested and found genuine).

So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding. Key words. “Pursue” (diōkō, chase). Peace and upbuilding (oikodomē, building a house) are goals to chase actively. Every choice should help to build others up, not tear them down (1 Corinthians 14:12; Ephesians 4:29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean peace at the expense of truth.

In a sentence. Anyone who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and receives human approval. Let us therefore make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification.

For worship. Pray for your church’s peace. Then do one thing this week that builds someone up.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.

Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Key words. The work of God is your brother, God’s workmanship (Ephesians 2:10), or the church God is building. “Destroy” (katalyō, tear down, demolish). Do not demolish God’s building for a plate of meat.

Everything is indeed clean. Key words. Paul repeats that the strong are right in principle.

But it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. Key words. Literally, it is evil for the person who eats with offence. Being right is not enough. How you use your rights matters.

It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble. Key words. Love may mean giving up a right altogether, at least in certain company. Wine is mentioned perhaps because it was also used in pagan offerings.

Where Christians differ: alcohol. Some say this verse requires total abstinence from alcohol for all Christians. Others say Christians can drink freely regardless of others. Verdict: Scripture presents wine as a gift of God (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; 13:13). Drinking in moderation is a matter of Christian liberty. But love will gladly give it up where it would cause a brother to stumble, for instance around someone struggling with alcohol. Those who choose to abstain may do so for the Lord, and should not judge those who drink moderately.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the strong must give up their liberty forever and everywhere because someone somewhere disapproves. Paul speaks of situations where a real brother might be led into sin.

In a sentence. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All food is clean, but it is wrong for a person to eat anything that causes someone else to stumble. It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything else that will cause your brother or sister to fall.

On a Tuesday. Is there a freedom you enjoy that someone near you finds hard? Consider laying it down when you are with them, for love.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.

The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Key words. The faith here is your conviction about liberty: that all foods are clean. You do not need to flaunt it. Enjoy it before God, privately, without making it a test of fellowship.

Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves. Key words. “Blessed”: happy, in God’s favour. The happy person is one whose conscience does not condemn him for what he does. A clear conscience is a great gift (Acts 24:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith in Christ should be kept private. Paul speaks only of convictions about matters indifferent.

In a sentence. So whatever you believe about these things, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves.

For worship. Thank God for the freedom you have in Christ, and for a clear conscience before him.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.

But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats. Key words. “Doubts” (diakrinō, to waver, be divided in mind). If someone is unsure whether something is right but does it anyway, they are condemned, by their own conscience and before God. They acted against what they believed was God’s will.

Because the eating is not from faith. Key words. Faith here is a settled conviction before God that this is right.

For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. Key words. A general principle. If you cannot do something in confidence that it pleases God, do not do it. Acting against conscience trains you to ignore God’s voice. In a wider sense, the Reformers drew from this that even good deeds done without faith in Christ cannot please God (Hebrews 11:6; Westminster 16.7).

Textual note: the doxology. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and most at the end of chapter 16. The best evidence places it at the end of chapter 16, where the ESV prints it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conscience is infallible. Conscience can be wrongly trained and needs to be taught by Scripture. But until it is better taught, do not go against it.

In a sentence. But whoever has doubts is condemned if they eat, because their eating is not from faith; and everything that does not come from faith is sin.

On a Tuesday. When in doubt, don’t. Then go to Scripture, so that your conscience can be better taught.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.

And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.<sup>5</sup>One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.<sup>6</sup>The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.<sup>7</sup>For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself.<sup>8</sup>For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.<sup>9</sup>For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.<sup>10</sup>Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God;<sup>11</sup>for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”<sup>12</sup>So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother.<sup>14</sup>I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.<sup>15</sup>For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.<sup>16</sup>So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil.<sup>17</sup>For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.<sup>18</sup>Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men.<sup>19</sup>So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.<sup>20</sup>Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God.
