15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Romans 15 brings together three threads: the conclusion of the weak/strong argument (vv. 1–13), the personal explanation of Paul's apostolic mission (vv. 14–21), and his travel plans and prayer requests (vv. 22–33). The chapter is held together by the theme of the worldwide scope of the gospel — Christ's own example of self-giving (vv. 1–3), the Gentile mission as the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy (vv. 9–12), and Paul's ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named (vv. 20–21).

The opening section (vv. 1–13) concludes the argument of chapter 14 by pointing to Christ as the model of the strong bearing with the failings of the weak. Christ did not please himself (v. 3) — He endured the reproaches of others for their sake. The strong who follow his example are not making a heroic sacrifice; they are imitating their Lord. And the doxological prayer of vv. 5–6 and 13 frames the whole argument in worship: the God of endurance, encouragement, hope, and peace is the one who enables the unity for which Paul prays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (v. 1). Paul has waited until now to identify himself with the strong — and he identifies himself only to place the obligation of the strong front and centre. The strong do not have the right to demand that the weak keep up with them; they have the obligation to bear with the weak, to build them up, to serve their good. "Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up" (v. 2).

The model is Christ: "For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me'" (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9). The Son of God did not come to be served but to serve — to bear not only the sins of the weak but their reproaches, their insults, the consequences of their failure. The one who is most perfectly strong became the servant of all. The Christian who follows this pattern — bearing the burdens of others rather than asserting the rights of the free — is walking in the footsteps of the one who bore our ultimate burden at Calvary.

The doxological climax of the section (vv. 5–6, 13) frames the whole practical argument in prayer and worship. Paul's wish is not merely that the Roman Christians be nice to each other; it is that they glorify God together with one voice (v. 6) — the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, all singing the same praise to the same God. And the God of hope fills with all joy and peace in believing (v. 13) — not the meagre joy of people who have resolved their differences, but the overflowing joy of people who have been given hope by the Spirit.

Between the example of Christ and that benediction stand four more things, and they carry the argument to its conclusion. The first is v. 4, which explains why Paul has just settled a first-century dispute about food by quoting a psalm: whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. The Old Testament was written for the benefit of readers who did not yet exist, and its stated product is not information but hope.

The second is v. 7, and it is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. The same verb Paul used in 14:1 for receiving the weak, and in 14:3 of God receiving him, now appears a third time with Christ himself as the measure. The strong were told to welcome; here everyone is told to welcome everyone, on the pattern of a welcome none of them deserved.

The third is vv. 8–9, where Paul states how one Christ serves two peoples. He became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs — that is, to demonstrate God’s truthfulness — and he did it so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. The two halves are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is the point: Israel receives a kept promise, the nations receive sheer mercy, and neither group has grounds to look down on the other.

The fourth is the chain of quotations in vv. 9–12, drawn deliberately from every part of the Hebrew Bible — the Law (Deuteronomy 32:43), the Writings (Psalm 18:49; Psalm 117:1) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11:10). Paul is not producing a proof text. He is showing that the inclusion of the nations was the settled expectation of the whole canon, and the chain ends on the word the benediction will pick up: in him will the Gentiles hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as the Model of Solidarity with the Weak

The Christological grounding of the strong's obligation in Romans 15:3 is one of Paul's most important ethical moves. Ethics derived from the example of Christ is not mere imitation-of-a-good-man moralism; it is participation in the pattern of the one who is Lord, whose servanthood was the shape of his sovereignty, whose self-giving is the source of the Christian's capacity for self-giving. When Paul says "bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), the law of Christ is precisely this: the pattern of the one who bore what he did not owe so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" — was not an abstract aspiration. The Roman church had real divisions: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people from different social classes and national backgrounds. The one voice of praise was the visible, social miracle that would demonstrate to the watching city of Rome that something genuinely new had entered the world. Now: The unity of diverse believers in genuine, cross-cultural, cross-social worship is still the most powerful apologetic the church has available. A community of people who have every reason to be divided — by race, class, culture, education, politics — worshipping together with one voice glorifies the God whose gospel is the only power that creates such unity.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.

Meaning first. Romans 15 has two parts. In verses 1–13, Paul finishes the argument about the strong and the weak that began in 14:1. The strong must bear with the weak, as Christ did not please himself (vv. 1–6); and all must welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, for Christ came to serve the Jews and to bring the Gentiles to praise God, as the Scriptures foretold (vv. 7–12). He ends with a prayer that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace (v. 13). In verses 14–33, Paul begins to close the letter. He explains why he wrote so boldly: his priestly calling to offer the Gentiles to God (vv. 14–21). Then he shares his travel plans: first Jerusalem with the gift from the Gentile churches, then Rome, then Spain, and he asks them to pray for him (vv. 22–33). Theology and mission, love and plans, all serve the glory of God among the nations.

We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak. Key words. Paul counts himself among the strong. “Obligation” (opheilō, we owe it, a debt). “Bear with” (bastazō, carry, shoulder a load, as in Galatians 6:2). “Failings” (asthenēmata, weaknesses): their scruples and tender consciences. The strong are not to put up with the weak grudgingly but to carry them.

And not to please ourselves. Key words. Strength is for serving others, not for doing whatever we like.

Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. Key words. Pleasing the neighbour does not mean flattering or giving in to every demand, but seeking his real good: “to build him up” (oikodomē, edification). Pleasing people for their good is different from being a people-pleaser (Galatians 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the strong must give up the truth about Christian liberty. It means they use their liberty for love.

In a sentence. We who are strong ought to bear with the failings of the weak and not to please ourselves. Each of us should please our neighbours for their good, to build them up.

On a Tuesday. Use your strength today, whether in knowledge, maturity, or resources, to carry someone weaker, not to please yourself.

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”

For Christ did not please himself. Key words. The supreme example. Christ, who had every right, gave them all up. He came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45; Philippians 2:5–8). If he did not please himself, how can we insist on our rights over food?

But as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.” Key words. From Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the suffering righteous one, often applied to Christ (11:9; John 2:17). The insults people hurled against God fell on Christ. He bore the scorn and hatred aimed at God, and he bore it for us. He carried a burden far heavier than any the strong are asked to carry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ never enjoyed anything, or had no joy. He did the Father’s will with delight (Hebrews 12:2). But he never put his own comfort first.

In a sentence. For even Christ did not please himself, but, as it is written: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”

For worship. Thank Jesus for bearing the reproach that should have fallen on you. Let that make you willing to bear a little for others.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,

For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction. Key words. Paul has just quoted a psalm and applied it. He explains why: the whole Old Testament was written for Christians too. “Instruction” (didaskalia, teaching). It is not just ancient history but God’s word to us (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16).

That through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. Key words. “Endurance” (hypomonē, steadfastness under trial) and “encouragement” (paraklēsis, comfort, exhortation) both come through the Scriptures. Their goal is hope. The Bible tells stories of God keeping his promises across centuries, which teaches us to keep trusting.

May the God of endurance and encouragement. Key words. A prayer. God is the source of the endurance and comfort that Scripture brings. Scripture is his voice.

Grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus. Key words. Harmony: literally to think the same thing (as in 12:16). In accord with Christ Jesus: according to his example and will. Unity is not uniformity of opinion on food, but one mind about Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament is only about us. It is first about God and his Christ. But because it is about him, it gives us hope.

In a sentence. For everything that was written in the past was written to teach us, so that through the endurance taught in the Scriptures and the encouragement they provide we might have hope. May the God who gives endurance and encouragement give you the same attitude of mind toward each other that Christ Jesus had,

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament not as a dusty record but as God’s word for you. Look for his faithfulness and take hope.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.

That together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The goal of unity is worship. “Together” (homothymadon, with one passion, as in Acts 1:14; 2:46) and “with one voice” (literally one mouth). A divided church cannot praise God with one voice. When strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, sing together, God is glorified.

Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you. Key words. “Welcome” (proslambanō) is the same word as 14:1. The measure of our welcome is Christ’s welcome. He received us when we were sinners, ungodly and enemies (5:6–10). So we can receive one another with all our differences.

For the glory of God. Key words. Christ welcomed us for God’s glory; and when we welcome one another, God is glorified again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we welcome unrepentant sin into the church (1 Corinthians 5). It means we welcome all whom Christ has welcomed.

In a sentence. so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring praise to God.

For worship. When you sing in church on Sunday, look around: Christ welcomed every one of these people. Praise God with them, with one voice.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”

For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised. Key words. Christ came first as a servant (diakonos) to the Jews, born under the law, ministering in Israel (Matthew 15:24; Galatians 4:4). He welcomed the Jews.

To show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs. Key words. Truthfulness (alētheia): God’s faithfulness to his word. By coming to Israel, Christ proved God true to his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (2 Corinthians 1:20).

And in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Key words. Christ also welcomed the Gentiles. For the Jews, his coming showed God’s faithfulness to promises; for the Gentiles, who had no promises, it showed pure mercy (Ephesians 2:12). Both have reason to praise.

As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.” Key words. From Psalm 18:49 (also 2 Samuel 22:50). David, the king, praises God among the nations. Christ, the Son of David, leads the praise of God among the Gentiles (Hebrews 2:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Gentiles were an afterthought. God’s plan always included them (Genesis 12:3), as the following quotations show.

In a sentence. For Paul tells you that Christ has become a servant of the Jews on behalf of God’s truth, so that the promises made to the patriarchs might be confirmed and, moreover, that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles; I will sing the praises of your name.”

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises. The same Christ who confirmed the promises to Abraham will keep every promise he has made to you.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.” And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”

And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Greek translation, at the end of the Song of Moses. Gentiles rejoicing together with Israel: exactly the unity Paul wants in Rome.

And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.” Key words. From Psalm 117:1, the shortest psalm. All the nations are summoned to worship the LORD. Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always meant the nations to praise him: Deuteronomy (Law), Psalms 18 and 117 (Writings), and Isaiah (Prophets, v. 12). The whole Old Testament agrees.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Gentiles replace Israel. They rejoice with his people.

In a sentence. Again, it says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.” And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles; let all the peoples extol him.”

For worship. Pray Psalm 117 today. Then pray for a nation where Christ is not yet praised.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.”

And again Isaiah says. Key words. From Isaiah 11:10 in the Greek translation.

“The root of Jesse will come.” Key words. Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line (Isaiah 11:1). When David’s dynasty seemed cut down like a tree stump, a shoot would grow from the root. Jesus is that root and offspring of David (Revelation 5:5; 22:16).

Even he who arises to rule the Gentiles. Key words. “Arises” (anistamai) is the word used for resurrection. The risen Christ rules the nations.

In him will the Gentiles hope. Key words. The nations will put their hope in Israel’s Messiah. Hope links this verse to verse 13.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule over the nations is only future. He reigns now, at God’s right hand, and the nations are coming to him through the gospel (Matthew 28:18–19).

In a sentence. And again, Isaiah says, “The Root of Jesse will spring up, one who will arise to rule over the nations; in him the Gentiles will hope.”

On a Tuesday. Put your hope in the risen king who rules the nations. The news headlines do not have the last word; he does.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

May the God of hope. Key words. A benediction to close the section. God is the source and object of hope. He gives it, and it rests in him.

Fill you with all joy and peace in believing. Key words. Joy and peace, two of the marks of the kingdom (14:17). In believing: they come through faith, as we keep trusting God. Not by trying to feel joy, but by looking to Christ.

So that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. Key words. “Abound” (perisseuō, overflow). Not a trickle of hope but a flood, and it comes by the Spirit’s power, not human optimism (5:5; 8:24–25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians never feel sorrow or anxiety. It means that God can fill a believer with joy and peace even in sorrow (2 Corinthians 6:10).

In a sentence. May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you trust in him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

For worship. Pray this verse for yourself and for someone you love, today, by name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theology and pastoral exhortation to autobiography and travel plans — and the transition is less abrupt than it appears. His account of his apostolic ministry is itself a miniature theology of mission. He describes himself as a minister (leitourgos — a cultic, priestly term) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing the priestly service of the gospel of God, offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). The mission to the Gentiles is not merely evangelistic strategy; it is priestly worship — the bringing of the nations as an offering to God.

The scope of Paul's completed mission (vv. 19–21) is staggering: from Jerusalem to Illyricum (modern-day Croatia), he has "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ." Not because every person has heard it but because he has planted the gospel in strategic centres throughout the eastern Mediterranean, from which the word can spread into every surrounding region. His ambition going forward is equally characteristic: not to build on another man's foundation, but to preach where Christ has not yet been named. The pioneer missionary impulse is written into the logic of the commission.

The prayer request of vv. 30–33 is one of the most moving passages in Paul's letters. He asks the Roman church to "strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" — the word for "strive together" (sunagōnizomai) is an athletic term, contending alongside someone in a contest. Prayer is work, and Paul wants co-labourers in it. He asks for three things: deliverance from unbelievers in Judea, acceptance of his offering by the Jerusalem church, and the joy of reaching Rome. All three will be granted, none in the form he pictured; the Rome visit will happen, but in chains.

Two stretches of the section deserve adding. The first is how it opens (vv. 14–15). Having written the most demanding letter in the New Testament, Paul tells its recipients that he is satisfied about them — full of goodness, filled with knowledge, able to instruct one another — and that what he has written is offered by way of reminder. He does not present a word of it as news.

The second is vv. 22–29, which contains the two most concrete things in the chapter. One is Spain (v. 24): Paul is not looking for another province but for the western edge of the known world, and he is asking Rome to become the base that sends him there. This is why the letter exists in the form it does.

The other is the Jerusalem collection (vv. 25–28), a relief fund gathered from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul is in Corinth, he intends to go west, and he is about to travel east instead — at real personal risk — to deliver money. And he does not call it charity. He says the Gentiles owe it to them (v. 27): having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, they owe material ones back. The collection is the argument of chapters 9–11 converted into currency and carried some eight hundred miles in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as Priestly Worship

Romans 15:16 is one of the most theologically rich descriptions of apostolic mission in the New Testament. Paul images his Gentile mission as priestly service — the offering of the nations to God as a sacrifice acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This means that evangelism is not merely a strategy for church growth or a duty to be discharged; it is an act of worship, the gathering of the nations to lay them as a living offering before the God who created and redeemed them. This priestly vision of mission has sustained every great missionary movement in the Reformed tradition, from Calvin's Geneva sending missionaries to France, to William Carey going to India, to the countless sent ones who have carried the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's completed mission from Jerusalem to Illyricum represents perhaps fifteen years of gruelling apostolic labour — multiple missionary journeys, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, cold and hunger. The nonchalance with which he refers to having "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel" in this vast region is the confidence of a man who has done what he was sent to do and is already looking at the next frontier. Now: The pioneer missionary impulse of v. 20 — to preach where Christ has not been named — remains the highest calling in the church's mission. There are still places, peoples, and communities where the name of Christ has not been proclaimed. The obligation Paul felt is the obligation the church still carries, until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God

I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers. Key words. “Satisfied” (peithō, persuaded, confident). After strong words, Paul reassures them. He did not write because he thought they were a bad church.

That you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. Key words. Goodness (agathōsynē, moral excellence, kindness). Knowledge: of the gospel. Able to instruct (noutheteō, admonish, counsel): ordinary church members are able to counsel each other from God’s word (Colossians 3:16).

But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder. Key words. “Very boldly”: Paul admits he has been direct. By way of reminder: much of what he wrote, they already knew. Christians need to be reminded of truths they know (2 Peter 1:12–13).

Because of the grace given me by God. Key words. His apostleship is a gift of grace, and it gives him the right to write this way (1:5; 12:3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that teaching is only for experts. All believers can and should instruct one another.

In a sentence. Paul himself is convinced, brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with knowledge and competent to instruct one another. Yet he has written to you quite boldly on some points to remind you of them again, because of the grace God gave him

On a Tuesday. You are able to encourage and counsel a fellow believer from Scripture. Do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.

To be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. Key words. “Minister” here is leitourgos, a word for priestly or public service (13:6).

In the priestly service of the gospel of God. Key words. “Priestly service” (hierourgeō, to act as a priest). Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God as a sacrifice. His altar is the gospel; his offering is people.

So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Key words. The offering is the Gentiles themselves (Isaiah 66:20). Once unclean in Jewish eyes, they are now made holy, not by circumcision, but by the Spirit. This is a powerful argument against the scruples of the weak: God accepts the Gentiles.

In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God. Key words. “Proud” (kauchēsis, boasting, glorying). Only in Christ Jesus: he boasts not in himself but in what Christ did through him (1 Corinthians 15:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that ministers are priests offering sacrifices of atonement, as in Roman Catholic teaching on the Mass. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Paul’s priestly language is a picture of evangelism. All believers are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5).

In a sentence. to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. He has the priestly duty of proclaiming the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Therefore he glories in Christ Jesus in his service to God.

For worship. Thank God that he accepts you, made holy by the Spirit. And offer him your life and witness as a priestly gift.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.

For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me. Key words. Paul will speak only of what Christ did. Paul was the instrument; Christ was the worker.

To bring the Gentiles to obedience. Key words. The obedience of faith (1:5; 16:26): believing the gospel and living under Christ’s lordship.

By word and deed. Key words. Preaching and actions: both proclaimed the gospel.

By the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God. Key words. Signs (pointing to something beyond) and wonders (causing amazement). Paul did miracles that confirmed his message (Acts 14:3; 19:11–12; 2 Corinthians 12:12).

So that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ. Key words. Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia (modern Albania, Croatia and nearby). Paul had preached in a great arc from Jerusalem through Syria, Asia Minor and Greece. “Fulfilled” means he had fully preached the gospel, planting churches in key cities, from which it would spread.

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Some teach that signs and wonders like those of the apostles should accompany all gospel preaching today. Verdict: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). They confirmed the apostolic message as Scripture was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and the canon complete, the miraculous sign gifts have ceased as a regular part of ministry. God still answers prayer and can heal and work wonders as he pleases, but the gospel is now confirmed by the written word. This is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

What it does not mean. It does not mean miracles are the main way the gospel spreads. Paul puts word first.

In a sentence. Paul will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through him in leading the Gentiles to obey God by what he has said and done, by the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, he has fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Speak only of what Christ has done through you. Let your stories of ministry glorify him, not you.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation, but as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.”

And thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel. Key words. “Ambition” (philotimeomai, literally love of honour; to aspire, make it your aim, as in 2 Corinthians 5:9).

Not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation. Key words. Paul’s pioneer calling: to go where no church yet existed. Others could water where he planted (1 Corinthians 3:6, 10).

But as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.” Key words. From Isaiah 52:15, from the great servant song. The servant’s message would reach kings and nations who had never heard. Paul sees his mission as fulfilling that promise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that building up existing churches is less important. Paul spent years teaching established churches. But some are called to pioneer.

In a sentence. It has always been Paul’s ambition to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that he would not be building on someone else’s foundation. Rather, as it is written: “Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

For worship. Pray for the unreached peoples of the world, and for missionaries who go where Christ has not been named.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,

This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. Key words. His pioneer work kept him busy elsewhere (1:13). “Hindered” (enkoptō, cut in on, blocked).

But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions. Key words. He has planted churches across the eastern Mediterranean. The foundation is laid; local believers can carry on.

And since I have longed for many years to come to you. Key words. Paul had wanted to see Rome for a long time (1:10–11; Acts 19:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in those regions was now a Christian. It means the strategic churches were planted.

In a sentence. This is why he has often been hindered from coming to you. But now that there is no more place for him to work in these regions, and since he has been longing for many years to visit you,

On a Tuesday. Your plans may be hindered for years by God’s work elsewhere. Wait patiently. His timing is good.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.

I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain. Key words. Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul reached it is uncertain: Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says he reached the limits of the west, which may mean Spain. Paul’s vision was to take the gospel to the ends of the earth.

And to be helped on my journey there by you. Key words. “Helped on my journey” (propempō, send forward) was a technical term for missionary support: supplies, money, companions (Acts 15:3; 1 Corinthians 16:6; Titus 3:13; 3 John 6). Part of Paul’s purpose in writing Romans was to win their support for the Spanish mission.

Once I have enjoyed your company for a while. Key words. Paul looks forward to fellowship, being filled up (empiplēmi) by them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul saw Rome as just a stopover. He loved them and wanted to share spiritual gifts with them (1:11–12).

In a sentence. Paul plans to do so when he goes to Spain. He hopes to see you while passing through and to have you assist him on his journey there, after he has enjoyed your company for a while.

For worship. Ask how your church can send others forward on gospel journeys. Give and pray for missionaries.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.

At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. Key words. “Bringing aid” (diakoneō, serving). Before Rome, Paul must make a long trip back east.

For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem. Key words. The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem took years to gather (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica) and Achaia (Corinth) were in Greece. “Contribution” is koinōnia, fellowship, sharing: the gift was an expression of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul cared only for spiritual needs. The gospel produces concern for the poor (Galatians 2:10).

In a sentence. Now, however, Paul is on his way to Jerusalem in the service of the Lord’s people there. For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the Lord’s people in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Generosity across cultural lines builds unity. Give this week to help poor believers somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.

For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. Key words. Glad giving, and also a debt. Both are true at once.

For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings. Key words. The gospel, the promises, the Messiah, the Scriptures: all came to the Gentiles from the Jews (11:17–18). “Share” is koinōneō.

They ought also to be of service to them in material blessings. Key words. Literally, in fleshly things: money, food. “Be of service” is leitourgeō, priestly service. Giving money is a form of worship (Philippians 4:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation can be paid for. It means gratitude for spiritual gifts shows itself in material generosity (1 Corinthians 9:11; Galatians 6:6).

In a sentence. They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in the Jews’ spiritual blessings, they owe it to the Jews to share with them their material blessings.

For worship. You have received spiritual riches from others: the people who taught you, your church, the saints of history. Give generously in return.

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.

When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected. Key words. Literally, having sealed to them this fruit. Sealing meant delivering it safely and officially. The gift is the fruit of the gospel among the Gentiles.

I will leave for Spain by way of you. Key words. The plan: Jerusalem, then Rome, then Spain.

I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ. Key words. Paul is confident that his visit, whenever it happens, will be full of Christ’s blessing. In fact he came to Rome as a prisoner in chains (Acts 28:16), but still in the fullness of Christ’s blessing: the gospel advanced (Philippians 1:12–13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul knew exactly how things would go. He planned, and God directed his steps differently (Proverbs 16:9; James 4:13–15).

In a sentence. So after he has completed this task and has made sure that they have received this contribution, he will go to Spain and visit you on the way. He knows that when he comes to you, he will come in the full measure of the blessing of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Make your plans, and hold them loosely. If God reroutes you, his blessing can still be full.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,

I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit. Key words. A solemn request. The love of the Spirit: the love the Spirit produces in believers, which binds them together. Notice the Trinity in verse 30: the Lord Jesus, the Spirit, and God (the Father).

To strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf. Key words. “Strive together” (synagōnizomai, wrestle together, from which we get agonise). Prayer is a fight (Colossians 4:12). Paul, the great apostle, asks ordinary believers he has never met to pray for him.

That I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. Key words. Paul knew Jerusalem was dangerous for him; many Jews there hated him (Acts 20:22–23; 21:10–14).

And that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints. Key words. He also feared the Jewish believers might reject a gift from Gentiles, because of suspicion about his ministry (Acts 21:20–21).

How God answered. These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem, but his life was spared; the believers received him gladly (Acts 21:17); he was protected by the Romans from a plot to kill him (Acts 23:12–35); and he reached Rome at the empire’s expense, as a prisoner (Acts 27–28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer is a way to control God. We pray, and God answers in his wisdom, sometimes better than we asked.

In a sentence. Paul urges you, brothers and sisters, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join him in his struggle by praying to God for him. Pray that he may be kept safe from the unbelievers in Judea and that the contribution he takes to Jerusalem may be favourably received by the Lord’s people there,

For worship. Wrestle in prayer today for a missionary or pastor by name. Ask for their safety and fruitfulness.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

So that by God’s will I may come to you with joy. Key words. By God’s will: all Paul’s plans depend on it (1:10). He did come, though not as he had planned.

And be refreshed in your company. Key words. “Refreshed” (synanapauomai, to rest together). Even apostles need rest and the encouragement of fellow believers.

May the God of peace be with you all. Amen. Key words. A benediction. The God of peace: who made peace with us through Christ (5:1) and gives peace within the church, between strong and weak, Jew and Gentile (14:19; 16:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter ends here. Chapter 16 adds greetings and a final doxology.

In a sentence. so that he may come to you with joy, by God’s will, and in your company be refreshed. The God of peace be with you all. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Be someone others are refreshed to be with. And let the God of peace be with you as you go.
