16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is sometimes treated as an appendix — a list of greetings to be skimmed before putting the letter down. It is far more than that. The twenty-six people Paul greets in vv. 3–15 (twenty-four of them by name), with several households besides, constitute a remarkable social portrait of the early Roman church: women who worked hard in the Lord, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, households that may have belonged to powerful men, and many names common among slaves and freedmen. The community Paul is writing to and for is not an abstraction; it is these people, in this city, with these names and these stories.

The chapter also contains a sharp warning against those who create division and cause obstacles contrary to the doctrine (vv. 17–20) — a reminder that the unity and the gospel Paul has laboured to establish require vigilance as well as love. And then the letter ends where it began: with the gospel. The doxology of vv. 25–27 is one of the most comprehensive summaries of Paul's gospel in the New Testament — the mystery kept secret for long ages, now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The list of greetings in Romans 16 is the most extensive in Paul's letters and has rightly been treated as a window into the earliest church. Twenty-six individuals are greeted, twenty-four of them by name, along with several households and groups. The social diversity is remarkable: Phoebe, a deacon and patron from Cenchreae; Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers and theological teachers; Andronicus and Junia, "well known to the apostles" and Christians before Paul; Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked very hard. Slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles — all members of the same body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) deserves special notice: Paul commends her as a deacon (diakonos — the same word used of male church officers) of the church in Cenchreae, and as a patron (prostatis) who has been of help to many, including Paul himself. She was almost certainly the letter-carrier — the person who bore the manuscript of Romans from Corinth to Rome and, as was customary for letter-carriers in antiquity, would have read and explained the letter to its recipients. The greatest theological letter ever written was entrusted to a woman for its first public delivery.

The greeting "holy kiss" (v. 16) — appearing in four of Paul's letters — was the physical expression of the family bond that the gospel created. In the ancient world, the kiss of greeting belonged chiefly to family. The church that greeted one another with a holy kiss was declaring, physically and publicly, that these people — strangers by blood, foreigners by origin, divided by every social category — were family. The gospel had done what nothing else could do: created a new human community that crossed every boundary the ancient world had erected.

Between the famous names and the holy kiss lies the bulk of the list, and it is worth not skipping. Verses 8–15 greet Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, Herodion, Tryphaena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus and his mother, then Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas.

Several of those are ordinary slave names, and three of them — Ampliatus, Stachys and Persis — Paul calls beloved. Two are greeted not as individuals but as households — and in one of them only those in the Lord. Three of the workers named in this stretch are women, and one man is remembered chiefly through his mother, who Paul says has been a mother to him as well (v. 13).

And the last two clusters are given no description at all — nine names and an unnamed sister, with nothing attached, followed by the brothers who are with them and all the saints who are with them, who are not named at all. That proportion is the honest shape of the church in every century: a few remembered for something, most remembered only for being there, and the majority not written down.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Humanity

Romans 16:1–16 is the embodiment in flesh-and-blood names of Paul's theological argument in chapters 1–15. The "no distinction between Jew and Greek" of 10:12, the olive tree of Jew and Gentile grafted together of 11:17–24, the "welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you" of 15:7 — all of these are visible in the list of names. This is what the gospel looks like when it has done its work: Phoebe and Priscilla and Andronicus and Junia, the patron and the tentmaker, the first convert and the former persecutor's associates, all belonging to each other in Christ. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a sociology.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The social mixing of Romans 16 was, by the standards of the first-century world, radical to the point of scandalous. Social boundaries in Rome were enforced with rigour; meals with social inferiors were a form of self-humiliation. The church that gathered Phoebe the patron and the slaves of great households and the Jewish tentmakers for common worship and common greeting was an institution the Roman world had no category for. Now: The contemporary church's ability or inability to embody the social diversity of Romans 16 is one of the most important tests of its gospel fidelity. A church that is racially, socially, or economically homogeneous by design has stopped short of what the gospel creates. The greetings of Romans 16 are not an antiquarian curiosity; they are the template for the new humanity the gospel is building.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.

Meaning first. Romans 16 closes the letter. It may look like a list of names to skip, but it shows what the gospel of chapters 1–15 produces: a real family of men and women, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, rich and poor, who love and serve one another. First, Paul commends Phoebe, who probably carried the letter (vv. 1–2). Then he greets twenty-six people by name in Rome, many with a word of warm praise (vv. 3–16). Then he warns against those who cause divisions with false teaching, and promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan (vv. 17–20). Then his companions send greetings, including the scribe Tertius (vv. 21–23). Finally, a great doxology sums up the whole letter: glory to the only wise God, who strengthens us by the gospel of Jesus Christ, the mystery now revealed to all nations to bring about the obedience of faith (vv. 25–27).

I commend to you our sister Phoebe. Key words. A letter of commendation (synistēmi, recommend, introduce): a common practice so that travelling believers could be trusted and received (2 Corinthians 3:1). Phoebe was probably carrying this letter to Rome. “Our sister”: a member of God’s family.

A servant of the church at Cenchreae. Key words. Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth, where Paul was writing (Acts 18:18). “Servant” is diakonos; the ESV notes that it can be rendered deaconess. It may mean she served in a general way, or that she held a recognised office of service.

That you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints. Key words. Receive her as a fellow believer should be received: with love, hospitality and honour.

And help her in whatever she may need from you. Key words. Perhaps she had business in Rome, legal or commercial, and needed help.

For she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. Key words. “Patron” (prostatis, benefactor, protector, helper): probably a woman of some means who used her wealth and influence to support Paul and others, perhaps opening her home and helping travellers.

Where Christians differ: Phoebe and women in church office. Some argue from Phoebe that women may hold any office in the church, including elder or pastor. Others deny that Phoebe held any office at all. Verdict: Phoebe was an honoured servant of her church, and she may well have held a recognised role of service, which some Reformed churches call deaconess (compare 1 Timothy 3:11). The office of deacon is one of practical service and mercy, not of governing or teaching the church with authority. The New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor, with its authority to teach and rule, for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). This is the complementarian view: men and women are equal in worth and in Christ (Galatians 3:28), with different callings in the church and home. Phoebe’s example shows how highly Paul valued women’s ministry, and churches should honour and use women’s gifts fully within Scripture’s pattern.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women’s service is second-class. Paul begins his greetings by commending a woman.

In a sentence. Paul commends to you our sister Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae. He asks you to receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of his people and to give her any help she may need from you, for she has been the benefactor of many people, including him.

On a Tuesday. Use what you have, whether home, money or influence, to help those who serve the gospel, as Phoebe did.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. Key words. Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’ expulsion of the Jews (Acts 18:2) was lifted. They were a married couple, tentmakers like Paul. Paul met them in Corinth, worked with them, and took them to Ephesus, where they taught Apollos the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:2–3, 18–26). They also hosted a church in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19). Prisca is often named first, perhaps because she was more prominent or of higher social rank.

My fellow workers in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Fellow workers” (synergoi): partners in gospel ministry.

Who risked their necks for my life. Key words. Literally, laid down their own necks: an image of offering one’s neck to the executioner’s sword. We do not know the event, perhaps the riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41).

To whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well. Key words. By saving Paul, they served all the churches he founded.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Priscilla held the office of elder because she helped teach Apollos. She and her husband explained the gospel to him privately, in their home, which is the kind of instruction every believer may give.

In a sentence. Greet Priscilla and Aquila, Paul’s co-workers in Christ Jesus. They risked their lives for him. Not only he but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.

For worship. Thank God for Christian couples who serve together, open their home, and risk much for the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.

Greet also the church in their house. Key words. Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings until the third century. Rome probably had several house churches (vv. 5, 14, 15). The church (ekklēsia) is the people, not the building.

Greet my beloved Epaenetus. Key words. “Beloved”: Paul’s warm affection for individuals.

Who was the first convert to Christ in Asia. Key words. Literally the firstfruits (aparchē) of Asia for Christ. Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital. The first convert is a pledge of the harvest to come. He may have been converted through Priscilla and Aquila’s ministry in Ephesus.

What it does not mean. It does not mean house churches are the only biblical model. They were the practical form in that time. The essentials are the word, the sacraments, prayer and fellowship (Acts 2:42).

In a sentence. Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet Paul’s dear friend Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.

On a Tuesday. Your home can be a place of church life: Bible study, prayer, hospitality. Open it.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.

Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Key words. “Worked hard” (kopiaō, toiled to the point of weariness). We know nothing else of her, but God knows all her labour.

Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen. Key words. “Kinsmen”: fellow Jews (9:3). They were probably a husband and wife. The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias, a man’s name, but Junia, a common Roman woman’s name, is more likely.

And my fellow prisoners. Key words. They had been in prison with Paul at some point, or for the same cause (2 Corinthians 11:23).

They are well known to the apostles. Key words. The Greek phrase can mean “well known to the apostles” (ESV) or “outstanding among the apostles” (ESV note).

And they were in Christ before me. Key words. They became Christians before Paul’s conversion, around AD 33–34, so they were among the very first believers, perhaps from Pentecost (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome).

Where Christians differ: was Junia an apostle? Some say Junia was a female apostle, and so women may hold any office. Others insist the name must be male, or the phrase must mean only “known to the apostles.” Verdict: The ESV reading, well known to the apostles, is grammatically well supported. But even if the phrase means outstanding among the apostles, the word apostle is used in the New Testament in two senses: the unique apostles of Christ (the Twelve and Paul), who had seen the risen Lord and laid the church’s foundation; and messengers or missionaries sent by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25). Andronicus and Junia could only be apostles in the second sense, as travelling missionaries. This does not overturn the New Testament’s teaching on eldership (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean their faithfulness was small. They suffered for Christ and were highly regarded by the church’s leaders.

In a sentence. Greet Mary, who worked very hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, Paul’s fellow Jews who have been in prison with him. They are well known among the apostles, and they were in Christ before he was.

For worship. Thank God for the believers who came to Christ before you and prayed and suffered for the church you now enjoy.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.

Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Key words. Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome. Ampliatus is found in inscriptions in the imperial household. A tomb in one of Rome’s oldest Christian catacombs bears this name.

Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ. Key words. “Our”: he had worked with Paul and others in the gospel. Urbanus (from urbs, city) was a common Roman slave name.

And my beloved Stachys. Key words. Stachys means ear of grain. Again, Paul’s love for individuals.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slaves were second-class in the church. In Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28). Some of the most honoured members of the Roman church were probably slaves or former slaves.

In a sentence. Greet Ampliatus, whom Paul loves in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in Christ, and his dear friend Stachys.

On a Tuesday. In the church, social status means nothing before God. Treat everyone in your church as beloved in the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.

Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Key words. “Approved” (dokimos, tested and proved genuine). He had been through some trial and stood firm.

Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Key words. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably include slaves and freedmen belonging to important men. Aristobulus may have been the grandson of Herod the Great, who lived in Rome. His household slaves would remain known by his name after his death.

Greet my kinsman Herodion. Key words. A fellow Jew. His name suggests a link with the Herod family, fitting the mention of Aristobulus.

Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus. Key words. Narcissus may be the powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, who was forced to commit suicide in AD 54. His slaves would have passed into the emperor’s household. “Those in the Lord”: only some in that household were believers. The gospel had reached into the imperial palace (Philippians 4:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a whole household had to believe for some members to be saved. Individuals came to Christ even in pagan households.

In a sentence. Greet Apelles, whose fidelity to Christ has stood the test. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, Paul’s fellow Jew. Greet those in the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.

For worship. Pray for believers who are the only Christians in their homes or workplaces.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.

Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Key words. Probably sisters, perhaps twins. Their names mean dainty and delicate, yet they were hard workers (kopiaō) in the Lord.

Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Key words. Persis means Persian woman, perhaps a former slave. Paul notes her past labour: she has worked hard, perhaps now elderly.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord. Key words. Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions (Mark 15:21). Mark wrote his Gospel probably for the church in Rome, and names Simon’s sons as people his readers knew. If so, the man who carried Jesus’ cross had a son in the Roman church. “Chosen” (eklektos): elect, or perhaps choice, outstanding.

Also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well. Key words. She had cared for Paul like a mother, perhaps in Antioch, where men from Cyrene were among the church’s leaders (Acts 11:20; 13:1). Spiritual motherhood is a precious ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Rufus was more elect than others. All believers are chosen in Christ (Ephesians 1:4).

In a sentence. Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, those women who work hard in the Lord. Greet his dear friend Persis, another woman who has worked very hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to Paul too.

On a Tuesday. Be a spiritual mother or father to someone younger in the faith. Feed them, pray for them, open your home.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.

Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Key words. Probably a house church, or a group of believers who lived or worked together. Most of these names are typical of slaves and freedmen.

Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them. Key words. Another group, perhaps another house church. Philologus and Julia may have been husband and wife, with Nereus and his sister as their children.

The names. Paul greets twenty-six people by name, about a third of them women, a mix of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free. He knew so many people in a city he had never visited because believers travelled, and many had met him elsewhere. The church in Rome was a network of house churches, held together by love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul greeted only important people. Most were ordinary. All were precious.

In a sentence. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas and the other brothers and sisters with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the Lord’s people who are with them.

For worship. God knows each of his people by name. Thank him that your name is known to him and written in his book (Luke 10:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. Key words. A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends in that culture, on the cheek. Holy: pure, set apart, expressing the love of brothers and sisters in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; 1 Peter 5:14). In the early church it became part of the worship service, before the Lord’s Supper.

All the churches of Christ greet you. Key words. The churches Paul had planted, or those he was representing, send their love. The church is worldwide.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians today must greet with a literal kiss. The principle is warm, pure, family affection, expressed in a way fitting for each culture: a handshake, an embrace.

In a sentence. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send greetings.

On a Tuesday. Greet your fellow believers warmly on Sunday. Learn names. Look people in the eye.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing doxology, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20) against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught. The letter has been, among other things, a sustained argument for the unity of the body across the strong/weak divide; it would be a bitter irony if the letter itself became a tool of division. Paul's instruction is clear: watch them, avoid them. The divisive person — whatever their theological credentials — is not serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive the naive with smooth talk and flattery.

The closing doxology (vv. 25–27) returns to the letter's great themes for one final, comprehensive statement. God is able to strengthen — the power of the gospel is not an argument but a strengthening. According to Paul's gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ — these are identified: Paul's gospel is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not a human theological construct. According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages — the gospel is not a new invention; it is the disclosure of what God planned from before time began. Now made known to all the nations — the universality Paul has argued throughout. For the obedience of faith — the phrase that bracketed the letter in 1:5 now closes it. To the only wise God — the doxology of chapter 11 returns, now applied to the whole letter's argument. Through Jesus Christ — the mediator of all grace and all glory. To whom be glory forever. Amen.

The letter that began with Paul introducing himself as a slave of Christ and set apart for the gospel ends with everything returning to God — from him, through him, and to him. The argument is complete. The doxology is the only adequate conclusion. Amen.

Two stretches sit between the warning and the doxology and should not be passed over. The first is v. 19, where Paul softens nothing but changes his tone: their obedience is known everywhere and he is glad of them, and what he wants is that they be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. It is the counterpart to the warning — the way to be undeceived is not to become worldly-wise about corruption but to know goodness well.

The second is vv. 21–24, a second greeting list, this time from Paul’s end of the journey: Timothy and three Jewish co-workers; Gaius, in whose house both Paul and the whole Corinthian church are lodged; Erastus, the city treasurer, whose name has plausibly been found on a paving inscription at Corinth; and Quartus. Between them stands v. 22, where Tertius, who wrote this letter, adds a greeting of his own — the only place in the New Testament where the man holding the pen speaks in his own voice.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Revealed: Gospel and Old Testament Unity

Romans 16:25–27 returns to the theme announced in 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets; the Old Testament is the gospel in anticipation; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. The "mystery" kept secret for long ages is not something the Old Testament was ignorant of but something it was pregnant with — the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant people, the extension of the Abrahamic blessing to all nations, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin's canon of interpretation applies: the two testaments are one Bible, one gospel, one covenant of grace, administered differently but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning of vv. 17–20 against divisive teachers was written into the most doctrinally comprehensive letter Paul ever wrote. The letter's very depth makes it susceptible to misuse: its teachings on election, freedom, and grace can all be distorted into weapons of division. Paul's warning is therefore structurally appropriate — the deeper the theology, the greater the need for vigilance against those who weaponise it. Now: Every generation produces its version of the smooth-talking divisive teacher who uses theological language to advance personal agendas and create factions. Paul's three-fold response is the standing instruction: watch them carefully; avoid them; trust the God of peace who will soon crush Satan under your feet (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.

I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions. Key words. A sudden warning. “Watch out” (skopeō, keep an eye on, mark). Divisions (dichostasiai, standing apart): splitting the church.

And create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught. Key words. “Obstacles” (skandala, traps). Contrary to the doctrine: the teaching of the apostles, which Paul has set out in this letter. The problem is not differences over food (chapter 14), but false teaching that undermines the gospel.

Avoid them. Key words. “Avoid” (ekklinō, turn away from). Do not give them a platform or follow them (2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14; Titus 3:10).

For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. Key words. Literally, their own belly. They serve their own desires: money, pleasure, influence (Philippians 3:19).

And by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. Key words. “Smooth talk” (chrēstologia, fine words) and “flattery” (eulogia, nice speech). False teachers are often charming. “Naive” (akakoi, innocent, unsuspecting).

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding every Christian you disagree with. Paul distinguishes between disputable matters (chapter 14) and teaching contrary to the gospel. The first calls for patience; the second for watchfulness.

In a sentence. Paul urges you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who cause divisions and put obstacles in your way that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Keep away from them. For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the minds of naive people.

On a Tuesday. Test teachers, books, podcasts and preachers by Scripture, not by how pleasant they sound.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you. Key words. Their faith was famous (1:8). Paul is not accusing them but protecting them.

But I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. Key words. Wise in good: knowing and doing it well. Innocent (akeraios, unmixed, pure) in evil: inexperienced, simple about it. Jesus said to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16; 1 Corinthians 14:20). You do not need to taste evil to understand it.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. Key words. The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden: the offspring of the woman would crush its head (Genesis 3:15). Christ has already won the decisive victory at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Now God will crush Satan under the feet of his people, as they share in Christ’s victory, finally at his return. The false teachers are Satan’s agents (2 Corinthians 11:13–15); their defeat is certain. “Soon” (en tachei, quickly, without delay). Soon does not set a date. Some of it came quickly: the false teachers at Rome would be exposed and the church preserved, a foretaste of Satan’s defeat. The final crushing comes at Christ’s return, which is always near, the next great event in God’s plan (see the note on 13:11–12). The point is certainty: the outcome is fixed, and the wait will seem short in the light of eternity (8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Key words. A benediction: the letter began with grace (1:7) and returns to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers defeat Satan by their own strength. The God of peace crushes him. We stand in Christ’s victory.

In a sentence. Everyone has heard about your obedience, so Paul rejoices because of you; but he wants you to be wise about what is good, and innocent about what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.

For worship. Satan is a defeated enemy. Praise the God of peace who will soon crush him under your feet.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.

Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you. Key words. Paul’s closest companion and spiritual son (Acts 16:1–3; Philippians 2:19–22).

So do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. Key words. Fellow Jews. Lucius may be Lucius of Cyrene (Acts 13:1). Jason may be the man who hosted Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5–9). Sosipater may be Sopater of Berea (Acts 20:4), who travelled with Paul to Jerusalem with the collection.

I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord. Key words. Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down. Here he adds his own greeting. Paul often signed the letter in his own hand at the end (Galatians 6:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). Using a scribe does not lessen the letter’s authority: the words are Paul’s, inspired by the Spirit (2 Peter 3:15–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Tertius composed the letter. He wrote down what Paul said.

In a sentence. Timothy, Paul’s co-worker, sends his greetings to you, as do Lucius, Jason and Sosipater, his fellow Jews. I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.

For worship. Thank God for faithful servants behind the scenes, like Tertius, who helped give us the book of Romans.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.

Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Key words. Probably the Gaius whom Paul baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). He hosted Paul while he wrote Romans, and his house was big enough for the whole church in Corinth to meet.

Erastus, the city treasurer. Key words. “City treasurer” (oikonomos tēs poleōs, steward of the city): a public official. An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a public square at his own expense in return for his office as aedile, a city official. He may be the same man. The gospel reached people of high position as well as slaves.

And our brother Quartus, greet you. Key words. Quartus means fourth: perhaps a slave name. Paul places a city official and a man known only as our brother side by side. In Christ, both are equally brothers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid public office. Erastus served his city as a believer.

In a sentence. Gaius, whose hospitality Paul and the whole church here enjoy, sends you his greetings. Erastus, who is the city’s director of public works, and our brother Quartus send you their greetings.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your position, whether city official or ordinary worker, you can serve Christ in it and use it for his church.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24, with this benediction. The earliest and best manuscripts do not have it, so the ESV leaves it out of the text, and it is shown here from the margin. Nothing is lost: the same benediction already appears in verse 20.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Key words. Grace (charis): the free favour of God in Christ, the theme of the whole letter. With you all: strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, slave and free.

What it does not mean. It does not mean manuscript differences undermine Scripture. The differences are few and none affects any doctrine. God has preserved his word.

In a sentence. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

For worship. Receive this benediction for yourself today: the grace of the Lord Jesus is with you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—

The doxology. The letter ends with a long sentence of praise (vv. 25–27), which gathers up the great themes of Romans: the gospel, Jesus Christ, the Scriptures, the nations, the obedience of faith and the glory of God. It mirrors the opening of the letter (1:1–5).

Textual note. In a few manuscripts this doxology appears after 14:23 or after 15:33 instead of here, and in a few it appears twice or not at all (see the note on 14:23). The best and widest evidence puts it here, at the end of the letter, and its words fit Romans closely, echoing 1:1–5. Nothing in the text of Romans is in doubt because of this; the question is only where the closing praise stood.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you. Key words. “Strengthen” (stērizō, establish, make firm, as in 1:11). God is able to keep them standing (14:4).

According to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. Key words. My gospel: the gospel entrusted to Paul (2:16), not a different one. The preaching of Jesus Christ: the proclamation about him. God strengthens his people through the gospel.

According to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages. Key words. A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (11:25; Ephesians 3:4–6; Colossians 1:26–27). The mystery is the gospel of Christ, especially that Jews and Gentiles together would be saved through faith in him. Kept secret (sigaō, kept silent) for long ages.

But has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations. Key words. Revealed in the coming of Christ, and explained by the prophetic writings, the Old Testament (1:2; 3:21). The prophets spoke of it, but its full meaning was hidden until Christ came.

According to the command of the eternal God. Key words. The eternal God commanded that the gospel be preached to the nations (Matthew 28:19).

To bring about the obedience of faith. Key words. The same phrase as 1:5, framing the whole letter. The obedience that comes from faith, and the obedience that faith is. The gospel aims at a people who trust and obey.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament was silent about the gospel. It means the gospel was there in promise, but could not be fully understood until Christ fulfilled it.

In a sentence. Now to him who is able to establish you in accordance with Paul’s gospel, the message he proclaims about Jesus Christ, in keeping with the revelation of the mystery hidden for long ages past, but now revealed and made known through the prophetic writings by the command of the eternal God, so that all the Gentiles might come to the obedience that comes from faith,

On a Tuesday. When you feel unsteady, go back to the gospel. That is how God strengthens you.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.

To the only wise God. Key words. Only God is truly wise. His wisdom is seen in the plan of salvation, which no one could have imagined (11:33; 1 Corinthians 1:24–25).

Be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Key words. Glory to God, through Jesus Christ: Christ is the one through whom God is glorified, and through whom our praise reaches God. The letter that began with the gospel of God concerning his Son (1:1–3) ends with glory to God through his Son.

Amen. Key words. So be it. Truly. The only fitting response to Romans.

What it does not mean. It does not mean glory is given to God apart from Christ. All true worship goes through him.

In a sentence. to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

For worship. Having read Romans, end where Paul ends: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ. Amen.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae,<sup>2</sup>that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.<sup>3</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,<sup>4</sup>who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.<sup>5</sup>Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.<sup>6</sup>Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.<sup>7</sup>Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.<sup>8</sup>Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.<sup>10</sup>Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus.<sup>11</sup>Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.<sup>12</sup>Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.<sup>14</sup>Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.<sup>15</sup>Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.<sup>16</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.<sup>17</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them.<sup>18</sup>For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.<sup>19</sup>For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.<sup>20</sup>The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.<sup>21</sup>Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.<sup>22</sup>I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.<sup>25</sup>Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages<sup>26</sup>but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—<sup>27</sup>to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
